Sports.title: Cristiano Ronaldo sends classy message to heartbroken Lionel Messi as he says 'I don't know how to go on' and hints he will QUIT football after his 'father, friend and businessman' dad's death
Sports.content:
Cristiano Ronaldo sends classy message to heartbroken Lionel Messi as he says 'I don't know how to go on' and hints he will QUIT football after his 'father, friend and businessman' dad's death

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Lionel Messi has hinted he will retire from football following the devastating death of his father Jorge.

Jorge, an integral figure in the career of his legendary son, died on Friday, August 7 following a battle with illness that overshadowed the Argentina captain's mesmerising World Cup campaign in the United States, in which he led his team to the final.

Messi, who broke down in tears following Argentina's group stage win over Algeria while Jorge's health was deteriorating, has shared a heartbreaking letter to his father on Instagram – in which he casts doubt over his playing future.

'Dad, I still can't believe you're gone. It hasn't sunk in yet, or rather, I don't want to accept it. It's very difficult for me to imagine never seeing you again, never talking to you again. I know you were suffering and that this is for the best, but you left too soon. We still had so much to enjoy together.

'I don't know what I'll do without you, I don't know how to go on. I only played football and now I have serious doubts that I'll continue doing that for much longer. You were by my side from the beginning, it was so close to the end. Why couldn't you hold on that little bit longer and we could have finished together?'

Messi revealed that his father was the driving force behind his decision to play at this summer's World Cup, but his ageing legs prevented him from bringing the trophy home – with Spain winning 1-0 in the New York final.

Lionel Messi has thanked fans for their support following the death of his father Jorge (left)

Messi's father and agent died in Rosario, Argentina on Friday August 7

Jorge's death saw an outpouring of emotional tributes from the football world, including from Messi's first team Newell's Old Boys, as well as Barcelona and Argentina.

'You kept asking me to play in the last World Cup, and just a few days before it started, you got worse. It was the first time you wouldn't be in a tournament, but Mom kept telling me you'd get better and be well enough to travel. I told you we were going to reach the final so you could travel.

'Every time a game ended, I waited and missed your message. That's when I realized the situation was really serious. Even so, I couldn't stop thinking about going as far as possible, to give you time and for you to see a game. We reached the final and you couldn't be there. I wanted to win it to bring it to you and show you a new one. I couldn't, my legs couldn't take it anymore. This time I tried to go against my physical limitations, but I couldn't. I never managed to feel well.

'When I arrived, you thought we'd lost the final on penalties. We couldn't talk about anything that happened. You couldn't enjoy any of it. We didn't win the championship, but you don't know how much we enjoyed every game. Once again, you were right: I had to be there and play.

'I'm telling you this because it was the only thing we couldn't talk about, because you already know everything else. We used to talk every day and see each other whenever possible, given my commitments.'

Messi missed Inter Miami's defeat by Monterrey on Sunday to return home in the wake of his father's passing, and thanked fans for their well wishes.

He added on his Instagram stories: 'I want to sincerely thank everyone for all the love, respect and enormous consideration you have shown me and my family during this incredibly painful time following the loss of my dad.

'Thank you for being there for us, for every message, every gesture and, above all, for respecting our grief and our privacy.'

Lionel Messi's father Jorge, pictured at the 2022 World Cup final, died at the age of 68

MESSI STATEMENT IN FULL 'Dad, I still can't believe you're gone. It hasn't sunk in yet, or rather, I don't want to accept it. It's very difficult for me to imagine never seeing you again, never talking to you again. I know you were suffering and that this is for the best, but you left too soon. We still had so much to enjoy together.' You kept asking me to play in the last World Cup, and just a few days before it started, you got worse. It was the first time you wouldn't be in a tournament, but Mom kept telling me you'd get better and be well enough to travel. I told you we were going to reach the final so you could travel. Every time a game ended, I waited and missed your message. That's when I realized the situation was really serious. Even so, I couldn't stop thinking about going as far as possible, to give you time and for you to see a game. We reached the final and you couldn't be there. I wanted to win it to bring it to you and show you a new one. I couldn't, my legs couldn't take it anymore. This time I tried to go against my physical limitations, but I couldn't. I never managed to feel well. When I arrived, you thought we'd lost the final on penalties. We couldn't talk about anything that happened. You couldn't enjoy any of it. We didn't win the championship, but you don't know how much we enjoyed every game. Once again, you were right: I had to be there and play. I'm telling you this because it was the only thing we couldn't talk about, because you already know everything else. We used to talk every day and see each other whenever possible, given my commitments. I don't know what I'll do without you, I don't know how to go on. I only played football and now I have serious doubts that I'll continue doing that for much longer. You were by my side from the beginning, it was so close to the end. Why couldn't you hold on that little bit longer and we could have finished together? I know that his happiness was seeing his family well, his wife, his children and, above all, without others knowing, seeing me play. It's always been like this since I was little. You'd take me to all the practices as soon as you got home from work. Many times, Mom would take me because you were working. Obviously, you never missed a game. How you suffered watching me, and how you enjoyed it, even though you never gave me many compliments. You were a father, a friend, and a businessman. You were always the person you needed to be in every situation and you never made a mistake. Aside from a few demands or arguments, you were always right. In the end, things always turned out exactly as you said. I will miss you very much, but you will always be present, especially in the upbringing of my children, because I teach and educate them as you did with me. Rest in peace and watch over us from up there as you did here. Thank you for everything. I love you, Dad.

Messi also posted a picture with his father, captioned: 'I love you, pa' in Spanish.

Football legend Messi was extremely close to his father, who also operated as his agent and de facto business manager throughout his career, overseeing his son's multi-million dollar empire off the pitch.

In recent months, though, the patriarch of the family had been dealing with an as-yet-unconfirmed medical issue that had seen him taken to hospital in his home country.

His illness first came to light when Lionel, 39, cried on the pitch at the World Cup in a rare public display of emotion.

After scoring a hat-trick against Algeria in Argentina's opening group game in Kansas City, Messi was questioned by journalists and said: 'No, honestly it's something completely unrelated to sports. It's been a few difficult days, complicated.'

Just hours later, journalist Eduardo Feinmann explained the reason for the tears in an interview on Radio Mitre, one of the country's most listened-to stations.

'This has to do with his father. His father is not in good health,' he said. 'For quite some time now, several months, since last year.

'And this week there were some situations that slightly worsened his health, and Messi is going through this internal struggle. In other words, like any human being.'

It has since been reported that Jorge suffered a 'medical episode' at his home in January of this year, and he was hospitalised as a result.

In the aftermath, he was said to have undergone cardiovascular and neurological tests, but no official diagnosis was shared by the family, who sought to keep Jorge's health out of the media.

Jorge's health became headline news again in June, when a broadcaster in Argentina falsely claimed he had died – before later issuing an emotional apology and stepping down from her job.

Lionel is the third of four children of Jorge and his wife Celia Cuccittini, and the pair remained together until his death.

They married in 1978 and split their time between Rosario and Miami, where their footballing superstar son currently plays for David Beckham's Inter Miami in Major League Soccer (MLS).

Before becoming Lionel's agent, Jorge worked for a steel manufacturer in Villa Constitucion, meeting his wife as a young man in Rosario – where the family then grew up.

Messi stands in front of his family (including father Jorge (third left) in Rosario in October 2003

Jorge arrives at son Lionel's wedding in 2017 with his wife Celia (L) and daughter Maria (R)

Messi has two older brothers, Rodrigo and Matias, and a younger sister, Maria Sol.

Jorge has been at Messi's side throughout his historic career, which began in Argentina with Newell's Old Boys, before he moved to Spain to join Barcelona's famed La Masia academy in 2000.

He became the greatest of all-time in an incredible 21 years in Barcelona, before stunning the world with a move to Paris Saint-Germain – orchestrated by Jorge – in 2021.

After two seasons in the French capital, he moved to MLS and Inter Miami, where he remains to this day at the age of 39.

While Lionel's career has been magical on the pitch, it has not been without controversy off it, with Jorge famously by his son's side throughout his tax fraud case in 2016.

The pair sat together in front of the court, with Jorge in his role as his son's business manager, with the prosecution alleging that Messi failed to properly pay tax on income from his image rights between 2007 and 2009.

Ultimately, both father and son were convicted of three tax offenses, initially each receiving suspended 21-month prison sentences.

Jorge's sentence was subsequently reduced to 15 months upon review in 2017 by Spain's Supreme Court, with the pair also hit with substantial fines.

Sports.title: Police launch new crackdown on 'dodgy Fire Sticks' - with 11 areas targeted for house raids - on the eve of new Premier League season
Sports.content:
Police launch new crackdown on 'dodgy Fire Sticks' - with 11 areas targeted for house raids - on the eve of new Premier League season

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Police have launched a fresh clampdown on 'dodgy Fire Sticks' ahead of the new Premier League season.

Law enforcement organisations across the UK are taking a tougher stance on these devices - and how they are used and distributed - with multiple people having been convicted and jailed in recent years for selling and supplying them.

This included the arrests of four men in Merseyside last month following a special two-day operation by police.

That followed six search warrants in the nearby area, with the four individuals detained on suspicion of supplying unauthorised access to TV, films and live sporting events.

The Federation Against Copyright Theft (FACT) plays a key role in the crackdown and investigations manager Nick Sumner highlighted the importance of their actions.

'These arrests demonstrate the value of FACT’s intelligence-led investigations and our close partnership with Merseyside Police,' he said.

Police have launched a fresh clampdown on 'dodgy Fire Sticks' ahead of the new season

'This sends a clear message that those involved in supplying illegal streaming services can be identified and held to account.'

FACT, the UK's leading anti-piracy body, had been sharing intelligence with Merseyside Police during the operation.

Detective Constable Andrew Gibson of the Cyber Dependent Crime Unit, added: 'This coordinated operation follows detailed investigative work with FACT and has enabled us to take action against six individuals suspected of supplying illegal streaming services on a significant scale.

'Those selling illegal subscriptions should not assume that operating online will protect them from detection.

'We will continue to follow the evidence and pursue those believed to be profiting from this activity.'

Reports have also added that 11 areas were targeted for house raids in relation to 'dodgy Fire Sticks' this summer, including seven places in Ireland, Wrexham, Prenton, Merseyside and Birkenhead.

A FACT spokesperson added: 'Illegal streaming services are often sold through websites, social media, messaging apps and modified streaming devices.

'Customers are typically offered unauthorised access to subscription television channels and pay-per-view content for a reduced fee.

'Alongside the damage caused to broadcasters and content creators, illegal streaming services can expose consumers to scams, malicious software and the theft of personal or financial information.

'FACT continues to work with police forces and rights holders across the UK to identify, disrupt and deter those involved in illegal streaming through intelligence-led investigations, enforcement operations, cease-and-desist notices and criminal prosecutions.'

Sports.title: What's really going on with Myles Lewis-Skelly: Why Arsenal may be forced to sell 19-year-old England star - and why £45m would be nowhere near enough
Sports.content:
Myles Lewis-Skelly's Arsenal future depends on key factors including compliance with UEFA spending rules and the ability to further strengthen the Premier League champions' squad, Daily Mail Sport understands.

Gunners fans were left stunned yesterday when it was reported that the club had invited offers for the 19-year-old academy product from Chelsea and Manchester United.

Arsenal have insisted that was not the case, however, an intermediary is believed to have told both clubs that the player would be available at the right price.

Sources have also disclosed that one of the main drivers behind the situation is UEFA’s rules on spending, which operate by the calendar year rather than season by season. That means that the summer window is the last opportunity to bring transfer revenue in, should it be needed. It is also the last chance to ship players out should you need to do so to facilitate more new arrivals.

A potential fee of £45million has been touted for Lewis-Skelly, who started in the Champions League final, however those with knowledge of the situation believe that the price would need to be considerably higher to convince Arsenal to sell.

Because Lewis-Skelly is a product of the club’s academy, any money received would be seen as ‘pure profit’ and come as a significant boost to the balance sheet. That element of the rules has seen other clubs reluctantly sell some of their prized, homegrown assets, to ensure compliance, such as Newcastle’s offloading of Elliot Anderson to Nottingham Forest in July 2024 (although that was to comply with Premier League rather than UEFA rules).

Arsenal fans were left stunned yesterday when it was reported that the club had invited offers for Myles Lewis-Skelly from Chelsea and Manchester United

United are in the market for a left back and are monitoring the situation

Arsenal have options. There are a number of players who are viewed as unlikely to play this season and, in a perfect world, they would depart ahead of Lewis-Skelly, who is liked by both Mikel Arteta and the club’s fans. It would not be a surprise to see Reiss Nelson and Gabriel Jesus, for example, leave the club this month.

However, the closer Arsenal get to deadline day on September 1 without others leaving, the more the likelihood of Lewis-Skelly departing increases.

As for interested parties, United are in the market for a left back and are monitoring the situation. Chelsea have completed a £16million deal for Spanish left back Pep Chavarria from Rayo Vallecano but Lewis-Skelly may well be an intriguing prospect.

Earlier this month, Arsenal signed Bruno Guimaraes from Newcastle for a fee of around £75million. In June, they also took the option to turn Piero Hincapie’s loan move from Bayer Leverkusen into a permanent transfer at a cost of £34.5million. They also paid £34million for Club Bruges forward Christos Tzolis, while last summer they spent around £250million on eight new players.

A spike in commercial activity and prize money from the Premier League title and run to last season’s Champions League final will have helped their position, although player bonuses have taken a sizeable chunk out of the coffers.

With regards to outgoings, the Premier League winners have brought in around £41million from the departures of Leandro Trossard, Jakub Kiwior and Christian Norgaard.

Sports.title: New England captain Joe Root makes decision over team curfew - after Ben Stokes and Gus Atkinson Chelsea nightclub incident led to questions over the team's alleged drinking culture
Sports.content:
Joe Root has ripped up England’s curfew rules just a month after they were drawn up.

Root, 35, takes charge of the first match of his second spell as Test captain next week and has confirmed the after-hours guidelines put together by director of cricket Rob Key will not be enforced.

Instead, he is telling his players to behave like ‘grown adults’ ahead of the series against Pakistan beginning in Leeds next Wednesday.

‘There's not going to be a curfew. I don't think this needs to be a big deal, to be honest,’ Root told the Sky Sports Cricket Podcast.

‘My view on the curfew is that the players are doing their work, and if you want guys to take responsibility on the field, they've got to feel like they can be grown adults and make good, strong decisions off it.

‘That's for us as a team to manage well, and police well for me and Stephen Fleming.

'We should be known for how we play cricket and what we do on the field. We should be on the back page of papers.’

The stance taken by Root and incoming Test coach Fleming is a bold move, just weeks after the ECB hierarchy felt it necessary to spell out exactly what players could and couldn’t do - including a ban on drinking the day before, during and after international matches.

New England Test captain Joe Root has decided to ditch the team curfew

Former skipper Ben Stokes was dropped from the squad for the second Test against New Zealand earlier this summer after breaking the curfew following the first Test

Key went to the length of distributing this amongst all senior men’s cricketers following Daily Mail Sport’s story that Root’s predecessor Ben Stokes had no case to answer in the Cricket Regulator’s probe into being in a nightclub in Chelsea post-midnight following a Lord’s Test win over New Zealand because he did not believe a curfew was in place once a match had finished.

Following that, any member of full England squads were to inform management if they intended to be outside of the team hotel by 10pm.

However, Root insisted: ‘Be adults, look after yourselves, look after each other, create a good, strong culture where you know when the right time is to celebrate and enjoy a win or to have a sensible beer, but remember - you've got to play for England.

‘I don't want people to feel like they can't enjoy winning a Test match because they want to have a beer or at the right time let their hair down and then that's absolutely fine. We're human beings at the end of the day.

‘You know what your responsibilities are, you know how you need to prepare for a Test match and what it takes, and the effects that these things can have on you. So be smart, be sensible, and just be an adult.’

An ECB spokesman told Daily Mail Sport: ‘We have a Test captain and coach, who are looking at how they set team standards and culture.

As part of this, the curfew will no longer be in place.

‘We will ensure all players have a clear understanding of expectations when they come together for the upcoming Test series.’

Sports.title: Gladiators legend and ex-England star John Fashanu hits out at his 'soon-to-be ex-wife' in family feud as he apologises to his daughter and threatens 'legal action against the liar'
Sports.content:
Gladiators legend and ex-England star John Fashanu hits out at his 'soon-to-be ex-wife' in family feud as he apologises to his daughter and threatens 'legal action against the liar'

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Former England footballer and Gladiators legend John Fashanu has publicly apologised to his daughter and revealed he is divorcing his wife in a scathing statement.

In a lengthy Instagram post, Fashanu, who presented the TV show for six seasons in the 1990s when he became associated with the catchphrase 'Awooga', took a brutal swipe at his 'soon-to-be ex-wife' and regretted spreading misinformation about his daughter, Amal.

Fashanu said: 'I’m here to clarify a few things, very important things. The video I previously did was wrong.

'I was misinformed by my wife Vivian, who I’m sorry to say I am divorcing. Now that I am aware of the truth I apologise to my daughter Amal and legal action will be taken against the liar.'

Fashanu was speaking to camera in the post, which was captioned: 'I was the one who called my daughter, Amal, to become involved in my business because she is my first daughter, and she has always held a very special place in my heart.

'Sadly, I allowed myself to be misinformed and influenced. My soon-to-be ex-wife, Vivian, created unnecessary division between me and my daughter, and I deeply regret allowing that to happen.'

John Fashanu has apologised to his daughter Amal and revealed he is divorcing his wife

Speaking more about their feud, the former Wimbledon star continued: 'Amal, I want to publicly say I’m sorry for that previous video. It was made at a time when I was listening to someone else’s anger instead of following my own heart.

'The truth is, Amal and I have a wonderful relationship. She will always be my first daughter, and she will always have a place by my side, helping me with my affairs.

'I couldn’t be prouder of the intelligent, strong and compassionate woman she has become. What makes me even prouder is that she never chose to retaliate. As she always says, "Two wrongs don’t make a right".

'Those words have stayed with me, and they say everything about the kind of person she is.'

The 63-year-old, who has been married three times, also insisted that 'life is too short for division' and that 'family is everything', before he hinted that he and his daughter are trying to repair things.

His latest post comes after Fashanu had bizarrely denied claims Amal made about him earlier this summer.

Fashanu apologised to his daughter Amal (pictured together in 2012) for how he had acted

Former footballer Fashanu presented Gladiators in the early 1990s alongside Ulrika Jonsson

She had said that they had reconciled ahead of her wedding and hoped that he would attend, but added he had been 'laid low by a mystery condition'.

Fashanu, however, refuted these claims and instead insisted his daughter was trying to defame him.

During his football career, the 63-year-old played for several clubs but was most associated with Wimbledon where he scored more than 100 goals and won the 1988 FA Cup.

After retiring due to injury in his early 30s, he presented Gladiators alongside Ulrika Jonsson.

Sports.title: Why Crystal Palace cut their losses on Brennan Johnson - despite team-mates wanting him to stay: His eye-watering salary, the problem Oliver Glasner identified and Palace insiders' instant regret, revealed by BOBBY MANZI
Sports.content:
Brennan Johnson, the second-most expensive signing in Crystal Palace history, has been shipped off to Everton in an unusual swap deal with Dwight McNeil heading the other way.

Johnson joined Palace in early January for £35million, a club-record fee trumped only by Jorgen Strand Larsen a few weeks later. Around the same time they landed Strand Larsen, Palace agreed a £15million deal for McNeil, before pulling the plug at the 11th hour.

Yet, seven months later, McNeil is a Palace player and Johnson is an Everton player despite no money changing hands. How did we get here?

Well, McNeil had one year remaining on his contract at Everton, while Johnson had four years left to run at Palace. Both players had been valued in January, at £15million and £35million respectively.

Take the housing market. If someone has their house valued at £500,000, they don’t accept an offer for £100,000 seven months later - unless the market crashes.

The football transfer market is more inflated than ever, and Palace have essentially acknowledged they overspent on Johnson in January by proceeding with this deal.

Brennan Johnson won the Conference League at Crystal Palace, but did little to contribute - failing to score in 26 appearances after joining in January

Swapping him for a £15million asset accepts a £20million loss, certainly in cash-flow terms. There are some clever accounting mechanisms to limit the brutal hit on the books. But even so, it is cash Palace will never see again – just seven months after investing.

They have, however, offloaded a top earner, with Johnson’s Palace salary thought to be £125,000 a week. McNeil is understood to be on significantly less. That frees up some much-needed funds.

Where did it all go wrong?

When Johnson spoke ahead of last season’s Conference League final, there remained a sense that all was not lost for him in a Crystal Palace shirt.

Despite a dismal start to life at Selhurst Park, Johnson was introspective in a bumper 17-minute interview.

Five Palace players spoke that day, but Johnson stuck around significantly longer than his counterparts. He was optimistic and portrayed his move to Palace as the right decision, even after a disappointing, goalless four months.

Yet behind that mask was a man without any self-belief. Damaged by a difficult half-season under Thomas Frank at Tottenham Hotspur, Johnson had seen his minutes limited despite being Spurs’ key man the previous season – scoring 18 goals in a campaign that ended in Europa League glory.

At Spurs, Johnson went from top dog to a player largely frozen out. From the highest point of his career, scoring the winner in a European final, to the lowest, all in a matter of months.

Brennan Johnson scored the winning goal in the 2025 Europa League final, but Ange Postecoglou's exit as Spurs boss saw his minutes drop

A fresh opportunity in January was welcomed, with Palace keen to bolster their forward options for the culmination of their Conference League campaign. In the end, however, it was a mistake.

The first problem for the 25-year-old was his incompatibility with Palace’s style of play. Johnson is an out-and-out winger. He thrives when starting wide, making lung-busting runs from the touchline before eventually finding himself in space at the far post. It is his trademark move.

But at Palace, he was shoehorned into a narrow position, playing as a No 10 – a role he had no experience of – meaning he rarely had the opportunity to showcase what he does best.

Then Palace boss Oliver Glasner felt he was overburdening himself, and his performances were floundering as a result.

‘I feel sometimes he puts himself under too much pressure so that he doesn't play with this freedom that maybe he should have,’ Glasner said in March.

‘He just should enjoy playing football because he’s such a great player. He has all the skills. With freedom I think then he will be the best version of himself and have his best performances.’

But as the weeks went on, his confidence continued to plummet. Johnson missed a crucial penalty in Wales’ World Cup qualification play-off against Bosnia in March, and he never recovered.

Johnson never got going at Selhurst Park and played like a player with very little confidence

There was rarely any conviction behind his actions on the pitch. That is not to say he was not trying; rather, he did not back himself.

There was a consistent absence of end product from the Welshman, who occasionally ventured into promising positions but stopped short of delivering the final ball or applying the finishing touch.

His performances were insipid – averaging just 1.72 dribbles per 90 minutes, 3.08 touches in the opposition box per 90 and losing possession 13.12 times per 90.

There was very little Johnson did well in a Palace shirt, which is not necessarily an indictment of his ability.

He showed more in training than he ever did in a game. Daily Mail Sport understands several Palace players wanted Johnson to remain at the club because they believed in his talent – from glimpses on the training pitch – and just felt he needed reassuring.

But members of the hierarchy are thought to have been unconvinced early on and were worried that they had misspent £35million.

As his wait to end his goal drought dragged on, his head continued to drop. The outside noise also increased, with supporters becoming irritated by his lack of output. Palace travel to his new club Everton on the opening day of the Premier League season, and Johnson will hope to prove those doubters wrong immediately.

How did the swap deal come about?

By the summer, Palace accepted he was the wrong fit and decided to cut their losses, with Johnson equally keen to find a new challenge. That presented an opportunity to Everton, who were among the potential suitors in January.

Toffees boss David Moyes has long been an admirer of Johnson, tracking him since his days at Nottingham Forest – he even tried to sign him while West Ham boss.

The club were amazed by Palace’s generous terms and negotiated a straight swap for McNeil. But it has been suggested that both Palace and Johnson believed it was best for him to move on, paving the way for a rare swap deal. The pair also share the same agency, Unique Sports Group.

David Moyes has finally got his man, having chased Johnson while West Ham boss

Merseyside may prove a more suitable landing spot for Johnson, playing in a familiar system and role, back on the right wing. He will be encouraged to embark on those wide runs that were rarely seen in a Palace shirt.

Moyes, too, is a good manager for wounded animals. Last season he rejuvenated Jack Grealish after a tough spell at Manchester City. He did similarly for Jesse Lingard at West Ham. The Scot will back himself to unearth the attacker that showed so much promise at Nottingham Forest and in his first two seasons at Spurs.

For Everton, there is little risk, aside from his hefty wages. They have acquired a player with a track record of delivering goals and assists – Palace aside – but one in desperate need of nurturing and guidance. All they needed to do was sacrifice McNeil, who they had been prepared to sell for some time.

Sports.title: Why 'overloaded' Youri Tielemans believes he can be Man United's marathon man: £35m star speaks for first time on Michael Carrick, beating Lionel Messi's record and Bruno Fernandes link-up
Sports.content:
When Youri Tielemans made his professional debut for Anderlecht against Lokeren, Michael Carrick, now his boss, still had five years left to run on his own playing career at Manchester United. That goes some way to underline Tielemans' longevity at the top.

Tielemans was a phenomenon in Belgium when he made his pro debut in 2013 aged 16. Only Lamine Yamal made double figures Champions League appearances at a younger age than Tielemans, who had achieved that by the time he was 17. At 18, he’d played more than 100 professional matches.

Now, at 29, with 668 career appearances in the legs, Tielemans is facing the very real prospect of surpassing Lionel Messi (701), and possibly Cristiano Ronaldo (720), for the most games played before he turns 30.

A return to the Champions League means United face a minimum 48-game season. The more likely number is somewhere in the mid-50s.

And so by the time a trip to Bournemouth comes on the final weekend of the season, Tielemans could well have cruised past Messi’s record. Deep runs in the cups and Ronaldo may be sweating too.

With that in mind, meet Manchester United’s new marathon man.

Youri Tielemans' longevity at the top since making his debut has been remarkable

The midfielder, still only 29, has made 668 career appearances already

Tielemans cannot stop smiling as he sits down to chat inside United’s five-star team base for this week’s training camp in Ireland.

There is plenty on the agenda: his first phone call with Carrick, his ‘really natural’ link-up with Bruno Fernandes, and also an insight into the role he expects to play for United this season.

But first it’s the issue of minutes, of wear and tear, and whether he can be counted on for what, if all goes to plan, could be a 60-odd game campaign for United.

‘Yes, I am [confident],’ he says defiantly. ‘I feel very good, actually. I had a little issue during the World Cup, which is sorted now, and I feel back 100 per cent fit.

‘Obviously, pre-season is all about building up fitness for the season, but, yeah, I feel great. I feel like I am ready to go, and in 10 days’ time [against Hull] we will be there.’

Tielemans is refreshingly honest. Thirteen years as a professional will do that.

He doesn’t shy away from the fact that he missed 21 games for Aston Villa last season through ankle and calf problems. Nor does he gloss over the fact he clocked up 62 appearances during a gruelling 2024-25 season.

At the World Cup this summer, Tielemans reached a limit that his body could not fight against.

‘It was just that last game,’ he explains. ‘It was just an overload of too many games, too many minutes, and unfortunately my body could not cope with it anymore.’

Tielemans senses a shift in the room as he, plainly, recounted Belgium’s final act in the United States.

But he knows his game, he knows his body, and where others hold reservations, he has trust and belief that, after signing a five-year contract, he’s still got plenty left in the tank.

‘The thing is, at the World Cup, I think we played 120 minutes against Senegal, and from there we had less time in between games,’ he continues.

‘So we played the US I think three or four days later, and then three days later we played against Spain. In the warm-up, my body just switched off for some reason.

Tielemans is part of the United squad on their pre-season tour of Ireland this month

‘Now, I do not think I am a player that I absolutely need a rest. Obviously, there is a lot of games and the manager needs to manage the team, but when I am good, I am good, you know… it does not happen often.’

There is a steeliness in Tielemans eyes that is befitting of someone who plays for a club the size of Manchester United. A club that, had things shaken out differently, he could have turned out for as early as 2019 when he was first approached.

That was when he was leaving Monaco, only for Tielemans end up at Leicester.

United came back in for him again in the summer of 2022, only to end up signing Casemiro and Christian Eriksen in central midfield instead. Tielemans would have been forgiven for thinking the opportunity to head to Old Trafford may have passed him by.

So, now he’s here, replacing the void left by Casemiro, does he feel any sense of pressure at stepping into the Brazilian’s shoes?

‘Not really, because we are all different players,’ Tielemans adds. ‘He has different qualities, he had a different career path than I have. I just try to be myself, to bring my own qualities to the team, and to enjoy my time here. But it does not add any pressure at all for me.’

At £35million, a release clause which we now know had been hiding in plain sight to the rest of the league, he is a bargain that those inside Manchester United believe could prove to be the pound-for-pound the league’s most valuable signing of the summer.

He played a central role in helping Aston Villa - a club he says he ‘owes the world’ for restoring him to his best level - win the Europa League against Freiburg in Istanbul and has the Premier League proven tag that Ineos and United hold in such high regard.

Beyond just the numbers, United have been crying out for a rhythm-setter. A metronome who can help the team control matches. In his own words, it’s the ‘smelling football’ philosophy Carrick is hoping to have Tielemans bring.

‘He wants to have the ball, he wants to press in certain ways,’ Tielemans explains, revealing one of his early tactical conversations with Carrick.

‘It might be different than what you are used to, what I have been used to before, but it is logical things in my opinion. It is just smelling football, and that is what I have been doing from when I was young at Anderlecht. So for me, nothing changes.

‘But it just needs to gel together. When you follow those principles, then you can add your offensive qualities, especially in the last third where everything is a bit more about freedom, without obviously overcommitting and keeping the defensive line in place. Then I think we can do good things.’

Having played as a deep-lying defensive No 6, a box-to-box No 8 and more advanced as a No 10, what does Tielemans see as his best role to help take United back to the top?

The midfielder signed this summer from Aston Villa - a club he says he 'owes the world' to for helping to reignite his career

‘I just try and play forward as much as I can,’ he says, ‘either to Bruno [Fernandes] or the front line, to try and put them in positions that they can attack with freedom and that they can create and use their qualities.

‘I have played different roles in my career. So yeah, I am not just glued to one system or one role. I try and do a bit of everything.

‘Being that link between the defence and the attack, I think that suits me the best.’

He will be a key mentor in a young group, too, alongside the likes of Tyler Fletcher (19), Kobbie Mainoo (21) and fellow new signing Andrey Santos (22).

‘I just try to be myself, and it all comes in a natural way,’ Tielemans concludes.

‘I do not try to boss anyone around because no one likes that anyway. So I just try to be myself, be natural, and then obviously with good performances it helps others to follow.’

Leading by example at the very top level is all Tielemans has known for the past 13 years. It’s why Messi, Ronaldo, a place in the record books, and the game’s biggest prizes, are all in his sights now he’s finally here at Manchester United.

Sports.title: Brennan Johnson hits back at Jamie O'Hara and Gabby Agbonlahor after pair poked fun at swap deal with Dwight McNeil: 'We'll give you c**p, we'll give you c**p back!'
Sports.content:
Brennan Johnson hits back at Jamie O'Hara and Gabby Agbonlahor after pair poked fun at swap deal with Dwight McNeil: 'We'll give you c**p, we'll give you c**p back!'

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Brennan Johnson has clapped back at Jamie O'Hara and Gabriel Agbonlahor after the pair mocked his latest transfer.

Johnson has joined Everton in a swap deal from Crystal Palace with Dwight McNeil going the other way.

Johnson's time in south-east London was brief, having only moved to the club in January from London rivals Tottenham.

Following confirmation of the transfer on Tuesday, O'Hara and Agbonlahor discussed the details while speaking on talkSPORT.

'I like Dwight McNeil,' O'Hara said during the discussion. 'Brennan Johnson has been a myth for a few seasons. He didn't do it at Spurs. He hides in games.'

Agbonlahor then chimed in with: 'You look at their output last season, it's a bit like "you give us him and we'll give you him!"'

😅 "Give us crap, we'll give you crap back!"



🤷‍♂️ "I like Dwight McNeil but Brennan Johnson has been a myth!"



O'Hara and Agbonlahor react to #CPFC and #EFC swapping Dwight McNeil and Brennan Johnson! 🔁 pic.twitter.com/Avc4VcR7y1 — talkSPORT (@talkSPORT) August 11, 2026

Brennan Johnson has hit out at Jamie O'Hara and Gabby Agbonlahor for their remarks about his output after joining Everton in a swap deal with Dwight McNeil going to Crystal Palace

O'Hara (top) and Agbonlahor (bottom) mocked the output of Johnson and McNeil (right)

I have to say, I rate Brennan Johnson for pushing back against them with this reply. He didn’t do it in our colours admittedly but it’s good to see him standing up for himself. https://t.co/jTA8Lhyf4J pic.twitter.com/MvlmGor8t3 — HLTCO (@HLTCO) August 12, 2026

As the duo laughed, O'Hara then threw in another jab, commenting: 'We'll give you crap, we'll give you crap back!'

Johnson though, hit back at the pair on Instagram, writing under the post: 'Won more than both of these put together.'

And the Wales international is not lying, having won two major trophies so far compared to the one combined between his two critics.

O'Hara won the 2007-08 League Cup with Tottenham, while Agbonlahor won nothing during his career. However, Johnson scored the winning goal in the Europa League final in 2024-25 for Tottenham and won the Europa Conference League with Palace last season.

Following criticism of his comments, O'Hara took to X on Wednesday to defend himself, writing: 'This the prob [problem] when you only listen to a clip and not full story.

'We were talking about Brennan and McNeil stats from last season which were C**P not that they were bad players, I'm a fan of McNeill [sic] and also said Brennan has all the attributes but he would admit his season was crap.'

Agbonlahor was on talkSPORT again on Wednesday morning and apologised for any outburst, directing the blame from O'Hara.

'What did I do wrong? It was Jamie that said 'c**p for c**p,'' Agbonlahor said tongue-in-cheek.

this the prob when you only listen to a clip and not full story,we were talking about Brennan and McNeil stats from last season which were CRAP not that they were bad players, I’m a fan of McNeill and also said Brennan has all the attributes but he would admit his season was crap — Jamie Ohara (@Mrjamieohara1) August 12, 2026

🤷 "What did i do wrong?!"

❌ "I thought Jamie O'Hara was out of order."



Gabby Agbonlahor forced to apologise to Brennan Johnson after he responded to his comments on Instagram 🔥#talkSPORT #BrennanJohnson pic.twitter.com/4CD4qFlAyP — talkSPORT (@talkSPORT) August 12, 2026

'I want to apologise to Brennan Johnson. I could have not laughed, but when someone makes you laugh it's normal to start laughing.

'I thought Jamie O'Hara was out of order. I think Jamie needs to apologise. You can't say 'cr*p for cr*p'. I thought Jame was out of order looking back at that now.'

Sports.title: 'Brutal, searing and punishing heat' - Babb on playing for Ireland at USA '94
Sports.content:
While none of the home nations qualified for the 1994 World Cup, the Republic of Ireland did.

It was a second successive appearance at the tournament for the Boys in Green, who were again led by 1966 World Cup winner Jack Charlton.

At Italia '90, the weather had been hot - but at USA '94, it was a different kettle of fish altogether.

The iconic image of Charlton launching an open bottle of water in the direction of Andy Townsend and Tommy Coyne always provides a reminder of that.

Image: Jack Charlton led the Republic of Ireland at Italia '90 and USA '94

He clashed with FIFA over their policy that bottles could not be thrown to the players on the pitch, so took to throwing the contents instead before FIFA later relented and allowed water bags to be thrown.

"They trust me to do what is right for them and I will continue to do it," Charlton said. "We have been right in pursuing this matter and FIFA's change of heart proves that."

Charlton was rarely seen without his white baseball cap that summer. Steve Staunton famously even wore one during the national anthem before the second group game against Mexico.

One of the players in the Ireland squad that summer was Phil Babb. The defender, then 23, had just completed his second full Premier League season at Coventry.

He made his international debut in a 0-0 friendly draw with Russia in March 1994, then played in the next four friendlies leading up to the tournament.

Image: Phil Babb played in all four of the Republic of Ireland's games at the 1994 World Cup

Nothing was set in stone, but he knew he would at least have a decent chance of being included in Charlton's 22-man squad, so started to physically prepare himself.

"A coach at Coventry asked me if I wanted to do anything specific - we ended up doing 12-minute sessions in a sauna!" Babb recalls, with a smile.

"We were doing burpees, press-ups, just trying to acclimatise to that intense heat. We did about six sessions - but I wouldn't recommend it for anyone now!

"I was a fit lad and had played pretty much all the Premier League games Coventry had played that season. I adapted to the heat pretty well, but I know some of the older lads really struggled."

Babb started alongside Paul McGrath in the heart of defence for Ireland's tournament opener at Giants Stadium in New Jersey.

Image: Ray Houghton's stunning strike earned a shock 1-0 win over Italy

That Saturday, they shocked an Italy side that featured Paolo Maldini, Franco Baresi and Roberto Baggio. John Aldridge's stunner sealed a memorable 1-0 win.

It was an achievement made all the more impressive by the fact the Azzurri went on to finish as runners-up - but also given the fact it was played in temperatures exceeding 30C.

"When we walked out onto the field, about two hours before kick-off, you could tell it was going to be absolutely roasting," he recalls.

"You could tell that straight away and we didn't stay out long. I just checked the grass to see which studs I wanted, then I went straight back in. I know some of the lads were walking around and taking the atmosphere in, but I thought: 'This is too hot'.

"I didn't go out for a warm-up with the rest of the lads, either. I stayed in the changing room. It was built for NFL, so they had a 40m sprint track. I warmed up in there and waited until we went out. It was brutal, it was searing, it was punishing.

"It affected everyone's game. You were saturated after just 10 minutes walking onto a pitch, so you had to conserve energy at the right times.

"Recovery was very basic and there was very little ball work because of the demands of the actual games and the fluids you lose. When you're that dehydrated, it's quite difficult. You want a drink, but you don't feel hungry and that is a key part of the recuperation."

Image: Babb, whose Ireland were knocked out by Dennis Bergkamp's Netherlands, joined Liverpool later that summer

Thirty-two years on from that tournament, football has evolved exponentially.

Sports science has taken on a key role in the game and, this summer, is likely to play into the way teams approach games tactically due to the heat. A slower tempo is expected in many.

Charlton was not prepared to facilitate the same in 1994, though.

"We only played one way, so if you tried to go off-piste, Jack would certainly let you know!" adds Babb.

"We had one style of play, with a lone striker. If it wasn't Tommy Coyne, it might have been Niall Quinn up there and we'd be putting long balls up to him, with either willing runners out wide or the midfield bombing on.

"That was the Irish way back then. Tommy ran tirelessly, to the point where he actually collapsed with heat exhaustion on the plane home.

"I think Jack's sports science was a barrel of Guinness in his room and he'd call the lads in and have a pint! I'm sure there's a high calorific content in that, so maybe he was ahead of his time!"

In spite of that, Babb's memories of the tournament are largely positive.

"I enjoyed it, I have to admit! I'd rather play in the searing heat than a wet Tuesday night in Hull," he says.

"I was a fit lad and it was quite easy for me playing alongside Paul McGrath, who was imperious in that tournament. I learned a lot from him and how he conserved his energy.

"I felt I got stronger because I got used to it. I guess our 0-0 draw against Norway would probably attest to the heat and the style of play.

"It all comes down to the individual. Footballers are supreme athletes now and they leave nothing to chance, so I think they'll cope a lot better than we did in the mid-90s."

The methods may have moved on since Charlton was throwing water onto the pitch, but Babb's memories from USA '94 provide a reminder this World Cup will be a battle against more than just the opposition.

Sports.title: Ogbene earns Republic of Ireland draw with Canada
Sports.content:
Chiedozie Ogbene's equaliser ensured the Republic of Ireland continued their good run of results as they drew 1-1 with World Cup co-hosts Canada in Montreal.

Canada went ahead in the 24th minute from an own goal by defender Jake O'Brien, heading a failed clearance into his own net from Stephen Eustaquio's corner.

Ireland were then awarded a penalty in the second half after Cyle Larin - who signed a two-year deal with Southampton earlier in the day - took out Jamie McGrath.

Canada goalkeeper Maxime Crepeau saved Troy Parrott's initial attempt, but Ogbene was on hand to slam home the rebound and tie the game in the 60th minute.

Image: Ireland's Jake O'Brien heads the ball into his own net

Ireland, who failed to qualify for this summer's World Cup, went close to a winner but Crepeau denied a charging run from Mason Melia late on.

The Orlando City goalkeeper missed out on the 2022 World Cup in Qatar after breaking his leg while playing in the MLS Cup final.

Canada, managed by former Leeds boss Jesse Marsch, officially open the World Cup on June 12 in Toronto against Bosnia and Herzegovina, before facing Qatar on June 18 and Switzerland on June 24.

They remain without captain Alphonso Davies, who is still nursing a hamstring injury he sustained while playing for Bayern Munich.

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland edge past Qatar in friendly as both sides end with 10
Sports.content:
Captain Nathan Collins headed the Republic of Ireland to a 1-0 friendly victory over World Cup-bound Qatar as both sides were reduced to 10 men.

Collins ensured Ireland got the better of a side managed by his former Wolves boss Julen Lopetegui with an early header.

However, just how the evening might have panned out had Jack Moylan not been dismissed as half-time approached, a sparse crowd inside the Aviva Stadium will never know.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's side, whose hopes of making it to the World Cup finals were dashed in heartbreaking fashion in March when they lost their play-off semi-final to the Czech Republic on penalties, were in complete control until Moylan's premature exit.

Qatar substitute Almoez Ali suffered the same fate 12 minutes from time.

Image: Jack Moylan was sent off before half-time at the Aviva Stadium

The game was played out against the backdrop of ongoing unease at the forthcoming Nations League clashes with Israel, and play was interrupted on several occasions during the first half as 'Stop the Game' protesters among a crowd of 28,981 repeatedly hurled tennis balls on to the pitch.

Ireland will now head for Montreal and their friendly against World Cup co-hosts Canada on June 6, while Qatar continue their preparations for the finals - they launch their Group B campaign against Switzerland in San Francisco on June 13 - against El Salvador in Los Angeles on the same day.

The Republic took the lead with just five minutes gone when, having been fouled by Ayoub Al-Oui wide on the left, Moylan curled the resulting free-kick on to the head of Collins, who glanced the ball effortlessly past 'keeper Mahmoud Abunada.

Image: Qatar's Almoez Ali was also sent off

There was a brief interruption after the protesters made their presence felt for the first time as Qatar's Pedro Miguel underwent treatment for injury, but once order had been restored, Troy Parrott whipped a first-time shot wide after being picked out by Seamus Coleman.

The Qataris simply could not get anywhere near Hallgrimsson's men and a mid-half drinks break did little to improve matters for the visitors with Abunada having to field Jayson Molumby's deflected 24th-minute shot from distance.

Lopetegui could not hide his frustration on the sideline and only the bravery of defender Ahmed Fathi denied Chiedozie Ogbene a second goal as he attempted to latch on to Liam Scales' header back across goal.

But the home side's night took a turn for the worse on the stroke of half-time when Northern Irish referee Jamie Robinson deemed Moylan's challenge on Jassem Gaber worthy of a red card, much to the Lincoln frontman's clear astonishment.

Image: Former Wolves and West Ham boss Julen Lopetegui is now in charge of Qatar

With defender James Abankwah having replaced Dara O'Shea at half-time, the 10 men found themselves under pressure for the first time on their return, although Coleman very nearly caught Abunada off his line with an audacious 52nd-minute attempt from the right wing.

Edmilson Junior dragged a long-range effort wide two minutes later after Molumby went down in midfield under Fathi's challenge and it took a fine 71st-minute reaction save by Caoimhin Kelleher - his first of the night - to keep out Yusuf Abdurisag's deflected shot.

However, Qatari hopes of salvation were dashed with 12 minutes remaining when Ali struck out at Molumby off the ball on several occasions and was also sent off.

Sports.title: Parrott out of luck as Republic of Ireland draw with North Macedonia
Sports.content:
Troy Parrott had two goals disallowed as the Republic of Ireland played out a stalemate against North Macedonia on the night on which they had hoped to book a trip to the World Cup finals.

Five days after their dreams came to an end for another four years in Prague, Ireland drew 0-0 with the Macedonians in a friendly encounter neither side wanted as the Czech Republic and Denmark fought for the big prize.

Even a third successive home victory for the first time since the 2015-16 campaign would have provided scant consolation for Thursday night's disappointment but Heimir Hallgrimsson's men had to make do with a disappointing draw.

AZ Alkmaar striker Parrott came closest to breaking the deadlock as 37-year-old defender Seamus Coleman received a standing ovation from a crowd of 39,560 at the Aviva Stadium when he was replaced during the second half of what could yet prove to be his final appearance for his country.

Nevertheless, the squad will reconvene for a series of friendlies at the end of the season ahead of next season's Nations League campaign and later Euro 2028 qualification having restored a measure of pride and established a momentum they hope will serve them well when they return to competitive action.

The hosts went on to the offensive from the off, although they were unable to find the final ball to allow either Parrott or Chiedozie Ogbene to threaten.

John Egan could not direct an 11th-minute corner at goal and Ogbene saw his snapshot deflected over three minutes later, but goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher had to parry Enis Bardhi's 21st-minute free-kick after it flicked off the defensive wall, with Bardhi volleying high over after the resulting corner had been only half-cleared.

Macedonia keeper Stole Dimitrievski saved Parrott's 23rd-minute header comfortably after Dara O'Shea and Finn Azaz had sparked a concerted attack, and Azaz failed to make the most of a free-kick two minutes later after he had been tripped just outside the penalty area.

Parrott was played into a promising position by Knight nine minutes before the break, only to miss the target by some distance.

The in-form striker - he scored his sixth goal in three games in Prague - might have done better again two minutes later after Azaz's clipped pass had caused problems for the Macedonian defence but he snatched at his attempt and fired high and wide.

Parrott twice had the ball in the net as time ran down but an offside flag stalled his celebrations on each occasion.

Ireland were unfortunate not to take the lead with 52 minutes gone when Azaz accepted Seamus Coleman's pass and found Parrott, who turned smartly before shooting against the upright.

Azaz curled an effort just wide and Tihomir Kostadinov denied Parrott a clear run on goal as the hosts began to turn the screw but it was veteran Coleman's 61st-minute departure as

Hallgrimsson made changes which attracted the biggest cheer of the night to that point.

Wholesale changes did not help the flow of the game, which rather petered out as the whistle approached, although Ireland substitute Johnny Kenny passed up a glorious opportunity to win it at the end with a weak shot at the keeper.

Sports.title: Szmodics out of hospital and 'on the mend' after collision
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland forward Sammie Szmodics has been released from hospital in Prague after being knocked unconscious during Thursday's World Cup play-off defeat by the Czech Republic.

The 24-year-old, who is currently on loan at Derby from Ipswich, was hurt in a collision with defender Stepan Chaloupek just two minutes after his introduction as an extra-time substitute at the Fortuna Arena, sparking concerned medics to rush to his aid.

Szmodics was carried from the field on a stretcher and taken straight to hospital, where Ireland head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson later revealed he would spend the night under observation.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Danyal Khan looks back on the heartbreaking result for the Republic of Ireland who lost their World Cup qualifying play-off against Czech Republic on penalties

A Football Association of Ireland spokesperson said on Friday morning: "Sammie Szmodics was transferred to hospital yesterday having sustained a head injury during extra time of the play-off against Czechia.

"Following further tests and a period of observation, he has been safely discharged from hospital and will continue his recovery under the care of the Republic of Ireland and Derby County medical teams."

Szmodics, who Hallgrimsson confirmed would have taken a penalty in the shoot-out which Ireland ultimately lost 4-3, took to social media to express his thanks to those who had helped him.

He posted on X: "Gutted the way it ended. Fans and boys immense all evening!! Appreciate everyone's messages. And thank you to the medical staff who acted so quickly to help me. On the mend."

Collins: Ireland must build on World Cup near miss

Ireland captain Nathan Collins is confident his side have laid the foundations to qualify for future tournaments having seen hopes of reaching this summer's World Cup finals come to an end.

Collins and his team-mates were agonisingly close to the play-off final when they led the Czech Republic 2-1 in Prague on Thursday evening with just four minutes of normal time remaining.

Image: A dejected Nathan Collins and head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson

However, Czech skipper Ladislav Krejci's late equaliser took the tie to extra-time and ultimately to penalties, where the hosts prevailed 4-3 to extend Ireland's wait for a first return to the big stage since 2002.

Asked about their progression to the play-offs, which was secured by back-to-back wins over Armenia, Portugal and Hungary, Brentford defender Collins said: "I'm not seeing many positives right now because we're in the gutter.

"But what we've created, the environment created with the fans and country, has been special. That's something we need to keep growing, to get even better at.

"That can help us get better on the pitch. We can push that and get fans to more tournaments."

Ireland had hoped to return to the Aviva Stadium on Tuesday for a showdown with either Denmark or North Macedonia for a place in the finals, but the Czechs will now host the Danes, who were 4-0 winners in Copenhagen.

Instead, Heimir Hallgrimsson's side face a friendly against the Macedonians.

Collins said: "The motivation has to be the same. We've to win to keep improving as a team and country. Any game we play at home is a big game."

Sports.title: 'Pain' - Irish heartbreak as Czech Republic win on penalties
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland's World Cup hopes were cruelly and heartbreakingly dashed as Czech Republic came from 2-0 down - to then beat them on penalties.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's side, who went two goals up after 23 minutes in Prague, were four minutes plus stoppage-time away from victory - before Wolves defender Ladislav Krejci headed in a corner to force extra-time.

Ireland were also a handful of penalties away from going through, as penalty saving expert Caomhin Kelleher saved from Mojmír Chytil in the shoot-out to give them a momentary advantage.

But Finn Azaz and Alan Browne both missed their spot kicks, allowing Patrick Schick and then Jan Kliment to win it for the hosts.

As a result, Czech Republic will go on to face Denmark on Tuesday for a spot at the World Cup - as Ireland's wait for a first World Cup appearance since 2002 goes on.

After Wales and Northern Ireland's semi-final exits, it also means England and Scotland will be the only teams from Great Britain and Ireland at the World Cup this summer.

Image: Ireland's players walk off the pitch after defeat

World Cup play-off finals - Europe Bosnia & Herzegovina vs Italy

Sweden vs Poland

Kosovo vs Turkey

Czech Republic vs Denmark

How Ireland threw away their lead

Ireland came flying out the blocks flying in Prague. Four shots in the opening ten minutes, including Nathan Collins crashing a shot off the bar from range, set the tone for a brilliant display - and they got their rewards.

A long throw caused chaos and Nathan Collins was deemed to have been caught slightly late by Vladimir Darida by VAR, who sent referee Glenn Byberg to the monitor for a review.

Troy Parrott, who else, crashed in the penalty for his sixth goal in the last three Ireland matches. And it got better for Ireland four minutes later.

Ryan Manning's corner found Dara O'Shea at the back post and his header across was cleared off the line by Vladimir Coufal - but off goalkeeper Matej Kovar and over the line.

Image: Czech Republic goalkeeper Matej Kovar scores an own goal to give Ireland a 2-0 lead

Ireland were in dreamland but a moment of Manning madness brought the Czech Republic back into it. The defender's needless tug back on Krekci - when the ball was heading out of play - was penalised by referee Byberg, with Patrick Schick pulling one back from the spot.

Ireland did, however, manage to settle the nerves down - right throughout the second half. Despite sustained Czech pressure in the second half, they barely threatened.

It was Ireland who had the better chances after the break, with Jayson Molumby striking the post and Parrott denied by a solid Kovar save at a corner. But then heartbreak struck with four minutes of normal time remaining, as Krejci bundled the ball in at the near post from a set piece.

Krejci could have even won it with the last kick of the game but scuffed his finish, as extra-time came.

Substitute Tomas Soucek missed a glorious chance for the hosts, with Adam Idah was denied a one-on-one chance by a goal-saving challenge from Stepan Chaloupek. Penalties came and the lottery fell in the hosts' favour.

Image: Jan Kliment scored the winning goal in the penalty shoot-out

Hallgrimsson confident in Ireland future despite 'pain'

Republic of Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrimsson:

"One word is pain. I feel pain. I feel pride for the performance of the players. They gave it all. I feel gratitude for all the supporters who supported us through the whole game, even after the loss. I feel pride being a part of that group. Personally, I know all the players will feel pain now. Only pain.

"We take with us that we can play teams higher in the FIFA ranking and can punch above our weight: Portugal, Hungary and here. We can compete with these teams. We came here with three wins in a row, a long time since that happened for this national team.

"So there's growth in this squad. It's maturing. These are been the biggest game most of these players have played. That's encouraging to know we're growing. It's strange to say that after we lost today.

"I know I'm biased in this, all the statistics and metrics of the team have improved. Big games, being on the line, crunch times all the time, we've managed to go through this. It showed the resilience, character of these players, that's why I feel confident going on."

Sports.title: Wilson key for Wales, NI aim for big upset while history beckons for ROI
Sports.content:
Sky Sports assesses Thursday's 2026 World Cup play-off semi-finals as Wales host Bosnia-Herzegovina, Northern Ireland go to four-time winners Italy and the Republic of Ireland face Czech Republic in Prague.

Thursday 7.45pm: Wales vs Bosnia-Herzegovina (winner will play Italy or Northern Ireland)

Harry Wilson is not the new Gareth Bale, but he's doing the job of Bale at his best, especially for Wales.

Fans have long been excited about Wilson's natural talent, but are now seeing his influence in the Premier League on a weekly basis for Fulham. This season, he has 10 goals and six assists for club, while for country, his stats are even better with five goals and two assists in his last five games.

If Wilson starts running the show, his confidence will feed to the other players and to the home crowd, and Wales will be very difficult to stop on their own patch.

Which World Cup group would Wales be in? If Wales qualify for the World Cup they would be in Group B with Canada, Switzerland and Qatar.

Craig Bellamy wanted to create an identity for Wales when he took over as head coach. It's now clear: he wants front-foot football coupled with intensity and energy.

Bellamy doesn't always see that in international football as he finds it slower at times compared with club football, but his Wales side will not be ponderous. You could see during the qualification campaign that Wales' intensity in winning the ball back very quickly and holding possession grew. Now it's about consistently doing it.

Apart from consistency in play, there needs to be consistency in selection. Much is always made about the 'spine' of a good team, from the goalkeeper to the glory hunter! Leeds United provide a fair chunk of Wales' spine with 'keeper Karl Darlow on form and in receipt of the No.1 keeper's jersey. Joe Rodon is the rock at centre-back that success relies upon, while team-mate Ethan Ampadu's versatility means he can link anywhere between defence and midfield. Throw in one of the in-form Premier League stars, Harry Wilson, and a strong spine can take a team a long way.

Ask Bellamy if he has thought about preparing for the play-off final against either Italy or Northern Ireland and you'll get glared at. It's Bosnia, Bosnia and Bosnia. He won't entertain anything beyond Bosnia until the game is over. It's a danger, a banana skin he wants to avoid. Thinking too far ahead isn't good on this occasion.

Geraint Hughes

Thursday 7.45pm: Italy vs Northern Ireland (winner will play Wales or Bosnia-Herzegovina)

On paper, perhaps in reality, it's David vs Goliath.

Northern Ireland enjoy David vs Goliath. Once upon a time it was David (Healy) vs England and David (Healy) vs Spain.

For smaller nations there is comfort in being the underdog. A loss would be met without a major backlash, a win makes you a hero. That's how Michael O'Neill's side will approach Thursday's assignment in Bergamo against Italy.

Which World Cup group would Northern Ireland be in? If Northern Ireland qualified for the World Cup they would be in Group B with Canada, Switzerland and Qatar.

Conor Bradley and Daniel Ballard are out. Between them they represent 50 per cent of the Northern Ireland players currently plying their trade in the Premier League.

The pair's absence is as much a blow to Northern Ireland's attacking prospects as it is defensively. Ballard represents their best aerial threat from set-pieces, Bradley their most dynamic player on the ball.

And yet for some reason that only football can explain, hope remains. The four-time World Cup winners are heavy favourites but far from the Azzurri powerhouse of old.

If Northern Ireland have it their way, it's unlikely to be a pretty spectacle. But can they frustrate their hosts? 0-0 at half-time? Pounce on the sense of angst that will exist among the home support?

To call it a free hit would be to downplay the importance of the game. But Northern Ireland are free from the weight of expectation.

Daring to dream of a result that becomes instant folklore.

Michael Morrow

Thursday 7.45pm: Czech Republic vs Republic of Ireland (winner will play Denmark or North Macedonia)

Image: Republic of Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrimsson and captain Seamus Coleman spoke to the media in Prague

History beckons for the Republic of Ireland here in Prague.

Make no mistake, this will be the biggest game to date for a lot of these Irish players as they attempt to take another step to this summer's World Cup but they must get past Czech Republic to do so.

Which World Cup group would Republic of Ireland be in? If the Republic of Ireland qualified for the World Cup they would be in Group A with co-hosts Mexico, South Africa and South Korea.

Still coming off the euphoria of the incredible back-to-back wins against Portugal and Hungary last November, this is an Irish team full of confidence.

Having spoken to a few people around the Czech Republic team, those results have been noted and they are particularly worried about Irish striker Troy Parrott, who scored five goals in those two games in November - including the 96th-minute winner against Hungary.

Head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson spoke ahead of this game about one of the key aspects is visually and mentally being ready for the challenge ahead of them, he seemed as calm and confident as usual.

However his key selection dilemma is does he bring back the experienced, tried and tested players such as Seamus Coleman, Robbie Brady and Chiedoze Ogbene - all three have had limited game-time this season for a variety of injuries.

Coleman and Brady especially are the only two players in the squad who were part of Ireland's last team in a major tournament which was in 2016 - their experience could prove vital.

Image: Can Troy Parrott recreate his Irish heroics in Prague on Thursday?

Their opponents are in a state of flux.

Czech Republic have a new head coach who takes charge of his first game on Thursday, with West Ham's Tomas Soucek also being stripped of the captaincy after November's internationals having caused shockwaves in the local media - Wolves' Ladislav Krejci has replaced him.

The pressure feels like it's all on the home side which could play into Ireland's advantage as they look to take another step to qualify for this summer's World Cup - their first since 2002.

Danyal Khan
