Sports.title: Jake Paul’s MVP Signs IBF Champion Elif Turhan
Sports.content:
Turhan gives Jake Paul’s promotion another major piece at 135 pounds. Caroline Dubois holds the WBC and WBO championships, while Stephanie Han owns the WBA belt.

That leaves MVP working with fighters who control all four major lightweight titles.

Turhan punched her way into that company last December in Monte Carlo. She broke down Brazilian Olympic gold medalist Beatriz Ferreira and forced a fifth-round stoppage to seize the IBF crown, registering the defining victory of her professional career.

She has since strengthened her position with wins over Taylah Gentzen in January and Gabriella Tellez in June.

Turhan brings pressure and finishing instinct to a division loaded with potential championship fights. She likes to close the distance, force exchanges and punish opponents once her combinations begin finding the target.

The Istanbul fighter becomes the first Turkish boxer to join MVP and follows Nicolson as the second addition produced by the promotion’s agreement with Matchroom.

Turhan believes the partnership can push her toward more championship opportunities.

“I am incredibly excited to be part of this powerful collaboration. This marks a major signal of the exciting initiatives we will undertake for women’s boxing globally, and I am deeply honored to be involved in this journey with all my strength and energy.”

Her next opponent has yet to be confirmed, but her ambitions reach beyond defending the IBF belt.

“I am excited for the opportunities that will come my way as I look to win more major World Titles.”

That pursuit creates an obvious pressure point at lightweight. Dubois controls two belts, Han holds another and Turhan carries the IBF championship.

If MVP eventually matches its lightweight champions, Turhan will have to establish her pressure against fighters capable of controlling distance, countering her entries and punishing her on the way inside.

Sports.title: Teremoana vs. DeAndre Savage Live Results and Fight Updates
Sports.content:
Teremoana Teremoana improved to 12-0 with a second-round knockout of DeAndre Savage after another destructive heavyweight finish. Savage survived the opening round despite absorbing several heavy shots as Teremoana began finding his distance and opening up. That resistance ended quickly in the second. Teremoana cracked Savage with a big punch that buckled the American’s legs but left him standing. The Australian kept hunting the finish, dropped Savage moments later, and watched as he failed to beat the referee’s count. Savage became only the third opponent to take Teremoana beyond the opening round, but the extra three minutes merely delayed another knockout for the Australian heavyweight.

Michael Zerafa broke down Alejandro Ortiz for a stoppage victory on the Gold Coast after taking command in the later rounds. Zerafa began forcing Ortiz onto the back foot, then cracked him with a heavy shot in the seventh as the pressure increased. His corner demanded he keep letting his hands go while staying smart, telling him Ortiz was hurt whenever he opened up. Zerafa responded by pressing harder and keeping Ortiz under fire. The breakthrough came when Zerafa dropped Ortiz and immediately looked to close the show. Ortiz climbed off the canvas but remained hurt, and the fight was stopped soon afterward when he had taken enough. The victory gave Zerafa the result he needed after entering the fight under pressure and facing questions over his recent form.

Sports.title: Jack Dempsey’s Harry Wills Problem Never Went Away
Sports.content:
Following Jack Johnson’s 1910 victory over Jim Jeffries, racial violence erupted across the United States. The possibility of another Black heavyweight challenging a white champion encountered resistance from promoters, regulators, and others concerned about another interracial title fight.

Wills paid heavily for that environment.

A Dempsey-Wills fight nearly materialized in 1922 when promoter Tex Rickard selected a date and had tickets printed for a proposed bout in New Jersey. The promotion collapsed when the financing needed to meet Dempsey’s guarantee failed.

Another attempt ran into opposition in New York, where athletic commission chairman William Muldoon resisted an interracial heavyweight championship fight over concerns about racial unrest.

Dempsey also gave his critics ammunition. He drew the color line early in his championship reign before later changing his public position. His long stretches of inactivity intensified criticism that Wills was being denied an opportunity he had earned. Yet Wills himself resisted blaming Dempsey.

“My only regret in life is that I never got a shot at Dempsey, [and] I’m sure I could have beaten him,” Wills later said. “It wasn’t Jack’s fault. He wasn’t scared of anyone. He was a great fighter.”

Dempsey lost the heavyweight championship to Gene Tunney in 1926. Wills never fought for the world title.

The missing fight should count when Dempsey’s championship reign is evaluated. Wills was precisely the type of challenger a champion needed to defeat to remove questions about his dominance.

Placing the entire responsibility on Dempsey, however, ignores the racial barriers, regulators, promoters and failed financing that repeatedly interfered with the fight.

More than a century later, nobody knows what would have happened if Jack Dempsey and Harry Wills had finally met. That unanswered question is why Wills remains an unavoidable part of Dempsey’s legacy.

Sports.title: Teofimo Sr. Dismisses Shakur Stevenson’s Vacant-Belt Championships
Sports.content:
“This fight is about Teofimo Lopez trying to get the world title again, become a real three-division world champion. No vacant belts,” Lopez Sr. said to Fighthype. “Shakur got like two vacant belts, right? So, to me, he’s not a real three-division world champion. My son is going to do it the right way. We’re going to go straight to the champion. No vacant belt.”

Stevenson has actually won world titles across four divisions. His first came against Joet Gonzalez for the vacant WBO featherweight belt in 2019. He then stopped reigning WBO junior lightweight champion Jamel Herring in 2021 before defeating Edwin De Los Santos for the vacant WBC lightweight title in November 2023.

The fourth belt is difficult for Lopez Sr. to dismiss under his own standard. Shakur took the WBO light welterweight title from Teofimo in January, giving him two divisional championships won by defeating reigning titleholders.

Lopez Sr. also criticized Shakur’s fighting style and questioned how much further Stevenson can climb through the weight classes.

“I would love to fight him again. Let’s hope that we can get him before we move up too high,” Lopez Sr. said. “I don’t think Shakur can go up in the weight divisions. He’s too chinny. He doesn’t like to get hit. He’s a boring fighter.”

He believes Teofimo fought the wrong fight against Shakur. In his view, Teofimo should have boxed from the back foot instead of following the southpaw to his right all night.

Sports.title: Liam Paro Answers Devin Haney’s IBF Call
Sports.content:
“Have the WBO.. I want the IBF,” Devin said on X.

Haney seems to have signaled his preferred opponent without directly naming him. The choice makes sense. Paro brings a large following in Australia and the potential for a PPV event built around two welterweight champions.

That separates Paro from Jack Catterall, another opponent who has been discussed for Haney. Catterall presents a difficult fight with his movement, defense, timing and awkward southpaw style.

Paro is a southpaw as well, but he’s much more willing to engage and turn fights into physical exchanges. Haney has generally performed well against aggressive fighters who come forward, giving him opportunities to box from range, counter, and tie up when they get inside.

Catterall offers a different challenge. He’s unlikely to chase Haney recklessly or provide the type of pressure that allows Haney to settle into his preferred rhythm. Taking that fight would mean accepting considerable stylistic difficulty without getting another world title in return.

Paro gives Haney the opportunity to unify the division while bringing an established Australian audience to the promotion. From Haney’s perspective, that combination makes the matchup easier to understand commercially.

Nothing has been finalized, but the exchange leaves little mystery about their interest. Both champions have publicly opened the door to putting the IBF and WBO titles together.

Sports.title: Archie Moore Silences Yvon Durelle in Montreal Rematch
Sports.content:
The rematch drew 11,555 spectators, generating a gate of $140,519 to set a Montreal boxing record. Former world heavyweight champion Jack Sharkey served as referee.

Moore, already well into his 40s, had held the light heavyweight crown since defeating Joey Maxim in December 1952. Durelle, 29, remained a leading contender after his ferocious effort in their initial meeting.

Rather than trading immediately with the heavy-handed challenger, Moore fought cautiously through the opening two rounds. His defense limited Durelle’s opportunities to land the kind of power shots that had caused so much trouble in their first fight.

Two judges had Moore in front after two rounds, while the third had the fight even.

Moore changed the fight completely in the third. A hard right hand dropped Durelle, who beat the count at seven and tried to fight back. The champion quickly closed in.

Three more knockdowns followed as Moore connected with rights and lefts. After the fourth knockdown of the round, Sharkey counted Durelle out at 2:52.

Moore had turned a rivalry born from one of the greatest scares of his championship reign into a decisive three-round knockout.

Durelle faced difficult circumstances before the fight. A boating accident left him with a back injury, and his hometown of Baie-Sainte-Anne suffered the tragic Escuminac Disaster in June, when 35 fishermen lost their lives.

Moore continued his remarkable run near the top of the sport. Durelle later challenged George Chuvalo for the Canadian heavyweight title in November 1959, losing by knockout in the 12th round.

The two rivals eventually became friends. Moore retained enormous respect for Durelle, remembering him as one of the hardest punchers and toughest opponents he faced.

Their first fight became the classic. On August 12, 1959, Moore made the rematch his answer.

Sports.title: Teofimo: Turki Alalshikh Pushed Benn, Ryan Garcia Wanted Me
Sports.content:
“Conor and Ryan are fighting because it’s a Turki thing. Turki pushed that fight,” Teofimo said to Fighthype. “It wasn’t something that Ryan wanted. Ryan wanted to fight me, but, you know, it’s a business at the same time.”

Ryan has since named Lopez among the opponents he wants to face after Benn, along with Rolando Romero and Shakur Stevenson. That shows the interest is there, although it doesn’t establish how close Garcia and Lopez were to actually fighting.

Teofimo has his own fight to win first. He challenges WBA welterweight champion Romero on August 22 in Las Vegas, attempting to capture a title in a third weight division.

Wins by Garcia and Lopez would leave both operating at 147 pounds with a marketable fight available between them. Teofimo would also own the WBA belt, giving Garcia another reason to pursue the matchup.

Garcia has mentioned Romero as a possible opponent as well, meaning Rolly could put himself in position for a rematch if he defeats Lopez.

Lopez believes money and promotional relationships are increasingly determining which fights get made.

“Everybody’s right now more on the money side,” Lopez said. “Everybody’s associated with somebody. Takeover is on his own with his own.”

Teofimo is coming off his January loss to Shakur Stevenson and will be making his welterweight debut against Romero. Rolly already owns a decision victory over Garcia, giving Teofimo a chance to strengthen his case for a Garcia fight with an impressive performance on August 22.

Ghana News.title: Scars From Dubai: 28-year-old fights to rebuild his life after acid attack disfigured him
Ghana News.content:
For 28-year-old Alex Degle, the pain of an acid attack he suffered in Dubai did not end when his wounds healed. Nearly three years later, he lives with a disfigured face, severe scars on his body and the daily struggle to provide for his family.

Degle travelled to Dubai in search of work and a better life for his wife, children and mother. Instead, he returned to Ghana after months of hospital treatment and plastic surgery, carrying injuries that have changed both his appearance and his ability to earn a living.

He alleges that a fellow Ghanaian he identifies as Michael attacked him with acid on December 23, 2023, following a disagreement at the house where they lived.

According to Degle, the dispute began over a 20-dirham [$6.00] debt and later resurfaced during a card game. He says Michael first attempted to strike him before leaving the house.

Degle was preparing food in the kitchen when Michael allegedly returned carrying a bottle containing a clear liquid. He says the substance was poured over his face and body without warning.

The liquid was acid.

Degle recalls an immediate and overwhelming burning sensation before losing consciousness. He was rushed to the hospital with severe burns and says he regained consciousness in January 2024.

He remained in hospital for several months, undergoing treatment and plastic surgery. The attack left his face completely disfigured and severe scars all over his body.

JoyNews has not independently verified Degle’s account of the attack or the subsequent legal proceedings.

Search for justice in Dubai

Degle says Dubai police arrested Michael and referred the case to the public prosecutor.

He also sought assistance from the Ghanaian Consulate in Dubai, which he says arranged for a lawyer to assist him. According to Degle, however, the lawyer failed to attend one of the court proceedings and later informed the family that they would need about 24,000 dirhams [$6,535] to cover legal fees and other expenses.

With no job, little money and mounting living costs, Degle says he could no longer remain in Dubai. He eventually returned to Ghana with his mother without securing the justice he had pursued.

Back home, Degle says he submitted documents relating to the case, including information about the man he accuses of attacking him, to Ghanaian authorities. Despite several follow-ups, he says he has received no substantive update.

He believes Michael remains in Dubai.

Rejected because of his appearance

Returning home did not end Degle’s ordeal. His injuries have made it difficult for him to return to the life and work he knew before the attack.

He now rides a commercial motorbike, popularly known as Okada, to support his wife, two children and ageing mother.

But even that work is uncertain. Degle says some passengers refuse to board his motorbike when they see his face. Others who know how he sustained the injuries deliberately patronise him to support his family.

On a good day, he earns between GH¢150 and GH¢200. From that amount, he must provide food, pay school-related expenses and meet the other needs of his household.

“Everything is on me,” he says.

Degle’s children sometimes struggle to obtain school uniforms, books and other essentials. The family lives in an unfinished structure without a toilet and a bathroom, and rainwater enters their room whenever it rains heavily.

Still, each morning, Degle gets back on his motorbike and searches for passengers because his family depends on what he earns that day.

An empty shop and an uncertain future

Degle has also tried to create another source of income for the family.

Using the little money he had after returning from Dubai, he constructed a container shop for his wife. The shop, however, remains empty because he cannot afford to stock it.

He does not want to spend the rest of his life relying on public assistance. His immediate wish is to secure a stable driving job.

Degle says driving is his profession and that he holds a licence permitting him to operate different types of vehicles. He also wants support to stock his wife’s shop so she can earn an income and share the financial burden.

But beyond rebuilding his livelihood, Degle wants the case against the man he accuses of attacking him to be pursued.

Nearly three years after leaving Ghana in search of a better future, he is back home fighting to reclaim his livelihood and obtain justice.

His appeal is simple: help him work again - and ensure the man he accuses of changing his life faces the law.

Ghana News.title: Climate action must put people’s pockets first – Expert says
Ghana News.content:
Country Programme Coordinator of the Climate and Development Knowledge Network (CDKN), Valerie Kplorm Nutakor, has urged stakeholders to move beyond climate change education and policy discussions and focus on practical actions that people can incorporate into their everyday lives.

She said climate action would remain limited if citizens were repeatedly told about the dangers of climate change without being given practical reasons and opportunities to change their behaviour.

Speaking at the WaterAid and JoyNews National Dialogue, Ms Nutakor said people were more likely to adopt sustainable practices when those practices were connected to their immediate realities.

“People say we've done a lot of climate education. We're talking too much, and when will it stop. But we're actually not talking too much; when people do not know, they can't do anything,” she said on Wednesday, August 12.

She said her own experience of growing up around people who practised simple forms of waste management demonstrated how everyday behaviour could contribute to sustainability even without people having a detailed understanding of climate science.

“The only reason I believe that I'm even in this space is because my parents are very interested in keeping things sustainable,” she said.

Ms Nutakor recalled that people in her community would keep plastic sachet materials because they could later be collected and sold.

“I grew up seeing it. I didn't know all about ozone layer cover and all of that, but that's where the greenhouse conversation comes in. I didn't care about it,” she said.

“All I knew is that, if I fold my rubber well, I can put this in the receptacle. The woman who comes around to come and pick it doesn't even want to stick their long pole into it anymore.”

“They just buy it, and then the school gets to get some money. We use it for our school garden. And then we are happy. I didn't know that it was sustainable, but I just knew that it was right.”

She said the experience illustrated the importance of creating systems in which environmentally responsible behaviour also delivers a direct benefit to individuals and communities.

Ms Nutakor argued that climate action should therefore be approached as a development issue rather than as an isolated environmental campaign.

“We have over the years made climate change a one-off conversation instead of looking at it in policy,” she said.

“Climate change is a sustainable development conversation. It should not be done out of this sustainable development conversation. Once you take it out of there, you have problems.”

She explained that the effects of climate change could increase the cost of development by reducing the lifespan of infrastructure and other investments.

“Climate change comes in because of what we call incremental costs,” she said.

She explained that a facility designed to operate for 30 years under normal conditions could face a shorter lifespan because of adverse climate impacts, creating additional costs that would have to be addressed.

“Now because the facility will now last only 15 years, the extra 15 years that will now have to be accounted for are what we call incremental cost. And that is what climate change needs,” she said.

Ms Nutakor said the challenge was therefore not simply to convince people that climate change was a problem, but to make climate action relevant to their daily decisions.

She pointed to farming as one example, saying farmers were primarily concerned with whether their crops would grow and provide an income.

“For instance, I'm going to the farm to say that I want to plant climate-smart seeds, the orange and the sweet potato, for instance,” she said.

“The reason I'm going to go and plant it is because I need money. I'm a farmer. At the end of the day, I need the crops to grow, and that's my business. I don't care about whether it is sustainable or whatever.”

“All I care about is that the market is ready for orange, the sweet potato, and so I'm going to plant it.”

She said climate-smart practices could gain traction when they were presented in ways that showed citizens how sustainability could support their livelihoods.

Ms Nutakor similarly cited the use of alternative transport technologies, saying economic benefits were often a stronger motivation for users than environmental arguments.

“The number one answer I've always received is that it's cheaper,” she said.

“If I get up, I can plug in the charging system, and then it lasts me more than necessary throughout the day. And I make my money, I make my returns, I pay everybody a fee, and I'm gone.”

“It's not because they are interested in these additional alternatives. It's because it makes sense to the pocket.”

She said policymakers therefore needed to pay closer attention to the economic incentives and practical conditions that determine whether people adopt climate-friendly practices.

“When I understand that I can still make my money and still be sustainable in doing it, then I'll be interested in actually defending it,” she said.

Ghana News.title: The Inconvenient Truth: Not everything called governance is the same thing
Ghana News.content:
Ing Prof Douglas Boateng

Political governance governs society; corporate governance governs institutions; boardroom governance governs oversight; and traditional governance governs communities through inherited legitimacy. Confusing their mandates does not strengthen governance. It quietly weakens accountability until nobody is truly responsible

A Word Stretched Too Thin

Governance has become one of those fashionable words that appears almost everywhere, rather like a favourite spice added to every dish whether or not the recipe called for it. Governments promise it, companies advertise it, and boards claim to practise it, while traditional authorities embody forms of it that predate the modern state itself. Yet beneath this impressive vocabulary sits an inconvenient truth. Political governance, corporate governance, boardroom governance, and traditional governance are related, but they are not technically the same thing. Treating them as interchangeable is rather like assuming a surgeon, a pharmacist and a hospital administrator are doing the same job because they all work in healthcare. Ask the pharmacist to perform heart surgery and the distinction becomes clear rather quickly, usually before the anaesthetic does.

Knowing Who Must Govern What

NyansaKasa (Words of Wisdom): "Good governance begins by knowing who must govern what, for whom, by what authority and with what accountability." That sentence carries more discipline than most governance codes manage in fifty pages. A president is not a chief executive with a national flag. A corporate chairperson is not a ceremonial president of a company. A traditional ruler is not simply an unelected mayor. When these roles blur, accountability usually blurs along with them.

One Word, Four Different Responsibilities

Political governance concerns the exercise of public authority, encompassing constitutions and the mechanisms by which those exercising state power answer to citizens; its legitimacy is derived from law rather than personality. Corporate governance occupies a different institutional universe, concerning how organisations are directed and held accountable to shareholders and wider stakeholders. Boardroom governance narrows the frame further, focused on how a board fulfils oversight through composition, independence and constructive challenge. Traditional governance sits apart from all three, resting not on statute or shareholding but on inherited legitimacy, exercised through chiefs, councils of elders and comparable institutions whose authority over land, custom and community life predates the modern constitution itself. The distinction matters because each system answers to a different master and a different measure of success, and corporate governance, in particular, is the wider ecosystem, while boardroom governance is where a meaningful share of that ecosystem is tested through simple human judgement, in a room, in real time.

A Framework Is Not a Character Reference

A company may possess a magnificent governance framework, and its board can still fail spectacularly. Enron had a board. Lehman Brothers had a board. Wirecard had auditors and formal regulatory oversight, yet its 2020 collapse still wiped out roughly twenty billion euros in market value within weeks once the fraud came to light. The architecture existed. It did not guarantee the behaviour. NyansaKasa (Words of Wisdom): "A governance framework can tell you where the fence should stand. Character determines whether you quietly move it when nobody is looking."

The Board Is Not Management With Better Catering

One persistent governance problem occurs when boards confuse oversight with executive management, fascinated with operational detail while management waits politely for permission to manage. The opposite failure is equally common, where boards grow so distant that management effectively supervises itself. A dominant chief executive can gradually turn independent directors into enthusiastic spectators, well fed and rarely disagreeable. Silence follows, the minutes record unanimous approval, and everybody goes home believing governance has had another successful day. NyansaKasa (Words of Wisdom): "The most dangerous boardroom is not one where people disagree. It is one where everyone has learned that agreement is safer." Institutional failure often begins exactly that quietly.

A Nation Cannot Discontinue a Citizen

The temptation to import corporate language directly into government can be misleading. A corporation may discontinue an unprofitable product line. A government cannot simply discontinue an unprofitable citizen, or the community whose needs are costly and whose returns are social rather than commercial. Singapore is frequently studied for administrative competence. Nordic nations demonstrate how high levels of institutional trust can support effective public administration, and Botswana has often been recognised for the prudent, transparent management of its diamond wealth across successive governments. Each illustrates that durable political governance depends on institutions built to outlast any single personality in charge.

The Bill Sent to the Next Generation

Political cycles everywhere can quietly encourage short-termism. Leaders understandably want citizens to see results before the next election, yet railways, education reform and water security often require decades rather than terms of office to mature. World Bank governance indicators tracked across more than two hundred economies show institutional quality correlating closely with long-run income growth, a relationship that rewards patience far more reliably than it rewards urgency. A nation governed exclusively for the next election eventually sends the invoice to the next generation.

Older Than the Modern State

Traditional governance remains perhaps the most misunderstood of the four, in part because it is older than the states that now sit alongside it. It cannot simply be dismissed as an outdated version of political governance, since these leaders often retain forms of social trust modern institutions still struggle to reproduce. Yet respect for tradition must not mean immunity from accountability, just as modernisation must not mean contempt for inherited wisdom. As one enduring aphorism teaches, two strong trees can grow beside each other once each understands where its own roots end.

When Governance Systems Collide

The greatest difficulty arises where these systems intersect, land being the clearest example, where a traditional authority may hold customary stewardship, local government may hold statutory planning powers, and central government may hold infrastructure ambitions, while investors and resident communities each hold legitimate interests of their own. Without clearly defined boundaries, multiple governance systems can produce not stronger accountability but organised confusion. NyansaKasa (Words of Wisdom): "Where authority overlaps without accountability, power develops many parents but failure becomes an orphan." The solution is not eliminating one governance system in favour of another. It is institutional clarity, agreed upon before the crisis rather than negotiated during one.

Where Regulation Ends, Character Begins

Despite their technical differences, political, corporate, boardroom and traditional governance eventually meet at one unavoidable point. A constitution cannot manufacture integrity. A board charter cannot create courage. A traditional title cannot guarantee wisdom, and no corporate governance code can force anyone to ask an uncomfortable question in the room where it actually matters. South Africa's King Reports have shaped sophisticated global thinking on stakeholder governance, and the United Kingdom's Cadbury tradition profoundly influenced modern board practice worldwide, yet no code, however well drafted, can anticipate every decision made behind a closed door. Character occupies the space where regulation ends, and that may be governance's most inconvenient truth of all.

What Must Change

Governance education should clearly distinguish political, corporate, boardroom and traditional governance while teaching where they legitimately intersect, rather than treating governance as one fashionable umbrella term. Board directors need rigorous preparation before and during appointment, and public officials need training in stewardship and long term policy planning. Traditional leaders deserve access to contemporary governance education without being asked to surrender the cultural legitimacy their institutions rest upon. Appointment systems, across all four domains, must increasingly prioritise competence, independence and character over familiarity or favour, because a board seat is a trusteeship rather than a thank you card, and elected office is a temporary responsibility rather than personal property financed by taxpayers. Boards must resist managing. Executives must respect oversight. Governance also requires a quiet mindset shift, away from treating authority as a reward for loyalty and toward treating it as a discipline requiring diverse voices, since institutions that widen who sits at the table tend to widen what problems they notice. Traditional authorities and statutory institutions need transparent frameworks for collaboration, agreed calmly rather than improvised under pressure.

The Most Inconvenient Truth

Perhaps our greatest mistake has been discussing governance as though it were a single profession with one universal operating manual. Political governance must protect citizenship and the public interest. Corporate governance must ensure responsible organisational direction. Boardroom governance must make oversight and judgement effective. Traditional governance must preserve legitimate communal authority while evolving alongside constitutional society. They overlap and influence one another, but technically and institutionally they remain distinct. NyansaKasa (Words of Wisdom): "Good governance is not everyone governing everything. It is the right people governing the right things, for the right reasons, within the right boundaries, and remaining answerable for the consequences." We rarely suffer from a shortage of people willing to exercise authority. What we occasionally lack is sufficient clarity about its purpose, its limits, and who answers when things go wrong. Because when everybody wants to govern but nobody wants to be accountable, governance becomes theatre, and history, unlike an audience, does not applaud the performance. It simply records the consequences.

About the Author

Ing. Professor Douglas K. Boateng is a strategist in governance, industrialisation and supply chains, and serves as a professional chairperson, an international Chartered Director (UK) and a Chartered Engineer (UK). A Pan-Africanist and social entrepreneur at heart, he has spent his career working across public institutions, corporate boards and industrial policy, in Africa and beyond, guided by the conviction that strong institutions are built one honest decision at a time. His contributions to industry and academia have been recognised with more than six lifetime achievement awards over the course of his career. He is the founder of NyansaKasa, Words of Wisdom, a collection of daily aphorisms he has written and shared since late 2019, distilling decades of experience advising governments, boards and enterprises on governance, accountability and institutional resilience into words meant to challenge and to endure. He convenes the Boardroom Governance Summit, Africa's largest boardroom-focused summit, and writes a widely read weekly op-ed series titled "Inconvenient Truth" and "What Is Wrong With Us," featured on some of the region's leading digital media platforms. Professor Boateng can be reached via LinkedIn or at info@panavest.com.

Ghana News.title: Police arrest two over alleged inciteful religious comments
Ghana News.content:
The Ghana Police Service has arrested two persons in separate incidents over alleged inciteful and offensive religious comments.

The arrests were carried out in collaboration with the National Signals Bureau (NSB) and the Police Cyber Vetting and Enforcement Team.

In the first case, police arrested 35-year-old Masud Abdullah, an Imam, over a video in which he allegedly advocated violence against people who speak ill of a revered religious figure.

According to the Police, information available to the Service indicates that the comments were made during a sermon at a mosque at Ntensere in the Atwima Nwabiagya North District of the Ashanti Region.

In a separate development, the Police Cyber Vetting and Enforcement Team arrested Daniel Junior Yaw Adjei, also known as Apostle Daniel JY Adjei.

He was arrested over a video in which he was allegedly seen making derogatory and offensive religious comments.

The Police said investigations into both cases are ongoing and that the suspects will be taken through due process.

Police caution against religious incitement

The Ghana Police Service has cautioned the public, particularly religious leaders, preachers, community leaders and social media commentators, against using freedom of religion or expression as a basis for inciting violence.

The Service stressed that freedom of religion and freedom of expression must not be used to encourage people to harm others.

It warned that utterances that incite violence constitute offences and that persons found engaging in such conduct would be arrested and prosecuted.

The Police also urged the public to exercise responsibility when expressing views on religious and other sensitive matters, particularly on social media.

Ghana News.title: Adamus Resources challenges mining lease revocation, accuses government of unlawful process
Ghana News.content:
Adamus Resources Limited has rejected the government’s decision to uphold the revocation of its mining leases, accusing the Minister for Lands and Natural Resources, Emmanuel Armah-Kofi Buah, of abusing his powers and disregarding Ghana’s mining laws.

In a statement issued on Wednesday, August 12, the mining company said it received the minister’s decision with “shock and disappointment” and described the process leading to the revocation as unlawful.

Adamus said the decision was contrary to procedures prescribed under the Minerals and Mining Act, 2006 (Act 703).

“The effort by the Minister to strip Adamus Resources Limited of its mineral rights was without regard to any of the statutory procedures laid down in the Minerals and Mining Act, 2006 (Act 703),” the company stated.

The company also rejected the allegations that formed the basis of the revocation, describing them as “unfounded, contrived and deliberately manufactured”.

Adamus accused the minister of using his office to deprive the company of its mining leases.

“The company has duly noted the abuse of power wrapped in the absolute disregard of law in the process leading to the contemptible revocation of its leases,” it said.

The dispute dates back to April 2026, when the minister, acting on the recommendation of the Minerals Commission, revoked three mining leases covering the Akango, Salman and Nkroful concessions.

The Minerals Commission’s initial investigations alleged several breaches by Adamus, including the unauthorised assignment of mineral rights to foreign nationals for independent mining operations without prior written approval from the minister.

The Commission cited Section 14(1) of Act 703 in support of that allegation.

Other alleged breaches included mining outside demarcated areas without an approved Operating Permit from the Chief Inspector of Mines, as well as failure to obtain environmental and forestry approvals from the Environmental Protection Authority.

Adamus subsequently petitioned the revocation, leading to the establishment of an Inter-Ministerial Committee to review the company’s challenge.

According to the government’s account, the committee affirmed most of the breaches identified in the initial assessment and uncovered additional financial liabilities.

These included US$2.56 million in unpaid mineral rights fees, GH¢86.8 million in unpaid royalties and GH¢290.5 million in tax arrears.

The committee also reportedly identified unexplained discrepancies in gold exports and found that US$224 million had been transferred to related parties outside Ghana between 2020 and 2024.

On Monday, August 10, Minister Buah announced that he had upheld the revocation and directed the Minerals Commission to take immediate administrative control of the mine.

Adamus has now served notice that it intends to challenge the decision through the courts.

The company said it would announce the specific steps it intends to take “in the coming days”.

It expressed confidence that a full and fair examination of the facts would demonstrate its compliance with Ghana’s applicable mining laws.

Minister defends process

Minister Buah has defended the government’s handling of the matter, insisting that Adamus was given an opportunity to respond to the allegations before the final decision was reached.

Speaking during a working visit to the mine, he said the government’s priority was to protect the national interest, workers and the integrity of the mining operation.

“We have given Adamus the right of hearing, and I think that we have gotten to this point where the priority is to make sure that the interest of the country, the mine workers who work here and the sanctity of this mine and the safety of it should be the top priority of government,” he said.

The minister also indicated that government intends to seek a court order compelling Adamus to settle outstanding royalty, tax and other financial obligations owed to the state.

With the minister’s determination bringing the administrative review process to an end, the dispute is now likely to shift to the courts.

Adamus said it would provide the public with details of the “cogent steps” it intends to take to challenge the revocation in the coming days.

Ghana News.title: Apostle Nyamekye recalls near-death experiences during six years in South Africa
Ghana News.content:
Apostle Eric Nyamekye — President, GPCC

Chairman of The Church of Pentecost, Apostle Eric Nyamekye, has recounted how he nearly lost his life during his six-year stay in South Africa, amid renewed concerns over attacks on foreign nationals in the country.

Apostle Nyamekye said his years in South Africa exposed him directly to some of the security challenges faced by Ghanaians and other migrants.

Speaking to the Communication Directorate of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, he recalled being confronted by armed robbers on two separate occasions, one of which he described as particularly dangerous.

“I lived in South Africa for about six years, and I suffered a lot from some of these things. I almost died in South Africa. Two times, I was accosted by armed robbers. The last one was too dangerous. When I was leaving South Africa, my luggage was stolen,” he said.

Apostle Nyamekye also recalled returning to South Africa more recently after a national deacon of The Church of Pentecost was kidnapped during a church service.

“And then recently, I had to rush to South Africa, about a year plus ago, when our national deacon was kidnapped in the midst of an offering, and I had to rush to South Africa. I was the right person to go, not because I was a chairman, but because they knew that I have also suffered from some of these things, so I needed to go in there and speak,” he added.

He said those experiences gave him a deeper appreciation of the insecurity and difficulties some Ghanaians encounter while living and working in South Africa.

His comments come amid renewed concern over the safety of foreign nationals in South Africa following recent xenophobic incidents and related security concerns involving Ghanaians.

Ghana News.title: Kidney patients call for more dialysis machines at Cape Coast Teaching Hospital
Ghana News.content:
The Forum for Kidney Patients Association Ghana has appealed to the government, corporate organisations, benevolent individuals and groups to urgently support the Cape Coast Teaching Hospital (CCTH) with more dialysis machines to enhance renal care services.

The Cape Coast Teaching Hospital, which is the only public dialysis centre in the Central Region, is under immense pressure, serving scores of patients from the region, as well as parts of the Western, Eastern and Ashanti Regions.

Despite the growing demand for its services, the centre currently has only five functioning dialysis machines serving more than 100 patients.

Consequently, each patient is allowed only about two hours per session instead of the recommended four hours, exposing them to the risk of complications and potentially endangering their lives.

The President of the Forum for Kidney Patients Association, Baffour Kojo Ahinkra, said the situation required urgent intervention from all stakeholders, given the rising incidence of kidney diseases.

He made the call when the Association donated consumables to the facility to facilitate the restoration of two dialysis machines that had been out of use due to a shortage of consumables.

The items donated included disposable bloodlines and dialysis powder, a concentrate that helps remove waste products and excess electrolytes from a patient's blood during haemodialysis.

Mr Ahinkra said the gesture was intended to complement the Government’s efforts to provide essential dialysis services to patients.

He called on the Government to expedite action to establish more dialysis centres in the region.

In the interim, however, he insisted that the CCTH dialysis centre must be beefed up to mitigate the pressure and give patients ample time on the machines.

“They are doing two hours per session instead of four and that does not give them any proper clearance in the system.

“When a patient from CCTH speaks to you, you smell urea in their breath, which is an indication that their blood is not being filtered well,” he said.

“I know the government is trying to set up more dialysis centres, but that is for the long term.

“For now, we have a place. Let’s beef it up with more machines and consumables because the cases keep rising every day,” he stressed.

A physician specialist at CCTH, Dr Samuel Doughan, noted that the recent surge in dialysis cases had put enormous pressure on the facility and its staff.

“We run out of consumables, and the machines are breaking down because constantly, they are in use due to the increased burden we have seen these days.

“We have about four to five machines averagely working. This means that we can only serve about 20 to 25 people if we are going to provide adequate dialysis for everyone,” he said.

He, therefore, reiterated the appeal for more dialysis machines to meet the increasing demand and provide patients with better treatment.

Dr Doughan expressed appreciation to the Association for the gesture, saying it would go a long way to support the dialysis unit.

To mitigate the rising incidence of renal cases, he entreated citizens to undergo regular check-ups, drink adequate water, and reduce their salt intake.

He also encouraged hypertensive and diabetic patients to take their medications religiously.

A patient from Akim Oda in the Eastern Region, Madam Gifty Tetteh, sharing her ordeal, narrated how she travelled for four hours to Cape Coast for her sessions each time.

She therefore called for a dialysis centre in her area while appealing for more dialysis machines at CCTH.

She also thanked the Association for the support gesture.

Ghana News.title: GAFET sets GH¢100m target to transform agricultural education by 2028
Ghana News.content:
The Ministry of Food and Agriculture (MoFA) has launched the Ghana Agricultural Fund for Education and Transformation (GAFET), a national endowment designed to provide sustainable financing for agricultural education and the human capital needed to transform the sector. The Fund was formally launched by the Minister for Food and Agriculture, Honourable Eric Opoku, at a ceremony in Accra attended by development partners, financial institutions, agribusiness leaders, traditional authorities, students and the media.

GAFET seeks to address a critical imbalance in Ghana’s economy. Agriculture contributes more than a fifth of the economy, yet only about 2 percent of tertiary students are enrolled in agricultural programmes, while agricultural education institutions face an estimated annual funding gap of GH¢12 million.

The Fund will pool contributions into a professionally managed endowment, with the capital preserved and invested and annual returns used to finance approved priorities across the agricultural education system. “If Ghana wants to transform agriculture, it must invest in the people who will transform agriculture,” Steven Nhyira Odarteifio, Lead Coordinator of GAFET said.

He added that GAFET would focus on closing the gap between classroom learning and the practical demands of modern agriculture by supporting laboratories, demonstration farms, mechanisation, digital agriculture, research and innovation, agribusiness incubation and faculty development. He said the objective was to ensure that graduates leave agricultural institutions with the technical and entrepreneurial capabilities required to participate meaningfully in a modern, technology-driven agricultural economy.

He also called for broader participation from the private sector, financial institutions, development partners, alumni associations and individuals, arguing that the fund’s long-term success would depend on its ability to build a broad national ownership base. “This fund does not end today. Today is only its birth. Let history recall that when the call came to rebuild Ghana’s agricultural future, government provided the vision, the private sector provided the confidence, and development partners provided their partnership, and together we built an institution that future generations will thank us for,” he said.

Delivering the keynote address, Hon. Opoku described GAFET as a human-capital pillar of the government's flagship Feed Ghana programme. “Before we can sustainably feed Ghana, we must equip Ghana. The quality of agricultural transformation will depend on the quality of agricultural human capital,” he said.

The Minister, who was flanked by high ranking personnel of the ministry, including his deputy, Hon. John Setor Dumelo, called on commercial banks, pension funds, insurance companies, agribusinesses, development partners, philanthropic foundations and alumni associations to support the Fund through contributions to laboratories, workshops, demonstration farms, scholarships and agricultural colleges. He also highlighted recent increases in funding to agricultural colleges, from GH¢35,000 to GH¢100,000 per institution, which he said had contributed to a 35 percent increase in enrolment.

GH¢3.5million raised at launch

GAFET has mobilised GH¢3.5 million in founding capital and aims to grow the fund to GH¢10 million by December 2026 and GH¢100 million by December 2028. The Fund is expected to transition to a full endowment structure in the fourth quarter of 2026, with a governing board, fund administrator, fund manager and custodian bank. It is ultimately expected to become a permanent statutory institution established by an Act of Parliament.

Its governance framework will include a Securities and Exchange Commission-licensed fund manager, independent annual audits, an approved investment policy focused on capital preservation and published annual summaries. GAFET will initially support 21 agricultural education institutions, comprising five standalone agricultural colleges and 16 universities and technical universities. Returns from the endowment will support practical training, mechanisation, research and innovation, digital agriculture, agribusiness incubation, faculty development and scholarships.

Secretariat Technical Lead Seyram Kofori-Ndinya said the Fund’s governance would be critical to maintaining public confidence. “Our objective is to show how the Fund will be governed, so that every contribution made today actually outlives all of us in this room,” she said.

Agribusiness coalition backs initiative

Five Ghanaian-led agribusinesses — AgriSolve, GrowForMe, New Age Agric Solutions, Tradeline Consult and Farmerline — have joined GAFET as founding partners. The partners highlighted the need to attract more young people into agriculture and equip them with practical skills, technology and access to modern agricultural infrastructure. Farmerline pledged to contribute capital and access to its technology platform, while GrowForMe committed to opening its crowdfunding platform to support the Fund’s growth.

Declaring GAFET formally launched, Minister Opoku urged stakeholders to focus on building institutions that would benefit generations beyond the present. “Generations yet unborn will remember not the speeches delivered but the institutions built,” he said.

For Mr. Odarteifio, the launch marks the beginning of a long-term national effort. “This fund does not end today. Today is only its birth. Together we can build an institution that future generations will thank us for,” Mr. Odarteifio said.

World.title: Trump pleads not guilty to 34 felony counts
World.content:
News outlets will not be allowed to broadcast former President Donald Trump’s arraignment on Tuesday in a New York state court, a judge said Monday night, but he will allow some photographers to take pictures in the courtroom before the proceedings formally begin.

Acting New York Supreme Court Judge Juan Merchan rejected the request by several media organizations, including CNN, for permission to broadcast the historic proceedings. Trump’s arraignment — like most arraignments in the Manhattan courthouse — is a public proceeding, but news cameras are not usually allowed to broadcast from inside the courtroom.

However, the judge is allowing five pool photographers to take still photos at the beginning of the proceedings “until such time as they are directed to vacate the jury box by court personnel.”

Earlier on Monday, Trump’s lawyers urged the judge to reject the media’s request for live cameras in the courtroom. The Manhattan District Attorney’s office told the judge they didn’t have a position.

The media outlets that tried to get cameras into the courtroom argued that “the gravity of this proceeding … and, consequently, the need for the broadest possible public access, cannot be overstated.”

Trump is now in Manhattan ahead of the arraignment. A grand jury indicted the former president last week.

The arraignment is also expected to bring the unsealing of the criminal charges against Trump, which have not yet been seen by his lawyers or the public.

The indictment stems from Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg’s investigation into hush-money payments, made during the 2016 presidential campaign, to women who claimed they had extramarital affairs with Trump, which he denies.

Trump denies all wrongdoing and his lawyers said last week that they’ll fight to get the charges dropped.

World.title: Russian authorities detain suspect over St. Petersburg cafe blast
World.content:
A Ukrainian tank is seen near the frontline area amid the Russia-Ukraine war, in Bakhmut, Ukraine, on April 02. (Muhammed Enes Yildirim/Anadolu Agency/Getty Images)

The Ukrainian military has reported little change to the front lines but heavy fire from Russian forces at various parts of the front line in the Donetsk region.

The General Staff said that more than 45 enemy attacks had been repelled over the past day, with the focus on Lyman, Bakhmut, Avdiivka and Mariinka.

It said there were 17 air strikes and more than 20 strikes by multiple launch rocket systems.

“In the Bakhmut direction, the enemy is trying to take full control over the city of Bakhmut and continues to storm it,” the General Staff said.

West of the city, Ukrainian defense forces repelled about 20 enemy attacks, according to the General Staff.

Oleksandr Syrskyi, commander of Ukrainian Land Forces, posted on Telegram that in Bakhmut he had met with “soldiers and commanders who destroyed the myth of invincibility of the Wagner fighters and Russian paratroopers.”

“The enemy is weakening and trying to cover up its failures with new fakes about the capture of Bakhmut,” Syrskyi said.

Syrskyi referenced the possibility of a future counter-offensive, saying that “the forward movement of our entire army depends on what every soldier is doing right now on their section of the front.”

Some of the most intense fighting is to the northwest and west of the city of Donetsk – as the Russians continue months-long efforts to dislodge Ukrainian defenses in Avdiivka and Mariinka. The General Staff said that some 20 assaults had been repelled.

“There are also some operational successes of our military in the Donetsk area. Our military have taken some positions. They have taken a more strategic and favourable position,” said Oleksii Dmytrashkivskyi, spokesperson for the military in that zone.

He also noted that Russian special forces had been introduced in the area.

“The enemy is trying to attack our positions between Avdiivka and Marinka. These attempts do not stop. It should be noted that the enemy has suffered quite significant losses,” Dmytrashkivskyi said.

He also claimed that the Russians “don’t have the same amount of equipment and, as they themselves say, they are on a ‘diet’ of ammunition for assaults.”

Social media video showed both sides engaged in heavy fire in the Avdiivka area, which the Russians have surrounded on three sides.

Denis Pushilin, the leader of the self-declared Donetsk People’s Republic, claimed that Russian forces were still advancing in the Avdiivka direction.

“It is still premature to speak of encirclement, but the situation is being created, if not critical, then extremely difficult for the enemy… After clearing Kamianka, our units are moving further. There are difficulties both with the terrain, which must also be overcome, and there are also similarities with weather conditions. But these difficulties are mutual — both for the enemy and for us,” Pushilin said.

World.title: Suspected Chinese spy balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing
World.content:
Washington —

The Chinese spy balloon that transited the US earlier this year was able to capture imagery and collect some signals intelligence from US military sites, a source familiar with the matter tells CNN.

The balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing in real time, the source said, and the US government still does not know for sure whether the Chinese government could wipe the balloon’s data as it received it. That raises questions about whether there is intelligence the balloon was able to gather that the US still doesn’t know about.

Still, the intelligence community has not been overly concerned about the information the balloon was able to gather, the person said, because it is not much more sophisticated than what Chinese satellites are able to glean as they orbit over similar locations.

A US intelligence official told CNN on Monday that “although analysis of the wreckage of the High Altitude Balloon remains ongoing, thus far, its flight over the United States does not appear to have provided critical new insights to the People’s Republic of China.”

The US also knew what the balloon’s path would be and was able to protect sensitive sites and censor some signals before the balloon was able to pick them up, officials have said.

As CNN has reported, the US intelligence community last year developed a method of tracking what it says is a fleet of these Chinese balloons operating across the globe, controlled by the Chinese military.

The FBI is still examining the balloon, but so far officials have been able to glean additional information about how the device worked, including the algorithms used for the balloon’s software and how it is powered and designed.

CNN has reached out to the National Security Council at the White House and the Pentagon for comment. NBC was first to report on the new intelligence.

Video Ad Feedback Justin Trudeau on what the world needs to do to handle China's threats 1:33 • Source: CNN Justin Trudeau on what the world needs to do to handle China's threats 1:33

The balloon first crossed into US airspace over Alaska in late January before passing through Canada and down into Montana, where it hovered for a few days, leading the US to believe it was trying to surveil sensitive military sites, like Malmstrom Air Force Base in Montana. It was eventually shot down by the US off the East Coast on February 4, and the incident further escalated tensions between Washington and Beijing, including the postponement of a diplomatic visit by US Secretary of State Antony Blinken to China.

A senior State Department official said in February that, as the balloon floated across the US, it “was capable of conducting signals intelligence collection operations.”

Gen. Glen VanHerck, the commander of US Northern Command and NORAD, said at the time that the US “did not assess” that the balloon “presented a significant collection hazard beyond what already exists in actionable technical means from the Chinese.”

The surveillance program, which includes a number of similar balloons, is in part run out of the small Chinese province of Hainan, officials told CNN. The US does not know the precise size of the fleet of Chinese surveillance balloons, but sources tell CNN that the program has conducted at least two dozen missions over at least five continents in recent years.

Roughly half a dozen of those flights have been within US airspace, although not necessarily over US territory, according to one official familiar with the intelligence.

China has maintained that the balloon was actually just a weather balloon thrown off course, and the US has been assessing the possibility that it was not deliberately maneuvered into the continental US by the Chinese government, CNN has reported.

Still, China did maintain some ability to maneuver the balloon, officials believe. And once the balloon was over Montana, China appeared to take advantage of its position to loiter over sensitive sites and try to collect intelligence.

This story has been updated with additional reporting.

World.title: Beijing promised to 'fight back' over Taiwan leader's US visit. But this time it has more to lose
World.content:
Hong Kong —

An anticipated meeting between Taiwan’s President Tsai Ing-wen and US House Speaker Kevin McCarthy in California this week has sparked concerns of a repeat of the pressure campaign China launched last year when then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi visited Taipei.

At that time, Beijing encircled the island democracy with unprecedented military drills – firing multiple missiles into its surrounding waters and sending dozens of warplanes speeding across a sensitive median line dividing the Taiwan Strait.

It also cut off contact with the United States over a number of issues from military matters to combating climate change, in retaliation for what it viewed as a violation of its sovereignty.

This time, Beijing has already threatened to “resolutely fight back” if a Tsai-McCarthy meeting goes ahead.

Video Ad Feedback See why tensions are rising between US and China over Taiwan 2:32 • Source: CNN See why tensions are rising between US and China over Taiwan 2:32

It also slammed Washington for allowing Tsai to stopover in the US while en route to and from official visits in Central America, warning it could lead to “serious” confrontation between the two powers.

A defiant Tsai staked out her own ground, pledging as she took off on her 10-day trip not to let “external pressure” stop Taiwan from connecting with the world and like-minded democracies.

But the optics of the meeting, taking place in California and not Taiwan, and its timing – at a particularly thorny moment in China’s foreign relations and ahead of a presidential election in Taiwan that could reset the tone of its relationship with Beijing – may see Beijing tread more carefully this time, or at least not escalate further, analysts say.

“This puts the burden on China not to overreact, because any overreaction is only going to push China further away from the world,” said Yun Sun, director of the China Program at the Stimson Center think tank in Washington.

That doesn’t mean, however, that Beijing won’t be closely watching Tsai’s movements as it calibrates its response – and decides how much military might to flex over her meeting with an American lawmaker on American soil.

The opacity of China’s system – and the potential for competing interests within its vast bureaucracy – also make it difficult to accurately predict its response.

“Every time Taiwan does anything that China doesn’t like, the Chinese react with their own military coercion,” Sun said. But in the current situation, “they have to consider the consequences of overreaction,” she added.

House Speaker Kevin McCarthy talks to reporters at the Capitol in Washington on March 24, 2023. J. Scott Applewhite/AP

Rising pressure

The expected meeting, which McCarthy’s office announced earlier this week would take place on Wednesday, also comes at a precarious moment in US-China relations.

Washington and Beijing are struggling to stabilize their communication amid flaring tensions over issues from a downed suspected Chinese surveillance balloon to semiconductor supply chains – raising the stakes of potential damage to that relationship if Beijing lashes out as it did when Tsai met Pelosi.

Taiwan is still feeling the fallout of that response last August, with Chinese military forces now regularly making incursions over what had previously been an informal but largely respected border of control between Beijing and Taipei in the Taiwan Strait. Taiwan’s official Central News Agency also reported Monday that Tsai would meet with McCarthy, citing Tsai’s presidential office.

Video Ad Feedback See image of a Chinese balloon hovering over Taiwan 3:05 • Source: CNN See image of a Chinese balloon hovering over Taiwan 3:05

But a meeting between Tsai and the leader of the Republican majority in the US House of Representatives, who ranks second in line to the Presidency, would mark another symbolic moment for Taiwan and the US, which only maintain unofficial ties.

For Tsai, who is entering the final year of her two-term presidency, “it’s clearly a capstone event,” according to Wen-Ti Sung, a political scientist at the Australian National University’s Taiwan Studies Program. “She has this image as the Taiwanese president who has taken US-Taiwan relations to new heights, and who … has been able to give Taiwan almost unprecedented international visibility,” he said.

That increased visibility – and enhanced cooperation with the US – has followed China’s mounting pressure on the island, which sits fewer than 110 miles (177 kilometers) from the mainland coast.

China’s Communist Party claims the self-governing island democracy as its own despite never having controlled it, and has vowed to take the island, by force if necessary.

The party has undertaken a sweeping expansion of its military capabilities over the past decade under leader Xi Jinping – and ramped up its pervasive economic, diplomatic and military pressure on Taiwan.

That’s driven concerns, among some in Washington, that Beijing is preparing for an invasion, though China’s official language still suggests that scenario is not its preferred option for achieving the claimed goal of “reunification.”

It is those pressures – and how to support Taiwan against unilateral actions by Beijing – that are likely to be on the table when Tsai, McCarthy and a bipartisan group of US lawmakers sit down on Wednesday.

Congress has been a pillar of increasing American support for Taiwan in recent years. Lawmakers regularly visit the island and drive bipartisan legislation enhancing support and cooperation.

While the US switched its diplomatic relations to Beijing decades ago, it maintains unofficial ties with Taiwan and is bound by law to provide the democratic island with the means to defend itself.

Under Washington’s longstanding “One China” policy, the US acknowledges China’s position that Taiwan is part of China, but has never officially recognized Beijing’s claim to the island of 23 million.

Though McCarthy does not have Pelosi’s decades-long record of advocacy regarding China, the California Republican is now a leading voice pushing for closer scrutiny of Beijing, and meeting Tsai could help him to burnish that image.

Last month, McCarthy told reporters that meeting Tsai in the US would not impact whether he travels to Taiwan in the future – something he had earlier said he wanted to do.

Fighter jets of the Chinese People's Liberation Army Eastern Theater Command conduct joint combat training exercises around Taiwan on August 7, 2022 in this photo released by Xinhua News Agency. Gong Yulong/Xinhua/AP

Beijing watching

A meeting in California, on US soil, is widely seen as less likely to provoke Beijing than a McCarthy visit to Taiwan.

Pelosi’s trip – the first from a lawmaker of that rank to the island in 25 years – generated a fever pitch of nationalist and anti-US rhetoric in mainland China.

This time, so far, domestic conversation in China’s heavily controlled media sphere has been significantly muted.

But the stakes remain high – including for Beijing itself – over how it responds, analysts say.

As Taiwan prepares for a presidential election in January, a fierce response could push voters away from Taiwan’s main opposition party Kuomintang (KMT), widely seen as more friendly toward Beijing.

It could also jar with another high profile trip happening now: a tour of mainland China from former Taiwan president and senior KMT member Ma Ying-jeou, the first visit from a current or former Taiwan leader since the end of the Chinese Civil War in 1949.

Ma’s tour is a “once in a half a century opportunity to send a conciliatory message between the two sides, Beijing shouldn’t want to tank that,” said Sung, the political scientist.

China is also acutely aware that its actions toward Taiwan are under a significantly brighter global spotlight following the invasion of Ukraine by Russian President Vladimir Putin, a close diplomatic partner of Xi. Putin’s rhetoric over Ukraine has echoes of how Xi speaks of Taiwan.

Beijing has recently sought to position itself as an agent of peace in that conflict – especially as it aims to repair frayed ties with Europe.

This week, as Tsai is expected to meet with McCarthy, French President Emmanuel Macron and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen will head to China – an important opportunity that Xi may not want to overshadow with military posturing.

An aggressive response also risks stoking confrontation with the US, not yet six months after Xi and US President Joe Biden called to enhance communication during a face-to-face meeting in Bali.

“(A less overtly aggressive response) would imply that Beijing does not wish to escalate tension with the US to a level that can risk getting out of hand,” said Steve Tsang, director of the SOAS China Institute in London.

“A reset in US-China ties is not on the agenda, but an easing of tension is not beyond the realm of possibility.”
