World.title: #OsunDecides2026: Meet candidates seeking to govern ‘State of the Living Spring’
World.content:
With 13 political parties fielding candidates for Saturday’s governorship election, the race for the Osun State Government House has entered its decisive phase.

Across the state’s 30 local government areas, the candidates are criss-crossing communities, selling their records, programmes and political promises to voters ahead of the poll.

Although 14 candidates were initially on the ballot, barely a week before the election, Adesina Adeyemi-Doro, the candidate of the All Progressives Grand Alliance (APGA), withdrew from the contest and endorsed the All Progressives Congress (APC) candidate, Bola Oyebamiji. Mr Adeyemi-Doro will still be on the ballot despite his withdrawal.

The contest has increasingly taken the shape of a three-way battle involving incumbent Governor Ademola Adeleke of the Accord Party, Mr Oyebamiji of the APC, and Najeem Salaam of the African Democratic Congress (ADC).

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

About 2.4 million people are eligible to vote at the 3,763 polling units, spread across the 332 wards in the 30 councils, for their preferred candidates on Saturday. The voters have a coterie of candidates drawn from different professions and endeavours of life to choose from. Among them are accountants, administrators, social scientists, bankers, economists, entrepreneurs, medical practitioners, estate developers and others.

Here are the 13 candidates on INEC’s list from whom voters will choose who will govern them for the next four years, beginning on 27 November.

Ademola Adeleke (Accord)

Ademola Adeleke, the incumbent governor and former senator, is a businessman and administrator. He was born on 13 May 1960 in Enugu, south-east Nigeria. His mother was Igbo from Abia State, while his father, a former senator, hailed from Ede in Osun State.

Mr Adeleke attended Jacksonville State University, Alabama, United States, where he majored in criminal justice and minored in political science. But after much controversy, he got enrolled at Atlanta Metropolitan State College, also in the US, where he earned a BSc in criminal justice in 2021.

He was executive director of Guinness Nigeria Plc and group executive director of Pacific Holdings Ltd.

Mr Adeleke hails from a political family. His father, Ayoola Adeleke, was a Second Republic senator, representing Oyo East on the platform of the defunct Unity Party of Nigeria (UPN). His late elder brother, Isiaka Adeleke, was the first executive governor of Osun and a former senator, while his younger brother, Adedeji Adeleke, is a businessman and founder of Adeleke University.

The governor is also the uncle of Nigerian musician David Adeleke, popularly known as Davido.

Mr Adeleke became governor in 2022 after defeating the incumbent, Gboyega Oyetola, in a keenly contested election. He secured 403,371 votes to Oyetola’s 375,027 and won in 17 of the state’s 30 local government areas.

The victory was particularly significant because Messrs Adeleke and Oyetola had previously faced each other in the 2018 governorship contest, which Mr Oyetola won by a very narrow margin.

Before becoming governor, the 66-year-old represented Osun West District in the Senate from 2017 to 2019. His entry into electoral politics was also closely linked to the influence of the Adeleke family.

The family connection remains an important part of his political identity.

Mr Adeleke’s political rise has therefore combined personal popularity, family name recognition and grassroots mobilisation.

Bola Oyebamiji (APC)

Bola Oyebamiji, aged 60, popularly known as AMBO, is a banker, economist, public administrator and politician from Ikire in Irewole Local Government Area of Osun State.

Mr Oyebamiji holds an OND and HND in banking and finance from The Polytechnic, Ibadan, Oyo State and later obtained a master’s degree in Public Administration from Lagos State University.

He bagged another master’s degree in Business Administration from the University of Ado-Ekiti.

He is also a Fellow of the Chartered Institute of Bankers.

His career spans the private and public sectors. He worked in the banking industry before moving into government and became the managing director of the Osun State Investment Company, now associated with Omoluabi Holdings.

He subsequently served as Commissioner for Finance under the administrations of former Governor Rauf Aregbesola and his successor, Gboyega Oyetola. His long involvement in managing the state’s finances has made fiscal management a central component of his political profile.

His public-service career later extended beyond Osun. President Bola Tinubu appointed him managing director and chief executive officer of the National Inland Waterways Authority (NIWA) in 2023. He resigned from the position in November 2025 to pursue the governorship race.

His political profile is also closely connected to the APC establishment in Osun. His years in government under Messrs Aregbesola and Oyetola place him within the political structure that controlled the state before Adeleke’s victory in 2022.

Najeem Salaam (ADC)

Najeem Salaam, 61, hails from Ejigbo. The man, popularly called “Iwaloye,” holds a doctorate in political science from the Obafemi Awolowo University, Ile-Ife.

He is an author, having co-authored a book, Rudiments of Government and Politics. It is a textbook used by students studying government and politics.

The ADC candidate is a former Speaker of the Osun State House of Assembly and a long-standing grassroots politician. He served as Speaker during the administration of former Governor Rauf Aregbesola and became a prominent figure within the progressive political bloc in Osun.

Mr Salaam’s emergence is significant because he represents a third political platform in a race otherwise dominated by the rivalry between Mr Adeleke and the APC.

His political strength comes largely from his long experience in Osun politics and his association with Mr Aregbesola, under whom he served as Speaker.

He has promised to prioritise workers’ welfare, education, youth empowerment, security, local enterprise and public confidence in government. He has also made electricity one of the key issues in his campaign, saying he has been engaging investors and stakeholders in the power sector to seek solutions to the state’s electricity challenges.

Olanrewaju Farinloye (AA)

Olanrewaju Farinloye is the candidate of the Action Alliance (AA). At 40, he is among the youngest candidates in the race.

INEC’s final list records his qualifications as the General Certificate of Secondary Education (GCSE) and the Certificate in Commercial and Economic Studies (CCECS). He is contesting alongside his deputy, Fadahunsi Olaniyi.

Olajide Esan (AAC)

Olajide Esan, 39, is one of the youngest candidates in the race. He is an entrepreneur and car dealer and emerged as the African Action Congress (AAC) candidate through a consensus arrangement at the party’s primary in December 2025.

Mr Esan is also a geographer. He studied at Osun State University, where he obtained a degree, and has described his professional interests as including Geographic Information Systems (GIS), spatial analysis and entrepreneurship. He has presented himself as a youth-oriented candidate and is popularly associated with the description “Youth Governor.”

His campaign has focused on economic diversification, agriculture, mining, and technology, as well as reducing the state’s dependence on federal allocations. His deputy is Bello Yekeen.

Yemisi Opawoye (ADP)

Yemisi Opawoye is the African Democratic Party (ADP) candidate and the only woman in the governorship race.

INEC records her qualification as a Bachelor of Education. She spent her professional life as an academic and is a retired school principal.

At 84, she is also the oldest candidate on the final list. Her candidacy adds an unusual dimension to the race, given both her age and experience in education.

She is paired with 43-year-old Atanda Babatunde as the deputy governorship candidate.

Adewale Adebayo (APM)

Adewale Adebayo is a prominent real estate developer and CEO of Tri Edge Real Estate.

He studied the mechanics of public administration and economic policy and is a former chairman of the Inter-Party Advisory Council (IPAC) in Osun State.

He served as the immediate past Osun State Chairman for the Allied Peoples Movement (APM), managing state-level party structures and grassroots organisation. In June, Mr Adebayoe received the endorsement of former Osun Governor Olagunsoye Oyinlola and members of the Kabiru Turaki-led faction of the Peoples Democratic Party in the state.

Jimoh Naheem is his deputy governorship running mate.

Clement Adesuyi (APP)

Clement Adesuyi is the governorship candidate of the Action Peoples Party. He emerged as the party’s candidate in December 2025 after being the sole aspirant at the party’s primary. He secured the affirmation of 39 delegates.

His manifesto is centred on the promise of transforming the state through investment in youth empowerment, health, education and infrastructure.

Masilo Adeleke (BP)

Masilo Adeleke is the Boot Party candidate.

He is a graduate of the University of Ilorin and contested the 2023 senatorial election but lost.

The party selected Aresa Adenike as its running mate

Taofeek Adeleke (NNPP)

Taofeek Adeleke is the New Nigeria Peoples Party (NNPP) candidate known for advocating inclusive governance, human-centred leadership, and grassroots development.

His campaign has placed considerable emphasis on education, healthcare, security and infrastructure. In July, he described education as one of the foundations of sustainable development and said his campaign was built around an “Education for All” message.

He is contesting alongside Adeyera Adesola as his running mate.

Saliu Oyelami (PRP)

Saliu Oyelami, popularly known as Orisunlagba, is the Peoples Redemption Party (PRP) candidate.

He is a medical doctor with more than two decades of experience in medical practice. His professional career has included work at Osogbo Muslim Hospital and the University of Ilorin Teaching Hospital, as well as medical practice in Taraba State.

Mr Oyelami is also the chief medical director of Shifauk Hospital Group.

His educational background includes studies at the University of Ilorin and the International University of Africa in Khartoum, as well as training in journalism at the International Institute of Journalism in Abuja.

The PRP candidate was a prominent governorship aspirant under the Action Democratic Party (ADP) in 2018, but he stepped down for another candidate before the final ballot.

In 2022, he also contested the Osun State gubernatorial election as the candidate for the New Nigeria People’s Party (NNPP).

His running mate is Adewale Solomon.

Olalekan Ogunsakin (YPP)

Olalekan Ogunsakin is the Young Progressives Party candidate, with Taye Oyetola as his running mate.

Outside of politics, he describes himself as an accomplished Nigerian-American physician-scientist, pathologist, board-certified toxicologist, and medical educator.

He earned a medical degree from Obafemi Awolowo University (OAU) in Ile-Ife, Nigeria, with a focus on healthcare awareness.

He also obtained a PhD from Tulane University School of Public Health and Tropical Medicine, specialising in pulmonary system research and earning the prestigious Tulane 34 award.

Olufemi Adesuyi (ZLP)

Olufemi Adesuyi is the Zenith Labour Party candidate, with Abdulsalam Olamide as his running mate.

He is a registered building contractor based in Akure, Ondo State. He operates Engr Adefemi Adesuyi Building Contractors, a business specialising in interior and exterior structural detailing, home ceilings, painting, wall screeding, and Plaster of Paris (POP) installations.

What voters are saying

While political parties and candidates are presenting their respective programmes, voters are assessing the contenders based on what they believe each candidate can offer the state.

For Bolanle Waheed, the APC candidate is the strongest among the major contenders because of his perceived relationship with the federal government.

“Among the major candidates contesting the Osun governorship election, I consider the APC candidate the strongest because I believe he has the backing of the President. I think this could give him better access to federal support and opportunities that could benefit Osun State,” Mr Waheed told PREMIUM TIMES.

However, he said the most pressing issue for him is the lack of employment opportunities in the state.

“The biggest issue I want the next governor of Osun State to address is unemployment and the lack of employment opportunities,” he said.

Mr Waheed said the next administration should focus on attracting companies and industries to Osun to create jobs for residents.

“I believe the government should focus on attracting and establishing companies and industries in the state to create more jobs for citizens, as many people are currently unemployed,” he said.

Despite his preference for Mr Oyebamiji, Mr Waheed said the candidate’s association with previous APC administrations gives him some reservations.

“Although the APC candidate has experience from serving in both the Aregbesola and Oyetola administrations, I have some concerns about this,” he said.

“The Oyetola administration was not favourable to many people in Osun State, and since the APC candidate was part of that administration, I am not completely convinced that he would do much differently from his former boss.

“However, I still think his experience and relationship with the federal government could be useful if he genuinely prioritises job creation and economic development.”

For Biodun Ogunlana, however, the incumbent governor remains the strongest candidate.

“Among the major candidates contesting the Osun governorship election, I consider Ademola Adeleke the strongest,” Mr Ogunlana told PREMIUM TIMES.

He attributed Mr Adeleke’s advantage to incumbency, name recognition and his grassroots network.

“On incumbency and popularity, Adeleke is widely seen as having the advantage of incumbency, name recognition and a strong grassroots base, especially in Osun West,” he said.

“He defeated an incumbent in 2022, which is often cited as evidence of his electoral strength.”

World.title: Osun election: Ex-PDP guber aspirant endorses Adeleke
World.content:
By Shina Abubakar, Osogbo

A former gubernatorial aspirant of the Peoples Democratic Party, PDP, in Osun State, Mr Adebayo Adedamola, popularly known as Fryo, has announced his endorsement of Governor Ademola Adeleke for the August 15, 2026 governorship election.

Adedamola was nominated by a faction of the PDP for the August 15 poll. He polled 919 votes out of 957 cast in the primary held in Osogbo, the state capital.

However, his name was not among the final list of candidates for the election announced by the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC).

Adedamola, alongside his supporters, said the decision followed extensive consultations, sober reflection and assessment of the political circumstances in the state.

“I have arrived at this decision based on my assessment of the political circumstances in our state and my conviction that, at this particular moment, this is the direction I am prepared to support.

“I encourage all PDP members, supporters and party structures across the state who believe in my leadership and judgment to support the emergence of His Excellency, Senator Ademola Adeleke, at the August 15 gubernatorial election,” Adedamola stated.

The PDP chieftain said he remains proud of his participation in the party’s primary and expressed gratitude to those who supported his candidacy.

He, however, stressed that politics is also about making difficult decisions at critical moments, adding, “Politics is not only about contesting elections. Politics is also about understanding the realities of the moment, making difficult decisions when necessary, and putting the larger interest of our people above personal ambition.”

Adedamola noted that he had already communicated his position to PDP leaders, members and stakeholders across the state.

Speaking on Saturday’s election, Adedamola called for a peaceful poll, urging political leaders, candidates and supporters to reject violence, intimidation and hate speech.

“Osun State is bigger than any individual. Osun State is bigger than any political party. And Osun State is certainly bigger than any election. We must allow the people to exercise their democratic rights freely and peacefully,” he said

Adedamola urged PDP members and structures across Osun to work towards the re-emergence of Governor Adeleke while conducting themselves lawfully and responsibly.

World.title: Osun election: INEC includes SDP on ballot, reprints result sheets
World.content:
Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) says it has included the Social Democratic Party (SDP) in the ballot for Saturday’s governorship election.

Mohammed Haruna, INEC National Commissioner, Chairman, Information and Voter Education Committee, stated this in a statement issued on Wednesday in Abuja.

The News Agency of Nigeria (NAN) reports that SDP is fielding Dr Francis Ajala and Faseke Oladipo as its governorship and deputy governorship candidates in the election.

Haruna also stated that the commission was already reprinting ballot papers and results sheets for the exercise.

He said that the action was taken in compliance with the judgment of the Federal High Court, Abuja, delivered on July 22 in Suit No. FHC/ABJ/CS/344/2026 between SDP and Ajala against INEC.

Haruna noted the court had ordered the commission to forthwith recognise, accept, upload, process and publish the name and particulars of Ajala as the SDP candidate for the governorship election.

“Consequently, the ballot papers for the election, scheduled to hold on Saturday, Aug. 15, are being reproduced to reflect this addition, bringing to 15 the total number of political parties contesting the election.

“The result sheets for the election are also being reproduced alongside the ballot papers to reflect the inclusion of the SDP candidate,” he said.

Haruna stated that the reproduced ballot papers would arrive in Osun on Aug. 13 and would, on the same day, be moved to the commission’s local government area offices across the state, in line with its standard distribution procedure ahead of the election.

“INEC assures political parties, candidates and the general public of its commitment to conducting a free, fair, and credible election in Osun,’’ he said.

World.title: Groups reject Foreign Aid Bill, urge Senate to withdraw it
World.content:
Senate

ABUJA — Five human rights organisations have called on the National Assembly and the Federal Government to withdraw the Foreign Aids (Regulation, Transparency and Disclosure) Bill, 2026 (SB. 1034), warning that its provisions could restrict civic space and undermine the work of human rights defenders and civil society organisations.

The organisations are the Nigerian Human Rights Defenders Network (NHRDN), Partnership for Justice, Front Line Defenders (FLD), West African Human Rights Defenders Network (WAHRDN) and Protection International (PI).

In a joint statement issued on Wednesday, the groups said the bill, sponsored by Senator Ibrahim Hassan Dankwambo (PDP, Gombe North), had passed second reading in the Senate in July.

They said the proposed legislation seeks to establish a Foreign Aid Regulatory Commission (FARC) with powers to register, inspect, audit, sanction and suspend or shut down organisations receiving foreign grants, donations or technical assistance.

According to the organisations, the proposed regulatory framework could affect independent civic groups, human rights defenders, legal aid providers and humanitarian organisations operating in Nigeria.

They argued that the bill was inconsistent with Nigeria’s commitments under the fourth cycle of the Universal Periodic Review (UPR), particularly recommendations relating to creating a safe and enabling environment for human rights defenders and civil society organisations.

The groups also noted that Nigeria is a candidate for election to the United Nations Human Rights Council for the 2027-2029 term, saying the country’s candidacy should be accompanied by stronger domestic protection of human rights defenders.

The organisations raised concerns over several provisions of the proposed legislation.

They said Section 6(1), which requires foreign aid to be registered within 30 days of receipt, could create difficulties for emergency funding, including legal defence, relocation assistance and support for survivors of rights violations.

The groups also criticised Sections 7 and 8, which provide for public disclosure of implementing partners and funded activities through a national register.

They argued that public disclosure of information involving human rights defenders, survivors, witnesses and individuals involved in sensitive documentation could expose them to security risks.

The organisations further raised concerns over Section 11, which requires foreign-funded activities to align with Nigeria’s national development plans and priorities.

They described the provision as broad and potentially capable of affecting organisations working on human rights, land and environmental rights, and support for vulnerable communities.

The groups also questioned the need for the proposed FARC, arguing that some of its functions could overlap with existing institutions, including the Corporate Affairs Commission (CAC), Special Control Unit Against Money Laundering (SCUML), Federal Inland Revenue Service (FIRS) and Nigerian Financial Intelligence Unit (NFIU).

The organisations called on the Senate, its leadership and the Federal Government to immediately withdraw the bill.

They also urged the authorities to ensure that any future legislation regulating civic space and foreign funding complies with the Constitution, the UN Declaration on Human Rights Defenders and Nigeria’s international human rights obligations.

The groups called for meaningful consultation with civil society organisations and human rights defenders in developing any future regulatory framework.

They also demanded explicit legal protection for confidential information concerning human rights defenders, survivors, witnesses and other at-risk individuals receiving support through foreign funding.

The organisations further called for an expedited framework for emergency and protection-related funding, including legal, medical, psychosocial and relocation support for defenders at risk.

They urged the government to reaffirm constitutional guarantees on freedom of association, expression and assembly.

While acknowledging the importance of transparency in the use of foreign funding, the organisations said regulatory mechanisms should not be used to restrict legitimate human rights activities.

They urged the National Assembly to withdraw SB. 1034 and ensure that any future regulatory framework protects the civic space and those working to defend human rights in Nigeria.

World.title: Police confirm recovery of 9 dead bodies in Niger community
World.content:
The Police Command in Niger has confirmed the recovery of nine dead bodies on the Wawa-Lumma road in Borgu Local Government Area of Niger.

The victims were suspected to have been killed by bandits while travelling on the road.

The Spokesperson for the Niger Police Command, SP Wasiu Abiodun, told the News Agency of Nigeria (NAN) on Wednesday in Minna that a team of police and military was dispatched and evacuated the bodies after information was received on Tuesday.

He said clearance operations had been intensified with a view to securing the area from any security threat.

“Police and military tactical teams were mobilised to the scene; the bodies recovered, while clearance operation was intensified to secure the area,” he said.

(NAN)

World.title: Arewa Youths laud Tinubu over creation of 10 division in Taraba
World.content:
By Femi Bolaji

JALINGO — Youths under the aegis of the Arewa Youth Assembly on Wednesday staged a rally in Jalingo, the Taraba State capital, to commend President Bola Tinubu for the establishment of the 10 Division of the Nigerian Army in the state.

Addressing journalists during the procession, the spokesperson for the group, Aliyu Mohammad Sani, described the development as a strategic intervention that would strengthen security operations in Taraba and the wider North-East region.

Sani said the establishment of the division demonstrated the Federal Government’s commitment to addressing security concerns affecting communities in the region.

He said, “This division is a fortress for Taraba and a shield for the entire North-East. For too long, our communities cried out for a force that understood our landscape, our fears and our hopes, and Mr President answered that call.”

He also commended the Federal Government for the recent increase in the salaries of military personnel, describing it as a morale booster for troops serving in frontline areas.

“It tells every man and woman on the front line that their sacrifice is seen and their blood is honoured,” he said.

Sani also commended the Chief of Defence Staff and the Chief of Army Staff for their efforts toward strengthening the country’s security architecture.

He said the establishment of the division had given residents renewed confidence in ongoing efforts to address insecurity.

Also speaking, the spokesperson for the Taraba People’s Movement, Comrade Umar Sani Bello, said the solidarity march was organised to convey the appreciation of residents to the Federal Government for the establishment of the military formation.

Bello said the development had renewed hope for improved security in the region, adding that the people of Taraba were ready to collaborate with the Nigerian Army and other security agencies to enhance security operations in the state.

World.title: Birth registration: NPC, UNICEF unite to give every child legal identity
World.content:
By Chioma Obinna & Rotimi Ojomoyela

The National Population Commission (NPC), National Identity Management Commission (NIMC), Association of Local Governments of Nigeria (ALGON) and the United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF) have intensified efforts to ensure that every Nigerian child is registered at birth and given a legal identity from the earliest stage of life.



The stakeholders are pushing for stronger integration of birth registration with primary healthcare services, greater decentralisation of registration centres to local communities and seamless interoperability between civil registration and national identity systems.



The renewed push is aimed particularly at newborns and children under one, with stakeholders stressing that timely birth registration can serve as the gateway to a child’s access to healthcare, education, social protection and other essential services.

The initiative forms part of efforts to strengthen Nigeria’s civil registration and vital statistics system and close the gap that has left millions of children without proof of legal identity.



At a media dialogue on birth registration for children under one year, UNICEF Child Protection Specialist, Mr. Denis Onoise, said the challenge was not simply about parents failing to register their children, but also about removing barriers that make registration difficult for families.



Onoise identified inadequate registration centres, long distances to service points, language barriers, inefficient registration processes and insufficient financial, human and material resources among factors limiting access to civil registration services.



He said: “The main challenges to accelerate civil registration and legal identity in Nigeria include limited accessibility to civil registration services, inadequate number of registration centres and associated long distances, language barriers, inefficient registration processes, and insufficient financial, human capacity and material resources.”



According to him, families also bear indirect costs, including transportation, time away from work and repeated journeys to registration points.



“The problem is compounded in hard-to-reach areas and among disadvantaged population groups,” he added.



The stakeholders, however, are seeking to turn the challenge into an opportunity by connecting birth registration with the country’s broader identity management system.



Under the proposed stronger collaboration, NPC would oversee birth and death registration, while NIMC would facilitate the linkage of registered births to the national identity database and prompt assignment of the National Identification Number (NIN).



Local governments would play a critical role by bringing registration services closer to families through ward and community-level registration points and integrating birth registration into primary healthcare services.



The approach is expected to reduce the burden on parents and ensure that registration becomes part of routine services provided when a child is born or taken to a health facility.



The partnership also involved UNICEF, which provides technical, financial and technological support, while Barnksforte Technologies Limited supports the development and deployment of the electronic civil registration and vital statistics system.



The stakeholders particularly advocated the integration of birth registration into primary healthcare, where mothers and newborns already interact with the health system.



Under the proposed model, birth notification at a health facility or community level would trigger the registration process, followed by issuance of a birth certificate and linkage with the national identity system.



This, they said, would make birth registration less dependent on parents making separate journeys to registration centres.



The strategy is also expected to improve the accuracy and timeliness of population data required for planning healthcare, education, social protection and other government programmes.



The stakeholders said birth registration goes beyond obtaining a certificate.



According to Onoise birth record establishes a child’s identity, including name, sex, place and date of birth, and provides the foundation for recognition before the law.



He said without legal identity, children may face difficulties proving their age or identity and can become more vulnerable to exclusion from education, healthcare, social protection and justice systems.



In his presentation, he further noted that an estimated 24.8 million Nigerian children under five have been registered.



Such children, it warned, may also face increased vulnerability to child marriage, trafficking, child labour, abuse, exploitation and family separation.



He said stakeholders are also relying on digitalisation to expand coverage and improve efficiency.

He explained that: “An interoperable digital civil registration system would enable registration records to be securely shared across relevant government systems while maintaining data protection and confidentiality.



“The approach is expected to reduce duplication, improve data quality and make it easier to track births from notification through registration, certificate issuance and identity enrolment.”



He however, acknowledged that gaps remain.



He noted that health-facility interoperability had stalled in some areas, with none of 371 targeted facilities live at the time of the assessment, while the birth notification pipeline was yet to record notifications in the reporting year.



There was also a significant gap between registrations and certificates issued, with 443,162 registrations compared with 120,469 certificates issued.



He further noted that parents remain key in the reforms being proposed.



He stressed that government systems alone cannot achieve universal birth registration.



Parents and caregivers remain central to ensuring that every birth is registered promptly.



He urged parents to take advantage of registration services when available at health facilities, local government offices and community registration points, while calling on traditional and religious leaders, women’s groups, young people and the media to strengthen public awareness.



He also called for stronger domestic financing, recruitment of permanent registrars, improved coordination among agencies and sustained community mobilisation.

He explained that the overall objective was to make birth registration a simple, accessible and routine part of every child’s entry into life, ensuring that no child grows up without a recognised identity.

World.title: Osun election: Adeleke’s campaign spokesman threatens N10bn suit against Fadahunsi
World.content:
Pelumi Olajengbesi, a campaign spokesman for Governor Ademola Adeleke’s re-election, has threatened a ₦10bn suit against the lawmaker representing Osun East Senatorial District, Francis Fadahunsi, “for defamation and injurious falsehood”.

In a letter dated August 12, 2026 and addressed to the lawmaker by Olajengbesi’s lawyer, Hammed Lasisi, Esq., Olajengbesi considered certain statements made by Fadahunsi about him during live television interviews on Viable TV on 2nd July 2026 and Channels Television’s Politics Today on 11th August 2026 as malicious and injurious to his personality.



Olajengbesi demanded an immediate retraction of the statements and an unequivocal public apology within 24 hours, after which legal proceedings would be instituted.



The letter read, “On 2nd July 2026, our Client’s attention was drawn to a live interview granted by you and aired on Viable TV, which was subsequently reproduced, republished and widely disseminated through Facebook, TikTok, WhatsApp, X, Instagram and other social and digital media platforms.



“During the said interview, you launched a direct attack on the identity, character and reputation of our Client by stating, among other things, that our Client was “not even from the same Ijebu-Jesha” and was “from somewhere in Ogun State.” You further accused him of “using thugs, Eiye and Aye.”



“These statements directly questioned our Client’s identity and origin as a son of Ijebu-Jesa and, more gravely, imputed that he sponsors, associates with and/or deploys thugs and members of the Eiye and Aye cult groups in furtherance of his political activities.



“Again, on 11th August 2026, during your live appearance on Channels Television’s Politics Today, you made another direct statement concerning our Client while commenting on the late Ajayi Aderogba, also known as Rogba, to wit: ‘Rogba is an Eiye man sponsored by Barr. Olajengbesi terrorising the whole … my own territory up and down through all these Eiye and Aye.’



“The natural, ordinary and unmistakable meaning conveyed by the above statement is that our Client sponsors, finances, supports and/or patronises members of the Eiye and Aye cult groups and deploys them to terrorise members of the public.”

Olajengbesi denied these allegations as false, defamatory and gravely injurious to his personal, professional and political reputation.

“The allegation of sponsoring cultists and persons engaged in acts of terror is particularly serious, as it imputes criminality and conduct wholly incompatible with our Client’s standing as a legal practitioner, public figure and candidate for elective office.



Olajengbesi said he has never sponsored, financed, supported, patronised or otherwise provided resources to any cult group or its members for criminal, political or other unlawful activities. Neither has he authorised any person to terrorise, intimidate or attack members of the public on his behalf.



Olajengbesi demanded that Fadahunsi retract the defamatory statements through the same media and platforms by which they were published and/or disseminated, and publish an unequivocal and unreserved public apology through appropriate national media and social media platforms.



Olajengbesi’s lawyer said that if he fails to do so within 24 hours, he will approach the court to compel Fadahunsi to pay ₦10,000,000,000.00 (Ten Billion Naira) as general and aggravated damages for defamation and injurious falsehood.

World.title: INEC reprints Osun ballot papers, result sheets to accommodate SDP candidate
World.content:
By Omeiza Ajayi

ABUJA: The Independent National Electoral Commission INEC said it has commenced the reproduction of ballot papers for the Osun State Governorship Election to accommodate the candidate of the Social Democratic Party SDP, Dr Francis Olugbenga Ajala, and his running mate, Faseke Babajimi Oladipo, who have now been added to the ballot.

In a statement signed by the National Commissioner and Chairman, Information and Voter Education Committee at INEC, Mohammed Kudu Haruna, the Commission said the action was taken in compliance with the judgment of the Federal High Court, Abuja, delivered on 22nd July 2026 in Suit No.

FHC/ABJ/CS/344/2026, in a matter between the Social Democratic Party and Dr Francis Olugbenga Ajala on one hand, and INEC on the other.

According to the statement, the court had ordered the Commission to forthwith recognise, accept, upload, process and publish the name and particulars of Dr Ajala as the candidate of the SDP for the election.

“The Commission wishes to inform the public that the reproduced ballot papers will arrive in Osun State on Thursday, 13th August 2026, and will, same day, be moved to Local Government Area offices across the State, in line with its standard distribution procedure ahead of the election,” the statement read.

With the addition of the SDP candidate, the total number of political parties contesting the governorship election, scheduled for Saturday, 15th August 2026, now stands at 15.

INEC noted that the result sheets for the election are also being reproduced alongside the ballot papers to reflect the inclusion of the SDP candidate.

The Commission assured political parties, candidates and the general public of its commitment to conducting a free, fair and credible election in Osun State.

World.title: UNICEF Seeks N1.2bn Nutrition Funding for Katsina
World.content:
Francis Sardauna in Katsina

The United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF) has called on the Katsina State Government to increase its investment in child nutrition by allocating N1.2 billion to the Child Nutrition Fund in the 2027 budget.

The Chief of UNICEF Field Office, Kano, Mr. Shafeeq Ur-Rehman, made the request when he led a delegation on a courtesy visit to Katsina State Governor, Dikko Umaru Radda at the Government House weekend.

Ur-Rehman said the proposed N1.2 billion contribution by the state would be matched by UNICEF to strengthen interventions aimed at tackling malnutrition among children and women in the state.

He said the funding would support the procurement of Multiple Micronutrient Supplements for pregnant women, as well as Ready-to-Use Therapeutic Food (RUTF) and other essential commodities for children under five suffering from severe wasting.

He commended the Radda administration for its consistent contribution to the Child Nutrition Fund, describing Katsina as one of the few states in Nigeria that had sustained its financial commitment to the fund over the years.

The UNICEF official stressed the need for increased investment in nutrition, particularly as the state continues to confront the challenge of child malnutrition.

He also disclosed that Katsina State was participating in a global pilot of the revised World Health Organisation (WHO) guidelines for the prevention and management of severe wasting in children.

Nigeria, he said, was one of only five countries selected globally for the pilot, which is currently being implemented in 10 local government areas of Katsina State.

Ur-Rehman said: “Katsina’s participation in this pilot is important because the lessons from here will not only contribute to nutrition programming in Nigeria but will also provide useful evidence for the global response to child malnutrition.”

He further commended Governor Radda for making Katsina the first and only state in Nigeria so far to appropriate N270 million for the implementation of a SMART Nutrition Survey.

He said the survey would generate reliable and timely nutrition data to identify vulnerable communities, guide resource allocation and strengthen interventions targeting women and children.

Ur-Rehman reaffirmed UNICEF’s readiness to support the state in conducting the Rapid SMART/SMART+ Nutrition Survey, stressing that evidence-based data remained critical to effectively addressing malnutrition.

Responding, Governor Radda pledged to include UNICEF’s additional N1.2 billion funding request in the state’s 2027 budget “despite the financial constraints facing the government”.

“We are not doing it for you; we are doing it for our people,” the governor said, assuring UNICEF of the state government’s continued commitment to interventions capable of producing measurable improvements in the lives of residents.

Radda said his administration had approved the release of N500 million as counterpart funding for the Child Nutrition Fund and described the investment as part of efforts to improve nutrition, healthcare and other development indicators in the state.

He said the collaboration between Katsina State and UNICEF had yielded encouraging results, particularly in the treatment of child malnutrition, adding that the number of children requiring treatment at stabilisation centres and outpatient treatment sites had begun to decline.

World.title: INEC Includes SDP Candidate, Ajala, On Ballot for Osun Guber Poll
World.content:
Adedayo Akinwale in Abuja

The Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) has announced that the candidate of the Social Democratic Party (SDP) for the Osun State governorship election, Dr. Francis Ajala and his running mate, Faseke Oladipo, have been added to the ballot for the election on Saturday.

INEC National Commissioner and Chairman, Information and Voter Education Committee, Mohammed Haruna, in a statement explained that the action was taken in compliance with the judgment of the Federal High Court, Abuja, delivered on July 22, 2026 in Suit No. FHC/ABJ/CS/344/2026, between SDP and Ajala on the one hand and INEC on the other.

He recalled that the court had ordered the commission to forthwith recognise, accept, upload, process and publish the name and particulars of Ajala as the candidate of SDP.

Haruna noted: “Consequently, the ballot papers for the election, scheduled to hold on Saturday, 15th August 2026, are being reproduced to reflect this addition, bringing to 15, the total number of political parties contesting the election.

“The result sheets for the election are also being reproduced alongside the ballot papers to reflect the inclusion of the SDP candidate.”

The commission informed the public that the reproduced ballot papers would arrive in Osun State on Thursday, August 13, 2026, and would, same day, be moved to local government area offices across the state, in line with its standard distribution procedure ahead of the election.

The commission assured political parties, candidates and the general public of its commitment to conducting a free, fair and credible election in Osun State.

World.title: Accord Appeals to EU for Urgent Intervention Over Rising Tension Ahead of Osun Poll
World.content:
* Peter Obi condemns threat-laden remarks, urges retraction, peaceful election

Sunday Aborisade in Abuja

Accord Party on Wednesday appealed to the European Union (EU) for urgent diplomatic intervention to de-escalate rising political tension in Osun State, condemn alleged electoral violence and intimidation, and help ensure a free, fair, credible, transparent and peaceful governorship election scheduled for Saturday.

The appeal was contained in a letter dated August 12, 2026, and addressed to the Ambassador and Head of the EU Delegation to Nigeria and ECOWAS, Gautier Migot, by Accord National Chairman, Chief Maxwell Mgbudem.

The party said the August 15 election was particularly significant as the last major off-cycle governorship election before the 2027 general election, warning that its conduct and outcome would have far-reaching implications for public confidence in Nigeria’s democratic institutions and electoral process.

Accord alleged that the political atmosphere in Osun had become increasingly tense amid reports of violence, intimidation, arrests, harassment and what it described as the deployment of state institutions and security agencies in ways capable of undermining political competition.

According to the party, at least 29 people had reportedly lost their lives, while several others sustained gunshot injuries in incidents linked to the political environment in the state.

It further alleged that more than 60 of its members and supporters had been arrested and detained in Abuja and Nasarawa State under circumstances it said required urgent clarification and independent scrutiny.

The party also raised concerns over the reported searches of residences of senior Osun State Government officials and the arrest and detention of some officials, including the Secretary to the State Government, as well as the reported freezing of the state government’s bank accounts by the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC).

Although the affected officials were later released and the accounts reportedly unfrozen following public concerns and presidential intervention, Accord said the incidents had heightened apprehension over the perceived use of state institutions in the political environment.

The party stressed that it did not seek to obstruct legitimate law-enforcement or anti-corruption activities, but urged that such powers be exercised impartially, transparently and in accordance with due process, particularly during an election period.

Accord’s appeal to the EU came against the backdrop of its demand for the immediate arrest and prosecution of Senator Francis Adenigba Fadahunsi, representing Osun East Senatorial District, over a viral video in which the party alleged that he incited supporters to kill Accord Party members and supporters in Ijesaland.

The party described the reported remarks as outrageous and reprehensible, arguing that they had further escalated political tension only days before the governorship poll.

It called on the Inspector-General of Police (IGP) and the Director-General of the Department of State Services (DSS) to investigate the senator’s alleged conduct and take appropriate action, while urging security agencies to protect all political actors and citizens.

The party also appealed for the immediate release of its members allegedly detained in Abuja and Nasarawa, insisting that their continued detention could prevent them from participating in Saturday’s election.

The party urged the EU, the United States, United Kingdom, African Union (AU) and ECOWAS to closely monitor developments in Osun and condemn actions capable of undermining democratic participation.

In a related intervention, the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) presidential candidate for the 2027 election, Peter Obi, has condemned what he described as the “inflammatory comments and threat-laden rhetoric” attributed to Fadahunsi.

Obi demanded an immediate retraction and apology, stressing that political leaders had a constitutional and moral responsibility to promote peace, democratic norms and unity.

He urged security agencies to monitor inflammatory statements and guarantee equal protection for voters, election officials and citizens before, during and after the poll.

According to Obi, the democratic mandate belongs to the people and no individual, irrespective of political office or status, should attempt to influence the electorate through fear, intimidation or coercion.

In its appeal, Accord urged the EU to use its diplomatic influence to encourage political parties, candidates and their supporters to reject violence, inflammatory rhetoric and intimidation.

It also called for strict neutrality and professionalism by security agencies and public institutions, while urging the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) to discharge its responsibilities independently, impartially and transparently.

The party further sought credible domestic and international observation, accountability for perpetrators of political violence and respect for lawful mechanisms for resolving electoral disputes.

Accord said it was not asking the EU to take sides, but to support democratic principles, political pluralism, rule of law and the right of Osun voters to freely choose their leaders.

It warned that the election represented a critical test of Nigeria’s democratic credentials, insisting that “preventive diplomacy” was needed before violence or institutional distrust could cause irreversible damage.

The party said a peaceful and credible election would strengthen confidence in Nigeria’s democracy ahead of 2027, while any perception of violence, intimidation or institutional manipulation could deepen public distrust.

Accord concluded by urging all stakeholders to allow the people of Osun State to determine their political future through a peaceful, transparent and credible electoral process.

World.title: NHRC Demands Immediate Suspension, Arrest of Fadahunsi Over Alleged Kill Order
World.content:
Michael Olugbode in Abuja

The National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) has called for the immediate suspension and arrest of Senator Francis Fadahunsi, representing Osun East Senatorial District, over alleged inflammatory remarks in a viral video ahead of the August 15, 2026 Osun governorship election.

The commission, led by the Executive Secretary, Chief Tony Ojukwu, said the remarks attributed to Fadahunsi amounted to incitement to murder, electoral violence and voter intimidation.

According to the NHRC, the senator allegedly instructed supporters to kill members of the Accord Party whenever they encountered them and warned that Accord members should not be allowed to vote, even if they possessed voter cards.

Ojukwu described the alleged statement as “a licence to kill”, warning that authorities must act before violence occurs.

“This is not politics. This is a licence to kill. A public officer who tells citizens to murder other citizens because of party affiliation must not be allowed to remain in office for one more day,” Ojukwu said.

The NHRC called on the Senate leadership to suspend Fadahunsi immediately, pending investigation, while urging the police and DSS to arrest, investigate and prosecute him in accordance with the law.

The commission also directed political party chairmen to instruct their members to refrain from hateful, inciting, intimidating or violent statements ahead of elections, adding that candidates or party supporters who violate such directives should be reported to law enforcement for prosecution.

The NHRC urged residents of Osun State to remain peaceful and report threats to the appropriate authorities. It said it has established a situation room to document and respond to human rights and electoral incidents during the election period.

The allegations against Fadahunsi require urgent investigation and due process, particularly given the seriousness of the alleged call for violence.

World.title: Within the Room, Again: The Variable Nigeria Finally Admitted
World.content:
Clifford Akpolo

About a year ago, I wrote from Brasília about the privilege of accompanying the Board of Nigerian Exchange Group (NGX Group) to meet President Bola Ahmed Tinubu. I argued then that much of the commentary on Nigeria’s economy suffered from omitted variable bias: that the story being told left out variables that changed its meaning. Last Thursday, at the Aso Villa, as the Board and management of Nigerian Exchange Group made another strategic visit to the president, I sat in the room again and watched a different omission being corrected, not in the critics’ model this time, but in the nation’s own.

For decades, Nigeria’s national economic conversation has been conducted in a narrow vocabulary: oil production, foreign reserves, inflation and the exchange rate. Budgets rose and fell with the price of crude; policy debate orbited the naira. The capital market, the mechanism through which successful economies finance enterprises, build infrastructure and distribute ownership and prosperity, was, at best, a footnote. In model terms, it was the omitted variable: present in the economy, absent from the specification.

What I witnessed on Thursday was that variable being formally admitted. The capital market is no longer a spectator subject in Nigeria. It was discussed at the highest table in the land in the same breath as fiscal and monetary policy: as an instrument of national strategy.

The evidence that earned it that seat is not rhetorical. “The picture today is that when you took office in 2023, the total value of stocks listed in Nigeria was just shy of N30 trillion. Today, Mr President, that figure is N160 trillion. By the end of this year, with the listings that we are seeing in our market, we expect that figure to rise to N230 trillion,” Group MD/CEO, NGX Group, Mr. Temi Popoola, told the president.

The All-Share Index tells the same story, rising from 52,000 points to 244,000. A sceptic will say asset prices are not the economy. I agree: a single indicator proves nothing. But markets are forward-looking aggregators of information; they price not simply what is, but what millions of independent decisions expect to come.

When domestic institutions, pension funds, retail investors and foreign portfolio managers converge on the same directional bet over three years, it deserves attention. That conviction has been expressed through market infrastructure built collectively by the Exchange, the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), Central Securities Clearing System (CSCS) and market operators, strengthened by June’s transition to T+1 settlement and validated through a Central Bank-led banking recapitalisation funded roughly 75 per cent from domestic resources.

This is no longer sentiment. It is revealed preference, at scale. That is what an admitted variable looks like: measured, priced, trusted. The Governor of the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN), Mr. Olayemi Cardoso, made the point from the regulator’s side of the table, recalling the doubt that greeted the recapitalisation announcement: “There was a lot of scepticism. People didn’t think it was possible. And now it was done very successfully; close to 75 per cent of the total was domestic resources. In the past, it was the other way around.” He was generous enough to add that NGX was up to the task and that the SEC played a major role in a seamless exercise, reinforcing the broader point: admitted variables are the work of an ecosystem, not an institution.

This is where the significance of NGX Group’s role becomes clearer. Economic reform creates the conditions for confidence, but confidence alone does not build factories, recapitalise banks or finance infrastructure. Someone has to convert that confidence into investable opportunities and mobilise savings into productive capital. That is the work of the capital market. Over the past three years, NGX and its ecosystem have increasingly occupied that space, helping translate the credibility created by reform into actual capital formation. NGX and Popoola’s role has been to keep that bridge between policy and markets visible, bringing concrete market mechanisms and opportunities to the highest level of economic decision-making.

What struck me most in the room, however, was not the data. It was how naturally the conversation flowed through it. “I can see the excitement in the room. All I can do is to celebrate you all today,” the president began, before offering the line that distilled the shift: “Nigeria can build a nation of prosperity by itself. If the stock market is doing well, then we are doing well.”

He then turned from celebration to consequence: what does this confidence make possible for the manufacturer seeking expansion capital, for the entrepreneur with a bold idea and for the millions of workers whose pensions participate in this growth? That is the right question.

Market performance is an intermediate variable; the dependent variable is the welfare of ordinary Nigerians. The clearest proof that the variable is now in the model came in a single announcement. Popoola had tabled four priorities for NGX Group: the privatisation and listing of commercially viable government assets; the domestic or dual listing of leading Nigerian companies; clarity on the capital gains tax treatment of listed securities; and greater use of capital-market instruments to finance infrastructure. Before the meeting ended, the president went on to disclose that NNPC Limited would be reformed and listed on the capital market.

That is consequential. When a state chooses to finance, discipline and distribute ownership of one of its most important commercial assets through the market, the market has ceased to be a footnote. A listed NNPC means audited accounts, market discipline and, most importantly, the opportunity for Nigerians themselves, directly and through their pension funds, to own a share of the national patrimony. It converts aspiration into presidential commitment.

The conversation ran wider than the delegation. The Minister of Finance and Coordinating Minister of the Economy, Mr Taiwo Oyedele, described the capital market as “one of the fastest ways to create wealth for millions of Nigerians,” challenging NGX and the SEC to target a trillion-dollar market. His sharpest observation concerned the next generation: “Many of our young people invest their money in virtual assets and gambling, whereas you can make more money from the capital market.”

NGX Group Chairman, Alhaji Umaru Kwairanga, matched the ambition with a timeline, telling the president that a one-trillion-dollar economy is achievable before 2030. He also recalled a recent panel where he attributed the market’s turnaround to leadership and consistency of reform: two inputs no market can generate for itself.

Let me be careful about what I am claiming, because precision matters. Nigeria’s cost-of-living challenge is real, and no index level pays a family’s bills. Every reform leaves residuals, and honest analysis names them. But the fairest answer to the transmission question, how any of this reaches the man on the street, came from the CBN Governor himself.

“Without stability, you don’t get the investments you are talking about. And without the investments, you don’t get growth.” Stability, investment, growth, welfare: that is the transmission mechanism. The boom-and-bust cycles of the past, marked by apparent stability followed by devaluation and then another cycle, were symptoms of a system whose plumbing, in Cardoso’s phrase, had never been done. The plumbing is the point.

Markets cannot create macroeconomic stability by themselves. Nor can monetary and fiscal policy, however well designed, deliver broad-based prosperity without mechanisms through which capital reaches productive enterprise. The capital market is part of that machinery: the bridge between savings and investment, between institutional capital and enterprise, between national assets and national ownership. That is why Thursday mattered beyond the day’s announcements.

The deepest significance of the meeting may be permanence. The truest compliment to any reform is that it is built to outlast its authors, a standard the president has set for himself in speaking of foundations for long-term, sustainable growth. The capital market’s new place in the national conversation is exactly that kind of achievement: institutional, not episodic.

Markets reward credible policy, disciplined institutions and consistent regulation. A market admitted to the heart of national strategy can serve every government that comes after. That is precisely what makes its admission an act of nation-building rather than a moment in a news cycle.

But being admitted is only the beginning. The task ahead is to make it irreversible: listing the assets, simplifying access, protecting investors, drawing young Nigerians from speculation towards ownership, deepening domestic participation, attracting long-term international capital, and building the bridge between policy and markets that we, as capital-market professionals, exist to build.

Nigeria’s future is still being written from within the room. The difference, one year on, is that the capital market is no longer waiting outside it.

* Akpolo, an economist and brand communication professional, is Head of Group Communications and Partnerships, NGX Group

World.title: Sara Foundation Prepares 700 Graduates for NJFP, Refers 696 Candidates
World.content:
Funmi Ogundare

Sara Foundation Africa has equipped 700 young Nigerian graduates with workplace-ready skills and referred 696 qualified participants into the candidate pool of the Nigerian Jubilee Fellows Programme (NJFP), following an intensive employability readiness initiative conducted in partnership with the Office of the Vice-President.

The Founder, Sara Foundation Africa, Sarah Inem Kalu, disclosed that the initiative, delivered through its Graduate Journey Pathway (GJP), attracted more than 1,000 applications within one week, exceeding its initial target of preparing and referring 500 graduates for the Federal Government’s flagship graduate placement programme.

The programme was implemented in collaboration with the Senior Special Assistant to the President on Delivery and Coordination, with the objective of strengthening the pathway between education and employment while preparing young graduates for opportunities in Nigeria’s evolving labour market.

According to her, several participants have already progressed to interviews, psychometric assessments and final-stage recruitment processes, with some securing placements with host organisations through the NJFP.

The five-day programme, delivered through 10 live virtual learning sessions, focused on practical workplace readiness rather than theoretical training.

Participants were trained in aptitude and psychometric assessment preparation, professional CV development, interview preparation, communication and presentation, LinkedIn optimisation and professional branding, artificial intelligence tools for workplace productivity, emotional intelligence, teamwork, goal setting, career planning and progression.

Kalu said the virtual format enabled graduates from different parts of Nigeria to participate while ensuring that the programme remained aligned with NJFP eligibility requirements, including graduation period, National Identification Number ( NIN) verification and completion of the National Youth Service Corps ( NYSC) programme.

She explained that the initiative demonstrated the impact that could be achieved when government and private-sector organisations collaborate to create practical pathways from education to employment.

She stated: “Talent is everywhere across Africa, but opportunity is not. At Sara Foundation Africa, we exist to bridge that gap by creating practical pathways that prepare young people for success in today’s digital economy.”

Kalu said the foundation measured the success of its programmes not merely by the number of people trained, but by the opportunities created and lives transformed through access to employment and further learning.

She added that the NJFP initiative formed part of the foundation’s broader commitment to digital inclusion and workforce development across Africa.

The founder noted that the GJP initiative was delivered using its learning and development infrastructure, Train AI, an AI workplace intelligence platform.

She added that its workforce development efforts were anchored on three flagship programmes; CAP, FLIP and Education Journey Pathways (EJP), designed to provide young people with access to digital education, mentorship, employability skills and structured progression opportunities.

“We currently work across 11 African countries in partnership with more than 35 universities, with a reach of about 6,000 Africans,” she said.

Also speaking on the partnership, the Senior Special Assistant to the President on Delivery and Coordination, Akubo Adegbe, noted that employers had a role beyond simply recruiting skilled workers.

“They are also partners in developing the quality of Nigeria’s workforce. Employers are not just consumers of talent, they are co-producers of workforce quality. Nigeria’s workforce transformation cannot be driven by government alone,” he said.

World.title: Insecurity: AWPUF Accuses Alia of Abandoning Agatu, Hails Council Chairman Over Army Battalion
World.content:
Onuminya Innocent

The Agatu West Peace and Unity Forum, AWPUF, has accused Benue State Governor, Rev. Fr. Hyacinth Alia, of abandoning Agatu Local Government Area to the mercy of armed herders, saying claims that the area has been “reclaimed” are far from the truth.

The group was reacting to a report published in Idoma Voice Newspaper on August 5, 2026, headlined _“We Have Reclaimed Agatu From Armed Herders”which was credited to the Agatu Local Government Council Chairman, Ambassador Melvin James Ejeh.

In a statement issued in Agatu and signed by its President, Comrade Ebi Lucky, AWPUF said the position of the council chairman does not reflect the reality on ground. According to the forum, 15 villages sacked by repeated attacks remain deserted.

“To set the record straight, the fifteen affected villages have not returned to their ancestral homes and farming activities are not taking place in those areas as claimed by the Agatu Local Government Council Chairman,” the statement read.

AWPUF further alleged that since the attacks began, Governor Alia has neither visited Agatu nor made any public comment on the killings. The forum described the silence as an indication that the LGA has been left on its own.

“Let us ask Mr. Governor: Is Agatu not part of the State? When did His Excellency ever comment on the killings of our dear people of Agatu since the consistent attacks by Fulani herders?” the group queried.

The forum said it has, since 2024, repeatedly called for the deployment of security operatives to Agatu Western Zone, but alleged that all appeals to the state government have been ignored. It claimed the only intervention was short-lived.

“It is pertinent to inform the public that the 25 soldiers deployed to Agatu Western Zone were redeployed back to Obagaji, the Agatu Local Government headquarters, within two weeks of their deployment,” AWPUF stated.

Despite its criticism of the state government, the forum commended the Agatu Council Chairman, Ambassador Ejeh, for facilitating the siting of an Army Battalion in the area. AWPUF said the move would strengthen security and boost community confidence.

The group lauded the chairman for what it described as “proactive steps that have brought relative peace to parts of the local government” and for providing logistics support to security agencies. It noted that hosting the battalion connects security to livelihood and could encourage displaced persons to return to their farms and markets.

While commending Chairman Ejeh, AWPUF urged the Benue State Government to take decisive action to end the killings and facilitate the safe return of displaced persons. “What we need are proactive measures to stop the incessant killings of our people. Crediting failed responsibility is not healthy in a true democratic setting,” Comrade Lucky said.

World.title: West African Regulators Intensify Move to Build Regional Fuel Pricing, Trading Hub
World.content:
*NMDPRA: Infrastructure, capital, data critical to price benchmark

*Lokpobiri: Deregulation has unlocked investment in Nigeria’s downstream

*Eyesan says rising refining capacity, oil output good for market integration

*Verheijen: Why refining capacity alone can’t guarantee energy security

*S&P advocates more liquidity to make regional benchmarks work

Emmanuel Addeh in Abuja

West African petroleum regulators Tuesday intensified efforts to establish an integrated regional refined petroleum products market capable of supporting credible pricing benchmarks and positioning the sub-region as a major fuel trading hub.

The push formed the central focus of the 2026 West African Refined Fuel Market (WAFRFM) Conference, organised by the West Africa Regulators Forum (WARF), the Nigerian Midstream and Downstream Petroleum Regulatory Authority (NMDPRA) and S&P Global Energy.

The conference, held under the theme: “Funding West Africa Infrastructure & Distribution to Create a Transparent Market for Regional Price Benchmarks,” brought together regulators, governments, refiners, traders, financial institutions, infrastructure investors and other industry stakeholders to deliberate on the development of the regional fuel market.

The discussions centred on the need to move beyond increased refining capacity to build the infrastructure, financing structures, regulatory systems, data architecture and market liquidity required to enable petroleum products to move efficiently across West Africa and allow prices to increasingly reflect regional market fundamentals.

Speaking at the conference, the Authority Chief Executive (ACE) of the NMDPRA, Mallam Umar Rabiu, said the region had made progress since the inaugural conference in 2025, but stressed that institutional developments must now be matched by investment and execution.

He said the 2025 conference had established a roadmap towards a West African refined products reference market, with emphasis on reliable refining capacity, stronger logistics and storage networks, interconnected ports, roads, rail and pipelines, harmonised standards, transparent market data and cross-border cooperation.

According to him, developments over the past year included the institutionalisation of regional regulatory cooperation through WARF, progress towards West African reference pricing and deeper collaboration with S&P Global Commodity Insights on market reporting and benchmark expertise.

However, Rabiu, who is the current chairman of WARF warned that a reference price alone could not create a trading hub.

“A reference price is not by itself a trading hub. A conference is not a market. Regulatory cooperation, important as it is, cannot substitute for the physical infrastructure, commercial liquidity, market information and operational excellence on which a credible trading hub must stand,” he said.

He identified infrastructure, capital, data and regulatory cooperation as critical foundations for creating a credible regional benchmark.

Rabiu pointed out that Africa has the resources, demand and increasingly the refining capacity, but needed to efficiently connect production to consumers through refineries, pipelines, storage terminals, jetties, ports, rail networks, roads, marine logistics, strategic reserves and digital trading platforms.

“The objective is not infrastructure for infrastructure’s sake. The objective is infrastructure that reduces the cost of moving energy, increases security of supply, improves inventory visibility, expands the number of credible market participants and creates the physical liquidity upon which transparent pricing depends,” he said.

Rabiu also urged investors to view the region’s infrastructure deficit as an opportunity, citing potential investments in pipelines, product transportation, storage, marine terminals, refinery expansion, road and rail logistics, gas infrastructure, digital commodity exchanges, product-tracking systems and integrated regional logistics corridors.

He noted, however, that capital would only flow into projects that were bankable, with predictable regulation, understood risks and sustainable returns. The NMDPRA chief also stressed the importance of operational efficiency, warning that infrastructure without operational excellence could create expensive bottlenecks.

“Our ports must become more efficient. Our terminals must improve turnaround times. Our pipelines and storage systems must operate safely and reliably. Our refineries must pursue sustained utilisation, reliability and competitive yields,” he said.

He further called for improved data transparency, noting that credible price discovery required sufficient transactions, willing participants, reliable reporting and confidence that market information reflected actual commercial activity. “Markets operate on information. Benchmarks operate on trust,” he said.

Also speaking, the Minister of State, Petroleum Resources (Oil), Senator Heineken Lokpobiri, said Nigeria’s deregulation of the midstream and downstream petroleum sectors had created renewed investor interest and opened opportunities for greater regional integration.

According to him, the federal government took a bold decision to completely deregulate the downstream sector, creating an environment capable of attracting investment and unlocking the potential of the industry.

“Before this government came, nobody had the courage to turn around the downstream. Not even the military leaders had the courage. But at the breaking point, he (President Bola Tinubu) took the boldest decision of completely deregulating.

“Today, the midstream and downstream are completely deregulated. That is why we are seeing renewed interest,” Lokpobiri emphasised.

The minister said Nigeria must look beyond its domestic market and position itself to serve the wider West African market, arguing that the region could benefit from the country’s growing refining capacity.

He stressed the importance of processing resources locally rather than exporting raw materials and subsequently importing refined products at significantly higher costs.

“We export our raw cashews. We export our raw agro-products outside. They refine them. We process them. And we buy them back ten times the price,” he said.

Lokpobiri said Nigeria should use its growing refining capacity to capture a larger share of the West African market, but noted that this would require a sustainable pricing mechanism and stronger collaboration among countries and regulators.

For her part, the Chief Executive of the Nigerian Upstream Petroleum Regulatory Commission (NUPRC), Oritsemeyiwa Eyesan, said developments across Nigeria’s oil and gas value chain were creating an opportunity for deeper regional market integration.

Eyesan pointed to the increase in refining capacity, rising crude oil production and improvements in the gas sector as evidence of significant changes in the Nigerian petroleum industry.

“We are seeing a spike in refining capacity. We are seeing Nigeria not only meet its refining needs, but attempt to also export. That is unprecedented,” she said.

She added that Nigeria’s gas industry was moving from a position of total deficit towards bridging the supply gap, while crude oil production had also increased. “We are now able to cross the barrier that OPEC has set for us. That, again, is unprecedented,” she said.

Eyesan explained that the next step was to close the loop by integrating West African petroleum markets, stressing that countries could no longer afford to operate in silos. “The West African market must be integrated. We can no longer afford to operate in silos,” she pointed out.

She called for integrated regulatory systems and appropriate infrastructure across the value chain, arguing that the region needed to build ready markets and systems that connected rather than isolated individual countries and industries.

Also speaking, the Special Adviser on Energy to the President, Olu Verheijen, said West Africa’s challenge was no longer primarily a question of resources or refining capacity, but whether the region could develop the systems required to efficiently move energy from where it is produced to where it is needed. “Refining capacity alone, as big as ours is, does not create energy security,” she said.

Verheijen said refined products could only deliver economic value when they could be financed, stored, transported and distributed reliably.

“A refined product only delivers economic value when it can be financed, stored, transported, and distributed reliably. Without infrastructure, supply remains stranded. Without transparent pricing, investors price uncertainty rather than opportunity,” she said.

She said the region needed pipelines, ports, storage facilities, coastal vessels, trucking networks and trading platforms, as well as greater access to trade and infrastructure finance.

Verheijen said Nigeria was increasingly refining the majority of the petrol consumed domestically, with imports falling significantly, while refined products were increasingly reaching markets outside the country.

She said the next phase should focus on connecting the growing supply with regional demand through infrastructure and transparent markets.

Head of Platts, S&P Global Energy, Vera Bleu, in her intervention, said significant progress had been made towards developing regional price references over the past year, but stressed that market participants themselves must create the liquidity required to make regional benchmarks credible.

She said S&P Global had expanded its regional pricing assessments, including more frequent updates for petrol and other refined products in response to increased market volatility.

“We can give the foundations, we can make the reference prices available. It’s time for everybody in this room to take bold steps to really bring them alive,” she said.

Bleu said the challenge was that market participants would naturally continue to gravitate towards established international benchmarks because of their liquidity.

“The reality is you will have to create them. We can give the foundations, we can make the reference prices available. It’s time for everybody in this room to take bold steps to really bring them alive,” she said.

Deputy Governor, Operations, Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN), Emem Usoro, said a well-functioning and well-priced refined products market could create significant opportunities for the financial sector, particularly in mobilising long-term capital for refining, storage, transportation and other critical infrastructure.

She pointed out that such developments could strengthen capital markets, improve foreign exchange efficiency, boost intra-African trade and enhance investor confidence across the region.

World.title: Transfer news: Pirates links swirl as Polokwane coach speaks on Matuludi
World.content:
Polokwane City coach Willy Moloto has addressed the absence of star defender Thabang Matuludi from the matchday squad amid continued transfer speculation.

The 26-year-old right-back has attracted interest from several top clubs, including Orlando Pirates and Mamelodi Sundowns, in recent months. He was heavily linked with a move away from Polokwane City during the current transfer window.

However, Moloto insists Matuludi’s absence has nothing to do with the ongoing speculation surrounding his future.



“There’s no such thing. Every time people don’t see a player, they start with the talk,” Moloto told FARPost.

The Polokwane coach explained that Matuludi has been dealing with minor knocks after being involved with Bafana Bafana at the 2026 FIFA World Cup.
