World.title: Zhu Rongji, who drove China's 1990s economic reforms, has died at 97
World.content:
Zhu Rongji, who drove China's 1990s economic reforms, has died at 97

Enlarge this image toggle caption K.Y. Cheng/South China Morning Post via Getty Images K.Y. Cheng/South China Morning Post via Getty Images

Zhu Rongji, former premier of China, has died at age 97. The cause of death was given as illness, according to state media.

Zhu, an acerbic technocrat and a trained engineer, was renowned for far-reaching economic reforms throughout the 1990s that sought to transition China from the chaos of its post-Maoist years to a more global market-oriented financial system, without completely ceding the Communist Party's control over the economy.

Despite staying almost completely out of the public eye after retiring from the premiership in 2003, he remains both loved and reviled in the country indelibly shaped by him. His reform legacy remains contested in China; in freeing up the country's enormous labor and financial resources, he helped to create vast amounts of wealth over the next three decades while also seeding institutions with future vulnerabilities.

Sponsor Message

"From the point of view of a policymaker, [he] embraced the notion of a China whose economic system was more compatible with that of the West. And by compatible, I mean vastly reformed, more open, less state-dominated, very limited state intervention," said Charlene Barshefsky, a lawyer and former U.S. trade representative who sat across the negotiating table from Zhu over years-long talks to let China enter the World Trade Organization (WTO).

In order to join the WTO, China first needed to get preferential trading status with the United States — which in turn demanded hard concessions and that it open up its closed economy to American companies. Zhu was under huge pressure to find compromise, and he let his views be known.

Enlarge this image toggle caption Joyce Naltchayan/AFP via Getty Images Joyce Naltchayan/AFP via Getty Images

In 2000, the U.S. Senate voted to give China that preferential trading status, and the following year, China joined the WTO. The agreement was a windfall for the nascent Chinese economy. The country became an export powerhouse, and foreign businesses rushed to China to establish a foothold.

The 6 1/2-year process let Zhu show off his flinty personality, though he struck U.S. officials as inquisitive and flexible. "This was not talking points. It was a lot of give and take," said Kenneth Lieberthal, a China expert who was a national security adviser for then-President Bill Clinton. He met Zhu multiple times during the negotiations.

Sponsor Message

Zhu was born in 1928 in the city of Changsha, in China's Hunan province. He graduated from Beijing's Tsinghua University, where he was also chosen as president of the student union, with a degree in electrical engineering, the winter before the Communist Party won control over China. In October 1949, when the new Communist-led republic was founded, Zhu officially joined the Chinese Communist Party.

His blunt, say-it-like-it-is style got him in trouble

Zhu's father died before he was born, and his mother died when he was 9 years old. Being an orphan, the need to survive helped shape his strong personality: thick-skinned and extremely direct.

"My defining characteristic is independent thought," he told bureaucrats in 1987, right before becoming mayor of Shanghai. "I say what I think."

When Chinese troops fatally fired on pro-democracy protesters in Beijing's Tiananmen Square in 1989, Zhu did not issue the standard propaganda line denying the tragedy. "The event that occurred recently in Beijing is a historical fact, and historical facts cannot be covered up by anybody. The truth will always come out," he wrote in an essay published in a Shanghai newspaper.

His blunt, say-it-like-it-is style got him in serious trouble. In 1958, he was labeled an ideological "rightist" and briefly expelled from the party for criticizing Chairman Mao Zedong's economic policies, but managed to hold on to a job in state planning. In 1970, he was purged again during the Cultural Revolution and sent to do five years of manual labor at a party reeducation school.

Zhu was rehabilitated after Mao died in 1976 and Deng Xiaoping came to power as China's leader. Zhu then worked his way back up the bureaucratic ladder with the same pragmatism he had learned as an engineer.

"Regardless of what country your company is from, when you arrive in China, you should receive fair and equal treatment. I just want you to pay taxes," he joked in 1999 to an audience of American businessmen, explaining that China was open for foreign investment.

Sponsor Message

A career state planner, Zhu nevertheless quickly adjusted to the economic chaos of the 1990s, as China careened between capitalism and state-led socialism. As central bank governor, Zhu successfully tamed runaway inflation. While vice premier, he also led a dramatic centralization of the tax system that incentivized land sales and huge wealth creation, along with hugely unsustainable levels of debt.

After being appointed premier in 1998, he entered office with a bold promise: He would reform the indebted state banks within two years and inefficient state enterprises within three. That earned him both instant enemies and fans.

"No matter whether what lies ahead is a minefield or a bottomless abyss, I will carry out my duties until the last breath in my body," he vowed.

Zhu's most controversial legacy by far remains restructuring China's bloated state-owned enterprises. He axed smaller, inefficient companies, leaving an estimated 30 million state workers suddenly jobless.

Worker protests erupted all over China. Zhu had the willpower — or callousness, as his critics would say — to ignore them.

"The central government decided that the laid-off worker problem could just be ignored and forgotten," said Dorothy Solinger, a professor emeritus of political science at the University of California, Irvine, who studies migrant labor in China.

Zhu tried to offset the layoffs' impacts. He created a basic social welfare system that exists to this day and made steps to boost basic health care, which had crumbled in rural areas. But pockets of China, especially in the northeast region of the country, where workers were reliant on state employment in heavy industry sectors, never fully recovered economically.

"I think their children also have a problem because they miss out on the things that the better-off part of the population could do, such as hiring tutors or going on extracurricular activities, going to the better schools," said Solinger. "It's a growing underclass."

Sponsor Message

Zhu took the criticism in stride. Unlike most Communist leaders, who read off staid and carefully prepared scripts, he loved engaging with and ad-libbing to the press.

"He loved answering all the questions, no matter how tough or sensitive," remembered Rose Luqiu, a former journalist for Hong Kong outlet Phoenix News who spent 10 years covering Zhu during his international state visits. "The only way he refused to answer was using a quite humorous way to dodge the questions."

His gallows humor allowed him to weather intense periods of criticism from senior ideologues within the Communist Party, once quipping during an anti-corruption campaign: "I have prepared 100 coffins: 99 for the corrupt officials and one for myself."

Other reforms of his did not materialize, in part because an austere Zhu never managed to cultivate the political patronage networks that would have allowed him to overcome fierce opposition within party ranks to his proposals. His efforts to reduce bad debt at China's state banks and reform the pension system floundered.

Enlarge this image toggle caption Greg Baker/AFP via Getty Images Greg Baker/AFP via Getty Images

Zhu "represented really a different time, a different era for China"

Zhu is now invoked with pleasant nostalgia. Under China's current leader, Xi Jinping, the country became more nationalistic, more beholden to the state and more closed off to the outside world.

"I think that Zhu Rongji represented really a different time, a different era for China: the time when China wanted to find its way in what, due to that time, was the best possible way, which was to move towards Western-style economics, to move toward Western-style rules," said Barshefsky, the former U.S. trade negotiator.

Zhu Rongji spent the last years of his life at his Beijing home in the western hills of the Chinese capital. He loved Peking Opera and spent much of his days listening to music — and quietly advising some of the newest generation of technocrats running China, though not all appear to have listened to him.

World.title: B.C. officials 'can't even think about' lifting Summerland evacuation orders until wildfire under control
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Latest:

Regional officials said they have heard frustration from families who evacuated their homes in Summerland, B.C., but said they "can't even think about" lifting evacuation orders until the Bald Range fire is better controlled.

Temporary access permits to Summerland are being triaged, with utility crews getting priority to ensure utilities can adequately sustain the community.

The B.C. Wildfire Service (BCWS) reminds people to stay clear of the Bonanza Creek wildfire, as it's a popular recreational area surrounded by numerous provincial parks.

of the Bonanza Creek wildfire, as it's a popular recreational area surrounded by numerous provincial parks. The province issued yellow and orange air quality warnings for regions across the central and southern Interior.

for regions across the central and southern Interior. The Ainslie Creek wildfire, one of two fires in the Brunswick Complex, saw growth towards Highway 8. The highway currently remains open as crews maintain 24-hour operations.

as crews maintain 24-hour operations. The BCWS says "new ignitions occurring during periods of hot and dry weather can establish and spread quickly."

Bald Range wildfire still burning out of control

During a Tuesday livestream from the Regional District of Okanagan Similkameen, Summerland Mayor Doug Holmes said they cannot consider lifting evacuation orders or alerts until the Bald Range wildfire is under control.

A BCWS update on Tuesday said overnight recoveries were poor due to clear skies and fuels remain "exceptionally dry and highly receptive to fire."

Officials say the volatile nature of the wildfire challenges their ability to plan ahead, as they are still responding to the fire as it progresses.

Ground crews are pictured battling the Bald Range fire overnight on Aug. 7, 2026. (B.C. Wildfire Service)

"We have to make sure it's safe," said Holmes.

Until then, temporary access permits are being granted in some circumstances.

Permits are "basically triaged," according to Deborah Jones-Middleton, the protective services manager with the district. She said utilities professionals, for example, will be permitted into the area as long, as it's safe to do so, to ensure utilities are adequately running to sustain a community.

There were 100 firefighters from Mexico battling the Bald Range fire on Tuesday, bringing the total number of ground personnel to 193. Heavy equipment, aviation personnel continue to construct control lines, while structure protection is in place around the community.

Brunswick Complex nears another highway

As of Tuesday afternoon, the Ainslie Creek wildfire had scorched roughly 614 square kilometres of land, and its northeastern edge was only about three kilometres west of Highway 8, which runs through Merritt.

The northeast edge of the wildfire is roughly 20 kilometres northwest of Merritt. The BCWS noted the Ainslie Creek fire hasn't crossed control lines or entered the community.

As a result of the growing fire, the Lower Nicola Indian Band expanded its evacuation alert to cover all properties in the Nicola Mameet Indian Reserve No. 1. It also issued an evacuation order for a property on its Speous Indian Reserve No. 8.

The BCWS said in its Tuesday update that the fire remains active along the northeast and southeast flanks, growing eastward throughout Monday. It added that as of Tuesday morning , the fire stopped about two kilometres short of control lines, and had not impacted Highway 8.

The Ainslie Creek wildfire has a pattern of showing aggressive behaviour and major growth, according to the service, when any two factors of elevated winds, low humidity and clear skies combine.

The Ainslie Creek fire burns along the Fraser River on July 27, 2026. (B.C. Wildfire Service)

The Brunswick Complex consists of the Brunswick Creek wildfire, burning on the east bank of the Fraser River above Boston Bar, and the Ainslie Creek wildfire, burning on its west bank. Highway 1 is directly affected by the wildfires and remains closed.

There were 236 firefighters, 20 helicopters, 59 pieces of heavy equipment and 85 structure protection personnel fighting the Brunswick Complex as of Tuesday.

Road closures

According to DriveBC , most of the major highway closures from previous days remain the same.

Due to the Bald Range wildfire, Highway 97 is closed between Peachland and the Pyramid Picnic Area in Kickininee Provincial Park. Traffic is being redirected to Highway 33.

Westside Road also remains closed due to the Bradley Creek Complex, burning on the west bank of Okanagan Lake, north of Penticton.

Other closures to Highway 1 north of Hope and Highway 97 north of Cache Creek remain in place.

World.title: Spain confronts influx of solar eclipse tourists while still battling wildfires
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Hundreds of thousands of tourists have descended on Spain in the hopes of experiencing Wednesday's solar eclipse.

But the celestial event comes amid elevated temperatures and an increased risk of wildfires in Spain, raising alarm bells for authorities hoping to ensure the boom in astrotourism doesn’t come with lasting fire damage.

"We've had an extremely tough summer in Spain, with yet another series of major forest fires. That's why we must restrict any kind of activity that could generate a spark," Virginia Barcones, secretary general for civil ​protection and emergencies at Spain's Interior Ministry, told Reuters.

A heat wave has been smothering much of Europe since May, and Spain is currently grappling with a devastating wildfire season. More than 603,000 acres (2,440 square kilometres) of land have been burned in around 400 fires so far this year, according to the European Forest ​Fire Information System.

To ensure that eclipse tourists don’t add to this number, authorities are deploying 35,000 officers on Wednesday to large, outdoor gatherings in the hopes of spotting and stopping any new fires that may start, according to Barcones.

Forest rangers work in a wildfire-scorched area near Casillas, Avila province, Spain on July 30. (AP Photo/Olmo Calvo)

Spain is one of the best viewing locations for Wednesday's solar eclipse — the narrow band of totality, around 200 kilometres across, also crosses northern Russia, eastern Greenland and western Iceland, clipping the northeastern tip of Portugal and curving across a wide swathe of northern Spain, ending at the Balearic Islands. Around 15 million people live in its path, mostly in Spain.

Only those in the path of totality will witness the moon fully covering the sun. In Canada, a partial eclipse will be visible, with those on the east edge of Nunavut and Newfoundland seeing the most coverage. Authorities are reminding viewers to always use eclipse glasses to protect their eyes.

This will be the first time a full solar eclipse has been visible from mainland Spain in 120 years, and the excitement has sparked a flurry of travel.

WATCH | How and when to see the partial eclipse in Canada: Where will the partial solar eclipse be visible in Canada? | Duration 3:26 Parts of Europe will see a total solar eclipse on Wednesday. Canada's not so lucky, but parts of the country will get to see a partial eclipse.

Earlier this summer, authorities in Spain announced that special measures approved by the Ministry of the Interior would be in place for the solar eclipse to handle the large crowds anticipated. Searches for lodging along the eclipse’s path of totality spiked as the event grew nearer, according to Expedia Group, with Valencia, Spain, seeing a 245 per cent increase in searches compared to the previous year.

A total of 660 official viewing sites have been outlined by regional governments in the hopes of handling the expected influx of more than 440,000 people. Authorities estimate around 1.5 million people could be on the road during the day to head to viewing sites. Both national and local authorities are warning tourists against using barbecues or going into dry countryside where fire risk is higher.

Are you currently in or travelling to Europe to watch the solar eclipse? We want to hear from you. Send us your photos or videos and share your experience at ask@cbc.ca.

The eclipse is anticipated to contribute more than 347 million euros to Spain's economy, according to a July economic impact study by the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Business.

Dry conditions, fire fears

Three major wildfires are still burning in the provinces of Huelva, Segovia and Huesca. Only one of the severe blazes is in the path of totality, according to Joe McNorton, a scientist with the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts: the Las Peñas de Riglos wildfire active to the north of Zaragoza, which "could pose a danger if astro-tourists venture into the area."

Burnt trees stand in an area scorched by a wildfire near Vila Vella, Valencia province, Spain, on July 30. (Damian Torres/The Associated Press)

But the forest fire index across much of the Iberian Peninsula and the Balearic Islands is expected to reach "very high or extreme levels" on the day of the eclipse, according to AEMET , Spain's meteorological agency. And the country is perilously dry: last month, only 4.3 millimetres of rainfall was recorded across mainland Spain, a quarter of the normal precipitation expected this time of year. It was the driest July on record, according to AEMET.

"Around 90 per cent of wildfires are human-caused, so the presence of many more people in rural areas inevitably brings more potential ignition sources," McNorton told CBC News.

WATCH | Heat wave in Europe threatens to fuel further wildfires: Heat wave threatens to further fuel Europe’s wildfires | Duration 2:02 Wildfires in France have forced 4,000 more people along the Atlantic coast to evacuate as another heat wave threatens to fuel the flames there and in neighbouring Spain.

AEMET is forecasting temperatures upwards of 35 C on eclipse day, with some regions reaching 40 C, although peak temperatures will be down two to five degrees by the time of the eclipse.

Reykjavík, Iceland, will see totality at 5:48 p.m. local time, but viewers in Spain won’t see the eclipse enter totality until just before sunset, with northwestern Spain entering totality starting at around 8:28 p.m. local time. At its maximum, totality will last two minutes and 18 seconds, although this will vary by location.

Eclipse fervor holding

Even amid a heat wave and wildfires, eclipse travelers have not been deterred. Jan Cami, a professor in the physics and astronomy department at Western University in London, Ont., says he is unsurprised.

"It’s an event where you don't need to be a scientist at all to actually enjoy that this is an absolute spectacle that nature has provided for us," Cami told CBC News.

During maximum totality, the temperature drops, and stars and planets become briefly visible during the day, an experience so "overwhelming" that those who witness it often start making plans for their next trip to see it again, he said. He has colleagues both in Spain and on a cruise in Iceland waiting for their chance to see the sun vanish on Wednesday.

A view of totality during the solar eclipse on April 8, 2024, in Hot Springs National Park, Ark. (Nick Ingram/The Associated Press)

"I think [travelling for celestial events] is a great opportunity at the same time to learn about other parts of the world."

It’s this sense of shared meaning that Cami is hoping will touch tourists in Spain – that those who battle the heat to see the eclipse will reflect on the struggles of the country they’re in, and how far-reaching the impacts of climate change are.

Maarten Savelkoel, 76, from the Netherlands, visits a campsite to see the total solar eclipse, in Arija, Spain, on Tuesday. (Borja Suarez/Reuters)

The 2026 eclipse is just the first in a trio of solar eclipses in the next few years that will be visible from Spain. Two more are expected, on Aug. 2, 2027, and Jan. 26, 2028, respectively.

The 2027 solar eclipse could prompt even more astrotourism, Cami predicts. The path of totality will cross southern Spain before continuing to Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia, Libya, Egypt, Saudi Arabia and Yemen.

"You can see the total eclipse of next year while [at] the pyramids of Giza," he said.

World.title: Manitoba mother whose 'little angel' died in CFS care says she was trying to get kids back
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A grieving mother says someone needs to be held accountable after her four-year-old daughter died in the care of Child and Family Services and her two other children were taken to a Winnipeg hospital with serious injuries.

Manitoba First Nations Police Service officers were called to a home in Long Plain First Nation on Sunday morning after the four-year-old was found by first responders with injuries and in medical distress, RCMP said in a news release Tuesday.

The girl was pronounced dead and her two sisters, a one-year-old and two-year-old, were taken to the hospital — one of them in critical condition.

Her mother said her four-year-old daughter was starting kindergarten in September and was about to celebrate her fifth birthday later this month.

"She was just a little angel. She loved her little siblings." the mom told CBC Tuesday. "She loved to sing, she loved to dance."

CBC is not identifying the mother to protect the identity of the two children who remain in the care of Child and Family Services.

RCMP Major Crimes Services said they took over the investigation from First Nations police due to the nature of the girl's death and the injuries to the siblings. No charges have been laid.

Children under care of CFS

The children were under the care of Waywayseecapo CFS, a western Manitoba agency based in Waywayseecapo First Nation, according to emails viewed by CBC.

A representative from Waywayseecapo CFS agency — which is under the umbrella of the Southern First Nations Network of Care authority — said the agency is not commenting on the death at this time.

The mom spent the last two days visiting her children at Health Sciences Centre's children's hospital.

"They're just babies and they're just sweethearts," said the girls' mother, who spoke to CBC Tuesday outside of the hospital.

The mother said her kids had been in care since October and the last time she saw them was in February.

At that time, she says they looked skinny and she could see bruising on one child's eyes — a concern she raised with her CFS worker.

"I had a gut feeling something was happening and nobody listened to me," she said.

Families minister to do internal investigation

Manitoba's Families Minister Nahanni Fontaine said her department will be doing its own internal investigation and they have reported the death to the Manitoba Advocate for Children and Youth to also investigate.

In an emailed statement, Fontaine said she is "deeply saddened by the tragic death of this young child."

She cannot comment further on the circumstances of the case due to the active RCMP investigation, she said.

Families Minister Nahanni Fontaine said the province will conduct its own internal investigation into the death. (Tyson Koschik/CBC)

Her government remains committed to "working with the Southern Network of Care and all authorities to strengthen supports and ensure children and families receive the care and services they need," she said in the statement.

A spokesperson for the Southern Chiefs' Organization, which represents 33 First Nations in southern Manitoba including Waywayseecappo First Nation, sent condolences to the family.

"Given the ongoing investigations into the circumstances surrounding the child’s death and the injuries sustained by the other children, SCO will not comment further or speculate at this time," the spokesperson said in an emailed statement.

'Time to take my baby back in a casket'

After her kids were apprehended in October, the mom says she went into a four-week treatment program in December, took parenting classes and was hoping to get her kids back this summer.

"I did everything, I went to treatment, I did the programs, I stayed sober. I cleaned my house," she said.

"Then just nothing was done about it. And now look, time to take my baby back in a casket and my other girls are just so broken."

She is speaking about what happened to her daughter because she doesn't want to see another death in care and she wants answers as to how this happened.

"I just want her voice to be heard and make sure it doesn't happen to any other kids. Some things need to be done about this," she said.

"All I wanted was them to be home with me where they were safe. And nobody listened."

World.title: What to know about the trial of Lindsay Clancy, woman accused of killing her 3 children
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

WARNING: This article contains details about violence against children and attempted suicide:

The Lindsay Clancy murder trial is making headlines around the world as jurors hear harrowing details of the Massachusetts mother who killed her three young children.

Clancy's legal team does not deny that she killed her children, but is arguing she shouldn't be held criminally responsible because she was mentally ill — in the grip of bipolar disorder and postpartum psychosis, a rare condition that the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health says occurs in approximately one to two cases per 1,000 births. Postpartum psychosis can cause extreme mood swings, delusions and confusion, according to the Society of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists of Canada.

Prosecutors argue Clancy is guilty of three counts of first-degree murder, having plotted to get her husband out of the house so she could carry out the murders.

The trial, which is being held in Plymouth, Mass., is being livestreamed on CourtTV and major Boston TV stations, as well as YouTube. On Tuesday, the trial moved into day 11, and proceedings are expected to continue for several more weeks.

Here are some details about the case and what court has heard.

The killings

Clancy, a former labour and delivery nurse, was struggling with her mental health and seeing multiple specialists in 2022. The court has heard she was prescribed 13 different psychiatric medications across different providers.

Her attorneys say Clancy did everything she could to seek help: She turned to multiple outpatient providers, tried various drugs they prescribed, called a suicide hotline, went to an emergency room and approached but wasn’t accepted into a hospital-based, full-day treatment program for women with postpregnancy mental health problems. Clancy also checked herself into a psychiatric hospital for several days.

Rather than improving her condition, her attorneys and family say the shifting cocktail of psychiatric medications made things worse.

Cellphone records show that on Jan. 24, 2023, she texted her husband Patrick late in the afternoon, asking him to pick up takeout and medicine.

During his absence from their Duxbury, Mass., home, prosecutors say Clancy used exercise bands to strangle their three children: five-year-old Cora, three-year-old Dawson and eight-month-old Callan. She then cut her own wrists and throat and jumped out of a second-storey window in an apparent suicide attempt.

Clancy, who turned 36 on Tuesday, was paralyzed from the waist down and has been attending the court proceedings in a wheelchair.

Court hears diary entries

Opening statements began on July 27, after an 18-member jury was selected.

Patrick Clancy, Lindsay's now former husband, took the stand early, detailing her mental health struggles and his experience on the day of the killings. Jurors were shaken when his 911 call was played in court.

The court later heard from Duxbury first responders, crime scene analysts and the family's nanny, who said Lindsay was a "wonderful mom who loved her kids."

Clancy's diary entries were also read in court, including a section where she wrote that she was “completely overwhelmed” trying to take care of her children.

“I feel like I’m drowning every day,” she wrote.

She sobbed in court when details of the autopsy reports were read.

Testimony from psychiatrists

Recent days have focused on Clancy's mental state, including testimonies from her psychiatrists and mental health experts.

On Monday her lawyer probed Dr. Jennifer Tufts, who saw Clancy via video meetings from September 2022 until the day before the killings.

Defence lawyer Kevin Reddington questioned Tufts' expertise, prescribing decisions and overall treatment, spotlighting her use of 25-minute video appointments and the series of recommended pharmaceuticals.

Defence attorney Kevin Reddington, left, questions psychiatrist Dr. Jennifer Tufts about her hand written notes on Monday. (Greg Derr/Pool/The Patriot Ledger)

"I do not believe that I've been negligent," Tufts testified.

Clancy is suing Tufts and other practitioners in civil court.

On Tuesday, another of Clancy's psychiatrists, Rebecca Jollotta, testified about a concerning mid-December call with the couple during which she heard Clancy had her "worst day" and was "having persistent, intrusive thoughts of suicide."

Prosecutor Shanan Buckingham has urged jurors not to view the trial as "a public debate about women's mental health and how the medical system treats women," but rather to focus on the specific actions Clancy took and the intent behind them.

If convicted of murder, Clancy faces life in prison without parole.

If found not guilty due to a lack of criminal responsibility, she would be committed to a state mental health facility.

Legal expert Margaret McLean told Parade that Clancy's case would then shift to a "civil commitment process" overseen by the court and mental health experts.

Clancy could eventually be released under strict conditions, or, if her illness is deemed "chronic and dangerous," she could remain institutionalized for the rest of her life.

World.title: From last place to the post-season? Here's how the 2026 Blue Jays could pull it off
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results. It's been a frustrating season for the Toronto Blue Jays after the team made it all the way to Game 7 of the World Series last year, but a winning surge in the past two weeks has kept their playoff hopes alive. The CBC's Greg Ross has more on the Jays' turnaround and their chances of making it to the post-season. Prime Minister Mark Carney says "you've got to believe" the Toronto Blue Jays can still make the playoffs. But can they, really? The Jays have played some scrappy baseball lately, as the team finds itself on the fringes of playoff contention with a quarter of the season to go and it's still possible they might find a way to the post-season in the anemic American League. Toronto beat the Boston Red Sox tonight, in a 5-3 victory that improved their season record to 58-63 and kept the team in the hunt for a potential playoff spot. Thanks for the sweater, Karla.

My message to Jays Nation: you've got to believe. pic.twitter.com/oP6IQ9dHmJ —MarkJCarney "At this point, you just kind of throw everything other than winning out the window and show up every day and try to win," Jays infielder and all-star Ernie Clement told CBC News, earlier Tuesday. There are a half-dozen teams, including Toronto, that are within four games of the last wild-card spot in the wider American League — and the Blue Jays would have to leap past all of them to secure a return to the post-season. Here's a look at why the Jays are where they are with just over 40 games to go, and what they have to do to get back to the post-season. From the World Series to last place? That's the reality: Toronto has gone from a team that competed for a World Series title last fall to a team curently sitting in last place in the American Leage East. They can't win the division at this point, so that means they'll have to claim a wild-card spot to reach the post-season. WATCH | The end of an era for some Toronto fan favourites: Blue Jays lose fan favourites in big trades | Duration 2:09 Less than a year after competing for the MLB championship, the Toronto Blue Jays made some big trades ahead of the deadline, including fan favourites Daulton Varsho and pitcher Kevin Gausman. The win over Boston Tuesday night improved Toronto's season record to 58-63 — 12 fewer wins than they had at the same point last year. At present, the Tampa Bay Rays lead the AL East, followed by the New York Yankees in second place, and the resurgent Boston Red Sox — who put together lengthy win streaks in July and August — in third. The Baltimore Orioles (with a 58-62 record) and the Jays sit in fourth and fifth place. Just 2 teams have done it According to Elias Sports Bureau, the official statistician of Major League Baseball (MLB), there are just two teams that have stood at 58-63 through 121 games — the same record the Jays have right now — that went on to make the playoffs in the wild-card era: The 2024 Detroit Tigers and the 2009 Minnesota Twins. Randy Robles of Elias Sports Bureau believes "there's some hope" for the Jays, noting that if there ever was a year for a struggling team to still have a chance, it would be this one, when so many American League teams have been playing so poorly. Blue Jays rookie Charles McAdoo runs the bases at Toronto's Rogers Centre after hitting a solo home run in Monday's game against the Boston Red Sox. (Getty Images) What it will take Toronto has begun to claw its way to a better record, claiming series wins against the Washington Nationals, the St. Louis Cardinals, the Houston Astros and the Philadelphia Phillies in the past couple of weeks. That winning trend has to continue for the team to have a shot at the post-season: "They gotta get to .500," Robles told CBC News, referring to the point when a team has won as many games as it has lost. The Texas Rangers, the team currently sitting in the third wild-card spot the Jays are vying for, was only one game above the .500 mark prior to Tuesday's matchups. All the teams seeking to take the Rangers' spot — Toronto included — currently have losing records. Summing up the challenge the Blue Jays face in climbing the standings, Toronto Star baseball columnist Mike Wilner saw a certain parity in the teams involved in the wild-card fight. "Every team in front of the Blue Jays kind of stinks," Wilner told CBC News. "The problem is, the Blue Jays kind of stink, too." Dylan Cease is the ace of the Blue Jays' starting pitching staff and in the hunt for a Cy Young Award this season. (Paul Beaty/The Associated Press) Cease leads the rotation The Jays are thin on starting pitching right now, but the rotation includes pitching ace Dylan Cease, the newly acquired José Soriano, Shane Bieber, as well as veteran Max Scherzer. Cease is on the hunt for a Cy Young Award, and has been in the midst of a sizzling run this summer that included bid for a no-hitter in July that he carried into the ninth inning. He started Tuesday's game against Boston, going five innings and striking out seven. Soriano was solid in his recent Blue Jays debut. Bieber, who missed most of the first half of the season, has been battling for consistency since rejoining the team in June. Scherzer has had two decent starts for Toronto this month — and the team will be counting on him to deliver more if they have a shot at a wild card. "We have a job to do: Every time we come to the park, we've got to win," Scherzer told CBC News. In the bullpen, the Jays will continue to look to closer Louis Varland and workhorse reliever Tyler Rogers in high-leverage situations. Rookie pitcher Spencer Miles, as well as relievers Braydon Fisher and Mason Fluharty will also be key to any push for the post-season. Kazuma Okamoto rounds the bases after a July 28 home run at Nationals Park. The rookie is leading the Jays in home runs this year with 24. (Brad Mills/Imagn Images/Reuters) What about the bats? Hitting has been a real problem for the Blue Jays this year. The team sits near the bottom of the major leagues in terms of home runs, runs scored and on-base percentage. Only two Blue Jays have a double-digit home run total: Kazuma Okamoto (24) and Springer (12). Last year, Toronto had four players who swatted 20-plus homers. This year, they'll be fortunate to have two.

World.title: What’s Quebec identity anyway? These Quebecers had a lot to say
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

There are two words that always seem to come up in political discourse in this province: Quebec identity or, in French, l’identité Québécoise.

But what does it mean ? Who defines it? Ahead of the Oct. 5 provincial election, I asked a cross section of Quebecers — and they offered a wealth of perspectives.

What follows is a series of those candid and nuanced conversations. I chatted with two women who left India and Pakistan in the 1970s for Quebec under René Lévesque. I met young sovereignists with Indigenous and Maghrebi roots, respectively.

I also caught up with one woman who identifies as a Montrealer — not a Quebecer — and two others who told me how they juggle their Quebec pride while fervently defending their English-language institutions.

Here's what they had to say.

A more ‘inclusive,’ welcoming Quebec

What does Quebec identity mean to these women with South Asian roots? | Duration 7:00 What does Quebec identity mean to Dolores Chew and Shaheen Ashraf? The two women immigrated to Quebec in the mid-1970s and one of them voted ‘Yes’ in the 1980 referendum.

Quebec has been home to Dolores Chew and Shaheen Ashraf for more than 50 years. And they still enjoy South Asian comforts like a cup of chai.

Over tea and snacks, they fondly recall a Quebec under René Lévesque. One of them voted ‘Yes’ in the 1980 referendum. But their sense of belonging changed after that.

The youth behind Quebec's sovereignty movement

2 sovereignists — with Moroccan and Indigenous roots — explain why Quebec should be a country | Duration 7:56 Nabil Ben Ali Ouriaghli and Benjamin Gingras say they identify with an independent Quebec that doesn’t assimilate anybody. But some values commonly promoted in Quebec, they say, are still up for debate.

Nabil Ben Ali Ouriaghli and Benjamin Gingras are both members of Oui Quebec, a citizen-led movement promoting sovereignty. They say their vision of an independent Quebec is one that focuses on inclusion and what brings people together.

Have a story about what Quebec identity means to you? Reach out to Sudha Krishnan at sudha.krishnan@cbc.ca

But they recognize there’s work to do in getting that message out.

A proud Montrealer — not Quebecer or Canadian

Why this Montrealer’s identity is rooted in the city – and not in Quebec and Canada | Duration 7:41 While Shereen Joseph proudly identifies as a Malaysian Montrealer, she says her identity is less tied to Quebec and Canada and wonders if she would feel as welcome if she left the city.

Western Canada didn’t quite feel like home, but Montreal sure did.

When Shereen Joseph moved to the Plateau-Mont-Royal borough, she found the identity that truly resonated with her: Montrealer. She explains how her Malaysian roots helped her embrace the city and the French language — and why the language tensions in this province seem so foreign.

Fighting for English-language institutions

What Quebec identity means to these 2 bilingual English school board commissioners | Duration 7:48 Allison Saunders claims her bilingual Quebec identity by living in both worlds — whether that means watching French TV or representing English education. As a young university student raised in the predominantly French-speaking neighbourhood of Rivière-des-Prairies, Susan Perera emphasizes the importance of bilingualism. But they both worry about young English-speaking students who are questioning their future in Quebec.

For Susan Perera and Allison Saunders, English-language schools are not just about education, they’re also about community and promoting a bilingual Quebec.

Both English school board commissioners proudly claim their Quebec identity. But at times, Saunders feels she "does not tick all the boxes" when it comes to how some people define what it means to be a Quebecer.

World.title: China's Zhu Rongji, economic reformer who helped lead country into WTO, dead at 97
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Former Chinese premier Zhu Rongji has died, according to state media. He was 97.

The official Xinhua news agency reported that Zhu died of illness in Beijing at around 11 a.m. on Wednesday. The impatient, sharp-tongued reformer helped ignite China's explosive economic boom by forcing wrenching change on state industry in the 1990s and leading the country into the World Trade Organization.

Once sent into rural exile to do manual labour for praising reforms in other communist countries, Zhu pushed through a dizzying array of changes as premier, China's top economic post, from 1998 to 2003.

Zhu clashed with Communist Party conservatives and state industry bosses as he pushed state-owned companies to become efficient and profitable. That cost millions of layoffs, but helped propel China to overtake Japan as the second-largest economy behind the United States, in 2010.

Building on former leader Deng Xiaoping's 1979 reforms, Zhu is credited with supplying the resourcefulness and tenacity to push through history-making changes such as China's WTO membership, which helped to transform China into the world's biggest exporter.

Those changes helped to keep economic growth above eight per cent a year from 2000 to 2010, peaking at 14.2 per cent in 2007.

Named premier in 1998 at age 69, Zhu became a popular figure by criticizing official bungling and graft and accepting blame when the government fell short. His demanding style earned him the nicknames Boss and Zhu Fengzi, or Madman Zhu.

"I have prepared 100 coffins here — 99 for corrupt officials and one for myself," Zhu said in 1998, according to the party newspaper People's Daily.

Zhu, centre, is shown waving to people outside Parliament Hill in Ottawa on April 16, 1999, while walking beside Prime Minister Jean Chrétien, left. (Tom Hanson/The Canadian Press)

Zhu ranked No. 3 in the party hierarchy behind President Jiang Zemin and Li Peng, chairman of the ceremonial legislature, the National People's Congress.

Zhu made his name as a deputy premier in the 1990s by crushing inflation. He enforced price controls and cut off loans to money-losing state companies, rebuffing resistance by local leaders — a pattern Zhu would repeat as he fought conservatives over the pace of reform.

Zhu led efforts to secure WTO membership following marathon negotiations that began in the 1980s. That status would enshrine free trade as a national commitment, giving Zhu a tool to force local officials to stop protecting favoured companies.

Zhu's campaign was nearly derailed when he went to Washington in 1999 with market-opening concessions to win U.S. endorsement of the WTO bid. The Clinton administration rejected the offer as inadequate while his political enemies at home accused him of offering too much, but Zhu survived and China went on to join the body in December 2001.

Zhu launched China's home ownership boom in 1998 with an initiative to sell apartments owned by state companies. Families rushed to buy, and within a decade the majority of urban housing was privately owned.

Still, Zhu showed no interest in privatizing the economy. He played a key role in drafting plans in the 1990s to turn banks, airlines, oil companies and other enterprises into profit-oriented corporations but to retain government ownership.

Years spent in political wilderness

Born Oct. 23, 1928, in Mao Zedong's home province of Hunan, Zhu paid an early price for his willingness to take risks and speak out.

After a start as an economic planner, his career went into a 22-year eclipse when he was labelled a "rightist" in 1957 for praising reforms in Hungary and Yugoslavia. He was banished to the countryside during the 1966-76 Cultural Revolution to do manual labour.

U.S. President Bill Clinton, right, gestures to Zhu during his state visit to Washington in April 1999. The visit came as China was looking for an endorsement from the U.S. to join the World Trade Organization. (Joyce Naltchayan/AFP/Getty Images)

Rehabilitated in 1979, Zhu rose swiftly, becoming deputy Shanghai party secretary in 1987 and mayor the next year.

As mayor in 1989, Zhu gained a reputation for moderation when he placated protesters and pledged not to call in the military.

"He managed to defuse, with considerable subtlety, a tense political situation that could have developed into localized violence or worse if the military had felt it necessary to intervene," wrote Australian diplomat Shelley Warner in the 1991 book The Pro-Democracy Protests in China: Reports from the Provinces.

Zhu's boss, Jiang, would soon be called to Beijing by Deng and made party leader. Zhu was named deputy premier in 1991 and joined the party's ruling Standing Committee in 1993.

Zhu broke with the leadership's stance of infallibility by admitting and taking blame for official failings.

In 1998, after summer floods killed 4,150 people and officials were accused of embezzling money meant for anti-flood dikes, Zhu complained some barriers were no stronger than bean curd.

Three years later, he apologized on national television for his cabinet's failure to protect the public after an explosion in a schoolhouse in southern China killed at least 42 people, most of them children.

Chinese President Xi Jinping greets Zhu at the 19th Communist Party Congress at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing on Oct. 24, 2017, one of Zhu's last known public appearances. (Greg Baker/AFP/Getty Images)

Zhu enlivened the party's bland image by cracking jokes in public, sometimes at his own expense. Laughter erupted at a 1999 news conference when he said a recent photo "made me look like a dead man."

One of Zhu's proudest triumphs as deputy premier was to craft a tax system that required local officials to hand more revenue to Beijing. He said in 1996 that he deserved a Nobel Prize in economics for that.

World.title: 'An absolute gut punch': Dozens facing unemployment as an Ottawa Metro converts to Food Basics
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A Metro grocery store in Ottawa's South Keys neighbourhood will be replaced by a Food Basics this fall, costing dozens of employees their jobs.

Metro Inc. says the store, which closed Wednesday, is being converted to a Food Basics to better meet customer needs in the area.

"We regularly assess our store network based on a range of factors, including local market conditions and store performance," a spokesperson with the company wrote in a statement to CBC. "Moving to a discount banner reflects the type of market and demand in the area."

The decision still came as a shock to employees at Metro's Southgate location, however.

"We were all just stunned," said Justin Braganza, a meat cutter who has worked at the store for more than 30 years.

Braganza, who's also a volunteer steward with the United Food and Commercial Workers union, said he and his colleagues were informed of the impending closure in May by their regional manager and another Metro representative who cited financial pressure.

"They said that rent had gone up and that they didn’t feel that our store was profitable enough to sustain the Metro model," he explained. "We were told very bluntly that we were all being terminated."

CBC asked Metro if the cost of rent contributed to its decision to convert the Southgate store, but the company maintained the change was made based on local market conditions and customer needs.

The Southgate Metro employed 72 people. Metro told CBC that under to the terms of their collective agreement, those workers don't have the option to transfer to other Metro stores.

"Employees who are interested in working at the new Food Basics store are invited to apply and will be considered through that process," the company wrote.

Employees blindsided

The collective agreement for the new Food Basics store requires Metro to hire a minimum of 10 part-time and five full-time employees who worked at the Southgate Metro and who apply to work at the new store, a spokesperson with the company explained.

Because Metro and Food Basics operate under different wage structures, if a former Metro Southgate employee is hired at the new store their seniority will be taken into consideration within the Food Basics pay band, the spokesperson said.

That's little comfort to employees like Braganza, however.

"It was just an absolute gut punch," he said. "They don’t use meat cutters at Food Basics, so I don't have a job waiting for me at this new store if I was even successful in the application process."

He said some of his colleagues could have even more at stake.

"One or two of our employees are even here on work permits, and them remaining in Canada depends on them having a job, and to not have a job, that really makes their situation so much more tenuous."

Some Metro customers were also disappointed at the news.

"To me, it's just disrespect for the workers. That's what bothers me very deeply," said Michael Vorobej. "I think Metro just wants to up their profit margin, and they want to do it on the backs of the people that have been working for them for so long."

The United Food and Commercial Workers union told CBC that representatives from locals 175 and 633 negotiated 'enhanced options' for its members including severance benefits and job opportunities at the new Food Basics store. (Dalson Chen/CBC)

Union negotiated 'enhanced options' for workers

The union representing workers at the Southgate Metro declined an interview, but in a statement to CBC said its representatives had reached out to Metro to advocate for its members' rights.

"As a result, UFCW Locals 175 and 633 negotiated enhanced options for our members at the Metro store, including job opportunities at the new Food Basics store and enhanced severance options," the union wrote.

It also said it held individual meetings with affected members to outline those options, "which was well received and appreciated by the employees."

A lawyer who specializes in employment and labour law reviewed the collective agreement between Metro Inc. and UFCW Local 175, and told CBC the deal does allow the company to lay employees off due to a shortage of work.

"That leaves the question ... if Metro is basically shutting down and then opening up and rebranding itself as a Food Basics, is there actually a shortage of work? Did they actually not have enough work for these positions, or is it more a change of corporate identity?” asked Nelligan Law partner Malini Vijaykumar.

Vijaykumar said a union may file a grievance challenging a company's claim of a work shortage. It may also argue that a company's actions constitute anti-union behaviour, opening the door to litigation.

"That can take months and months, and all the while your employees are out of work and out of pay," she said.

Malini Vijaykumar is a partner with Nelligan Law who specializes in employment and labour law. (Nelligan Law)

Alternatively, these cases can be resolved through settlements between the union and the employer. Vijaykumar explained that these deals often include confidentiality clauses and bar unions from filing grievances.

"Unions are typically pretty vocal," Vijaykumar said. "Where you're not seeing that and where an enhanced severance arrangement and job opportunities and that kind of thing seem to have been worked out, it may be a sign that there has been a sort of agreement worked out between the parties."

If that has happened, both sides will be cautious about communicating details of any deal, she said.

Meanwhile, Braganza said he and other employees are feeling sidelined and without much recourse.

"It illustrates that workers have very few rights in this situation," he said. "The employer holds all the cards."

Braganza said he's been reflecting on the relationships he’s built with colleagues and customers that he'll have to leave behind.

"It's like we were a little family, and now with this closure we're all going to go our separate ways and it’s going to be hard," he said.

World.title: YPF divests its stake in gas distribution for 780 million dollars
World.content:
YPF divests its stake in gas distribution for 780 million dollars

12th Wednesday, August 2026 - 06:28 UTC Full article

YPF will transfer 70% of the capital of Metrogas, the country's largest gas distributor, and 5% of Metroenergía, its trading arm

Argentine oil company YPF, 51% state-controlled, has accepted Edenor's offer to buy its stake in Metrogas and Metroenergía for 780 million dollars, according to a filing submitted on Monday to the securities regulator. The deal takes the company out of the natural gas distribution business.

YPF will transfer 70% of the capital of Metrogas, the country's largest gas distributor, and 5% of Metroenergía, its trading arm. Metrogas supplies around 2.4 million customers in the city of Buenos Aires and eleven surrounding districts, more than a quarter of the national market. Edenor supplies electricity to 3.4 million customers in the northern part of the metropolitan area.

The buyer is controlled by the Edelcos consortium, made up of businessmen José Luis Manzano, Daniel Vila and Mauricio Filiberti. Manzano, a former interior minister under Carlos Menem, already held 9.23% of Metrogas through his investment vehicle. Once completed, the deal will place a single group in charge of the largest gas and electricity distributors in the metropolitan area, with close to 5.8 million customers combined.

The competitive process began in April with thirteen non-binding offers and narrowed to five finalists: besides Edenor, Central Puerto, MSU, Grupo Pierri and Litoral Gas took part. Citigroup advised the oil company. Edenor bid alongside British firm Andina PLC and will have to launch a tender offer for the remaining shares, held by the national social security administration, investors on the Buenos Aires stock exchange and Manzano's existing stake.

YPF said the sale forms part of a review of its asset portfolio and that proceeds will go to Vaca Muerta, the unconventional hydrocarbons field at the center of the strategy pursued by its chairman, Horacio Marín. Argentine law also bars vertical integration between gas production and distribution, an incompatibility the company had carried since taking control of Metrogas in 2012.

The timing coincides with improved results at the distributor. Between 2023 and 2025, Metrogas doubled its gross profit, quadrupled its operating result, cut its debt to a third and resumed dividend payments for the first time since 2001. The tariff adjustments introduced by Javier Milei's government and a five-year review setting an indexation formula shape the regulatory framework of the business.

Metrogas's licence, granted in 1992 for 35 years, expires in December 2027. The gas regulator has sent the executive a recommendation to extend it by two decades, to 2047, a decision not yet formalized. Completion of the transaction is conditional on authorizations from energy sector regulators.

World.title: Michelle and Flávio Bolsonaro appear together for the first time since their June rift
World.content:
Michelle and Flávio Bolsonaro appear together for the first time since their June rift

12th Wednesday, August 2026 - 06:21 UTC Full article

“We have set our disagreements aside. What family is perfect? Let anyone without family problems raise their hand,” the former first lady said at the end of the event

Brazil's former first lady, Michelle Bolsonaro, and Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, the Liberal Party's presidential candidate, appeared together in public on Tuesday for the first time since the falling-out between them in late June. The meeting took place at the party's headquarters in Brasília, where they recorded campaign material and prayed together.

“We have set our disagreements aside. What family is perfect? Let anyone without family problems raise their hand,” the former first lady said at the end of the event. She added that both had put their differences behind them to unite “in favor of something much greater,” and confirmed she will take part in the campaign. “He can count on me on social media and he can count on the strength of women spread across Brazil,” she said.

The dispute erupted in late June, when Michelle Bolsonaro released a video accusing her stepson of mistreating and humiliating her over internal party matters, leaving her support for his candidacy in doubt. “They treat me as if I were an idiot. As if I had arrived yesterday,” she said at the time. Flávio Bolsonaro posted an apology video in July inviting her to join the campaign, and she responded positively, although they had not appeared together in public until Tuesday.

The former first lady heads PL Mulher, the Liberal Party's women's wing, and her backing is considered significant among evangelical and female voters. On August 2 she was nominated as a Senate candidate for the Federal District, at a convention she was unable to attend because of a hospitalization; her brother read the speech she had prepared.

The reunion comes four days before the official start of campaigning for October's elections. Flávio Bolsonaro has not secured alliances with the parties of the so-called Centrão and is competing for conservative voters with former governor Ronaldo Caiado, governor Romeu Zema and political figure Renan Santos.

Polls differ in scale but agree in placing President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, who is seeking re-election, ahead. A Datafolha survey from mid-July gave him 48% against the senator's 43% in a potential runoff; later measurements cited by international agencies put the two at 44% and 39% respectively.

Jair Bolsonaro, Michelle's husband and Flávio's father, is under house arrest after being sentenced to 27 years for attempting a coup. He is barred from holding public office, has appealed the ruling and is seeking a legislative pardon.

Lula will open his campaign at the stadium in São Bernardo do Campo, in greater São Paulo, where he was a union leader. Flávio Bolsonaro will do so at Copacabana beach in Rio de Janeiro.

World.title: Argentina to mark every July 15 with the World Cup win that revived the Falklands dispute
World.content:
Argentina to mark every July 15 with the World Cup win that revived the Falklands dispute

12th Wednesday, August 2026 - 06:13 UTC Full article

The decision was approved unanimously on August 5 at an executive committee meeting held at the association's Ezeiza complex

The Argentine Football Association (AFA) has established July 15 as National Football Teams Day, in tribute to the 2-1 win over England in the 2026 World Cup semi-final, the same match after which several players displayed a banner asserting a sovereignty claim over the Falklands that prompted a FIFA disciplinary case.

The decision was approved unanimously on August 5 at an executive committee meeting held at the association's Ezeiza complex. According to its statement, the date commemorates the “great and historic victory” of the side coached by Lionel Scaloni, which came from behind in Atlanta through goals by Enzo Fernández and Lautaro Martínez, both set up by Lionel Messi. The AFA specified that the recognition also covers all national teams — youth, men's and women's, futsal, beach football and field football — that train at the Lionel Andrés Messi complex. Argentina went on to lose the final to Spain.

After the final whistle on July 15, a group of players unfurled a sheet reading “Las Malvinas son argentinas” — “The Falklands are Argentine” — in front of the stands. The British government condemned the gesture and asked FIFA to investigate, considering it a political demonstration at an official competition. A spokesperson for then-prime minister Keir Starmer said, as reported by the Daily Mail, that “the World Cup might not be ours, the Falkland Islands definitely are”, adding that self-determination rests with the islanders.

FIFA rules prohibit political messaging at its competitions. The governing body's disciplinary committee opened proceedings against the AFA and several players, among them Giovani Lo Celso, Cristian Romero and Lisandro Martínez. The case remains open and no sanction has been decided. There is a precedent: FIFA had already begun proceedings over a similar banner displayed at a friendly against Bosnia in La Plata before the tournament.

Argentine President Javier Milei backed the players. He called the celebration “perfectly valid” and said it reflects a sentiment shared by Argentines, though he anticipated a fine from the governing body.

The AFA also said the banner will be handed to veterans of the Falklands War. It was made by a group of fans from a bedsheet and paint at a cost of under ten dollars, taken into the stadium without authorization and retrieved from the pitch by a member of the delegation's staff.

The United Kingdom has administered the Falklands since 1833. In the 2013 referendum, islanders voted overwhelmingly to retain their status as a British overseas territory. Argentina maintains a sovereignty claim over the islands.

World.title: US disables a Panama-flagged container ship off the coast of Pakistan
World.content:
US disables a Panama-flagged container ship off the coast of Pakistan

12th Wednesday, August 2026 - 00:16 UTC Full article

A Navy MH-60 helicopter fired two Hellfire missiles into the vessel's engine room after its civilian crew ignored repeated warnings

US forces struck the Panama-flagged container ship Vela Nova in the Gulf of Oman on Tuesday, leaving it unable to steer, after it attempted to head for an Iranian port in violation of the naval blockade imposed by Washington, US Central Command (CENTCOM) confirmed.

A Navy MH-60 helicopter fired two Hellfire missiles into the vessel's engine room after its civilian crew ignored repeated warnings, the command said in a statement. The strike disabled the ship's steering gear. A senior US official quoted earlier by The Wall Street Journal had said the shot was aimed at the rudder, and that the crew was subsequently transferred to another vessel.

The incident took place some 71 nautical miles — around 131 kilometers — off the coast of Pakistan, while the ship was sailing westbound. Maritime security firm Vanguard reported that the impact started a fire, later extinguished, and that all 17 crew members are safe. The British organization UKMTO had initially reported an incident involving a tanker.

The Panamanian flag corresponds to an open registry and does not imply any link to the Panamanian state or Panamanian ownership. Shipping records list Golden Valley Marine INV as registered owner and commercial manager, with Sino Hellenic Ships Management as technical manager and classification by the Korean Register.

It is the third vessel disabled since the United States reimposed the blockade on July 14. As of Tuesday, CENTCOM has redirected 55 commercial vessels attempting to cross the line, disabled three and boarded two, according to its own figures. The previous cases were the Curaçao-flagged Belma and the Mozambique-flagged Lavine, on July 24. In June, three Indian sailors died during a blockade enforcement operation, according to an Indian official at the time.

Charlie Brown, an adviser to the US organization United Against Nuclear Iran, told Reuters that the Vela Nova recently called at Mumbai and Port Klang, ports also used by vessels linked to Iran, and that the episode underscores the heightened scrutiny now being applied to Iran-related shipping.

The strike comes during a period of relative calm following the apparent collapse of the memorandum of understanding signed by the two countries in June and a thirteen-day escalation in July. Tehran and Washington exchanged mutual demands for compensation over war damage on Monday. In July, the Houthis declared a naval blockade of Saudi Arabia and struck two Saudi tankers in the Red Sea.

World.title: Colombia asks for supplies but not foreign rescue personnel after the earthquake
World.content:
Colombia asks for supplies but not foreign rescue personnel after the earthquake

12th Wednesday, August 2026 - 00:05 UTC Full article

The Colombian government issued a diplomatic note on Tuesday requesting support from the international community with specific requirements

Colombia's government has requested international aid in the form of supplies for those affected by Monday's magnitude 7.4 earthquake, but has not called for foreign rescue teams, despite offers from at least six countries and multilateral bodies.

El Salvador's president, Nayib Bukele, was the one who made Colombia's position public. “The government of Colombia has requested humanitarian aid solely in the form of supplies to assist the families affected,” he wrote on social media. “We have been informed that its rescue teams, doctors and other emergency services are deployed and attending to the situation, so at this time they do not require personnel support.” El Salvador will send two cargo planes with a hundred tons of humanitarian aid.

Several governments have contingents on standby. Ecuador offered a search and rescue team of 47 personnel with specialized dogs and seven days of operational autonomy. Mexico assembled a unit with four tons of medicines and 8.4 tons of tools and rescue equipment, similar to the one deployed in Venezuela after June's earthquakes. “We are waiting for a formal request from the government of Colombia, but we are ready for the moment they tell us we can go and help,” President Claudia Sheinbaum said. Chile, Brazil, Peru, Guatemala and Spain, among others, also offered assistance.

The exception is the United States, which announced 15.5 million dollars in aid for emergency shelter, food, protection and damage assessment. The State Department said it activated a Disaster Assistance Response Team on Monday, due to arrive in the country on Tuesday.

The Colombian government issued a diplomatic note on Tuesday requesting support from the international community with specific requirements, a mechanism that does not formally amount to an international appeal. United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres said the organization remains in contact with the authorities and supports “the government-led response, as requested.” China's ambassador in Bogotá, Zhu Jingyang, called for a liaison official to be designated as soon as possible to coordinate assistance.

Colombia's emergency cooperation system is centralized in the National Disaster Risk Management Unit, which must set out requirements before the foreign ministry passes them to donors. “The government is learning on the go how the mechanism works,” said international relations scholar Sandra Borda, who added that cities cannot channel aid directly. President Abelardo de la Espriella, who took office on August 7, announced the appointment of geological engineer David Suárez Tamayo to head the unit.

World.title: At least 132 dead in the magnitude 7.4 earthquake that struck western Colombia
World.content:
At least 132 dead in the magnitude 7.4 earthquake that struck western Colombia

11th Tuesday, August 2026 - 10:51 UTC Full article

Pereira and its metropolitan area account for most of the dead

At least 132 people were killed and 570 injured by the magnitude 7.4 earthquake that struck western and central Colombia on Monday, according to the latest report submitted by the Colombian Association of Capital Cities at 7:00 p.m. local time. Authorities warned the figure is preliminary and that rescue work is continuing.

The quake struck at 07:34, with its epicenter near the municipality of San José del Palmar, in Chocó department, at a depth of more than 80 kilometers, according to the Colombian Geological Service. It is the strongest recorded in the country in the past decade.

Pereira and its metropolitan area account for most of the dead. Departmental tolls released by governors and mayors correspond to different cutoff times and do not match one another: Chocó governor Nubia Carolina Córdoba-Curi reported 12 dead and 84 injured in that department, while the mayor of Manizales confirmed two deaths. Fatalities were also reported in Valle del Cauca and Antioquia.

| URGENTE: Momento del derrumbe de un edificio de 3 pisos tras el terremoto de magnitud 7,4 en Pereira, Colombia. pic.twitter.com/r3v2lW5pU3 — Alerta News 24 (@AlertaNews24) August 10, 2026

The government put the number of damaged homes at more than 1,500, with 37 destroyed and 61 buildings completely collapsed, along with damage to 18 health centers, 52 schools, 17 community centers and 18 roads. The civil aviation authority suspended operations at seven air terminals: Cali, Pereira, Manizales, Quibdó, Armenia, Cartago and Buenaventura.

Damage to the hospital network is among the most critical. In Cali, the Hospital Universitario del Valle partially collapsed and seven large health care institutions were closed and evacuated because of structural damage. Valle del Cauca governor Dilian Francisca Toro said at least five intensive care patients were trapped under rubble. Cali mayor Alejandro Eder reported at least twenty collapsed structures with people trapped inside and requested rescue teams from Bogotá and Medellín. The capital's mayor, Carlos Fernando Galán, dispatched a hundred rescue workers.

De la Espriella agreed to declare a national disaster situation and is leading a unified command post at the National Disaster Risk Management Unit, with additional posts in Armenia and Quibdó. The foreign ministry is coordinating international cooperation. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the bloc was ready to provide assistance.

The Colombian Geological Service reported two aftershocks, of magnitude 2.8 and 4.8. The agency also recorded an emission of ash and gases from the Puracé volcano, in Cauca department, on orange alert since July, coinciding in time with the earthquake.

World.title: Colombia and Venezuela quakes are unconnected despite similar magnitude, experts say
World.content:
Colombia and Venezuela quakes are unconnected despite similar magnitude, experts say

11th Tuesday, August 2026 - 10:11 UTC Full article

“The Venezuelan earthquakes are shallower and involve a different mechanism, a strike-slip mechanism. This one is deeper, a subduction earthquake,” a seismologist stressed

The magnitude 7.4 earthquake that struck western and central Colombia on Monday has a different tectonic origin from the earthquakes recorded in Venezuela in June, despite comparable magnitudes, said Viviana Dionisio, a seismologist with Colombia's National Seismological Network.

“It was a tectonic earthquake associated mainly with a subduction mechanism,” the specialist said. That process occurs when the Nazca plate, beneath the Pacific Ocean, slides under the South American plate, on which Colombia's mainland territory sits. Energy accumulated at the contact between the two can be released in large earthquakes, of the kind historically recorded around the Pacific Ring of Fire.

The Venezuelan earthquakes of June 24, of magnitudes 7.2 and 7.4, responded to a different mechanism. According to Dionisio, they originated in the interaction between the Caribbean and South American plates through lateral displacement, known as strike-slip faulting. “The Venezuelan earthquakes are shallower and involve a different mechanism, a strike-slip mechanism. This one is deeper, a subduction earthquake,” she stressed.

Depth is the factor explaining why two earthquakes of similar magnitude can cause very different damage. The focus of the Colombian quake was located at around one hundred kilometers, according to revised data from the Colombian Geological Service, which in its first bulletin had placed it at 82. In shallow earthquakes, waves travel a shorter distance and reach areas near the epicenter with greater intensity; in deep ones they pass through more material and lose energy along the way. The seismologist warned, however, that depth alone does not determine the extent of damage, which also depends on the vulnerability of buildings and ground conditions.

The epicenter was located in San José del Palmar, in Chocó department, on the boundary with Risaralda and Valle del Cauca. Dionisio said it is not unusual for an earthquake of these characteristics to originate in that region, given the tectonic dynamics of western Colombia.

The Colombian Geological Service has recorded more than thirty aftershocks, the strongest of magnitude 4.8. “An earthquake of this magnitude generates a certain number of aftershocks that generally decrease in frequency and magnitude over the following days or weeks,” the seismologist said.

Rodrigo León, of the Geosciences Department at Universidad de los Andes, noted that earthquakes cannot be predicted, nor is it possible to anticipate when an aftershock will occur or to rule out larger movements. He also considered that, given the magnitude of the event, the damage could have been worse. The provisional toll exceeds 130 dead.

World.title: American Airlines resumes its seasonal Montevideo-Miami route in December
World.content:
American Airlines resumes its seasonal Montevideo-Miami route in December

11th Tuesday, August 2026 - 10:00 UTC Full article

The operation is not the restoration of a discontinued route but the reopening of a service the company suspends each year outside the tourist season

American Airlines will restart its seasonal service between Carrasco International Airport and Miami International Airport on December 3, once again becoming the only carrier offering nonstop flights between Uruguay and the United States during the peak summer season.

The operation is not the restoration of a discontinued route but the reopening of a service the company suspends each year outside the tourist season. The change from the previous cycle is the extension of the daily-frequency stretch: in 2025-2026 daily flights ran until February 11, while this season they will continue until March 2, 2027, some three weeks longer.

From that date, the connection will operate three times a week, on Mondays, Thursdays and Saturdays, until March 28, 2027, when the scheduled season ends.

The route will be flown by a Boeing 787-8 with capacity for 234 passengers, in a configuration of 20 Business class seats, 28 in Premium Economy and 186 in the main cabin. According to the itinerary released by the airline, flights from Miami will depart at 22:55 and arrive in Montevideo at 10:10 the following day. In the opposite direction, departures from Carrasco are set for 22:30, landing in Miami at 05:45. Times are local and subject to change. The journey takes approximately nine hours.

“After nearly three decades of dedicated service to Uruguay, we are delighted to resume our daily seasonal flights in Montevideo for the busiest period of the summer,” said Pascual Álvarez, the company's managing director of operations for South America, Central America and the Caribbean. He said the route targets both international travelers visiting Uruguay and Uruguayan passengers connecting from Miami to other destinations.

Miami is the airline's main international connecting hub, with more than 400 daily flights in peak season to over 200 destinations, according to company figures.

At Aeropuertos Uruguay, the concession holder for the Carrasco terminal, commercial director Matías Carluccio said the reactivation “strengthens Uruguay's access to the United States and broadens travel options for passengers seeking to connect our country with new international destinations.” He added that the company would continue working to support the growth of air connectivity.

American Airlines has operated in Uruguay for close to thirty years. The Miami connection is the only direct route between the South American country and US territory, and its calendar coincides with the busiest tourist season in the River Plate.

World.title: Made in Mexico: Why UNAM is more than a university
World.content:
Listen to this article

As 58,000 university applicants sit a rerun of an entrance exam this month, it’s worth asking where exactly they are competing to enter. Their goal, the National Autonomous University of Mexico (UNAM), is an institution with 475 years of history, a campus built on a lava field, and a claim on Mexican public life that no other university comes close to.

Between Aug. 12 and 19, tens of thousands of Mexican teenagers are filing into convention centers in León, Oaxaca, Tijuana and Mexico City to take an entrance exam most of them had already passed. UNAM ran its undergraduate admissions test entirely online for the first time this year, with AI-supervised proctoring.

It did not hold. Some 2% of exams were annulled outright, score distributions looked nothing like the previous five years, enrollment was frozen across every degree program, and a technical commission recommended that a large slice of the applicant pool prove their results again, in person, with human invigilators watching.

That a single university can pause its own school year and hold the country’s attention for a month is itself the story. Here is why it can.

A university older than the country
