World.title: Riesgos y consejos para proteger a los niños durante el eclipse de Sol total
World.content: La falsa sensación de seguridad durante el eclipse solar de este miércoles es uno aspectos que más preocupan a los expertos ya que durante este tipo de fenómenos el Sol no deslumbra como en un día normal y la radiación puede dañar la retina de la misma manera. ¿Y si vamos a ver el eclipse con niños? Pues a todas las recomendaciones de seguridad se unen algunas específicas para los menores, como explica en este vídeo Julio Álvarez, Jefe de Pediatría del Hospital General de Valencia. Álvarez recomienda explicar bien a los niños lo que va a ocurrir, plantear juegos y evitar la exposición. “No hay un tiempo mínimo seguro de exposición. No se puede mirar al sol sin las gafas”, alerta el pediatra, que incide en que la radiación puede provocar lesiones en la retina que no se pueden tratar.

World.title: Colombia se vuelca en el rescate de los supervivientes del terremoto: “No se desgasten aquí, la única señal de vida es en el otro lado”
World.content:
El sismo de magnitud 7,4 deja más de dos centenares de muertos en un país que lanza un despliegue urgente de bomberos, militares y vecinos

El alcalde de Pereira, Mauricio Salazar, no puede contener las lágrimas al hablar de sus vecinos: su municipio concentra 73 de los 224 muertos que ha dejado hasta ahora el terremoto de este lunes. Un reportero de televisión termina consolándolo en directo. Poco después, vuelve a quebrarse frente a los micrófonos. Las poblaciones afectadas se debaten entre la conmoción y la urgencia de sacar sobrevivientes de entre los escombros. Las primeras 72 horas, el plazo que dan los expertos en rescates antes de que la esperanza se empiece a apagar, no tardarán en llegar.

La larga sacudida, de magnitud 7,4, ha dejado al menos cuatro departamentos del suroccidente de Colombia con decenas de edificios colapsados, miles de viviendas inhabitables y un número de desaparecidos que va cambiando en cada actualización. Tan solo 24 horas después del temblor —que llegó a sentirse durante cuatro eternos minutos—, las labores de rescate continuaban en las regiones más afectadas con ayuda de maquinaria pesada, rescatistas y militares.

Pereira, puerta de entrada al Eje Cafetero, uno de los destinos turísticos más buscados de Colombia, vive una extraña normalidad. La mayoría de los comercios de esta ciudad de más de 800.000 habitantes están cerrados, pero el tráfico es intenso a pesar de las restricciones de movilidad. Se oyen ambulancias de vez en cuando. Pocas. Algunos de sus vecinos cocinan en enormes ollas que calientan en fuegos improvisados en la calle.

Voluntarios trabajan en los escombros de un edificio en busca de sobrevivientes, en el centro de Pereira, este martes. Chelo Camacho Un ciudadano se refresca tras los trabajos de remoción de escombros. Chelo Camacho El centro de Pereira, una de las zonas más afectadas tras ekl sismo de este lunes. Chelo Camacho Rescatistas trabajan durante la noche en busca de sobrevivientes en edificio al sur de Cali, sector Tequendama. Jair F. Coll

En una zona que una noche normal daría miedo, este martes decenas de hombres buscaban a Luis Carlos Valera, el barbero, de 60 años y sin familiares cercanos en la ciudad. El local donde trabajaba quedó aplastado bajo los restos de un hotel de mala muerte, de 8.000 pesos o dos euros la noche. Entre sus rescatadores hay bomberos, vecinos y pequeños delincuentes del barrio. “¡Silencio!”, gritan. Esperan algún sonido para saber dónde buscarlo. “Luis Carlos, da un golpe si nos oyes”, le pide uno de ellos. Se escucha algo, imperceptible, y siguen escarbando. “Denos instrucciones y las seguimos”, pide con educación el líder de los rescatistas improvisados.

El capitán de bomberos Luis Reyes se pasea por la zona intentando ordenar los esfuerzos. “No se desgasten por aquí, la única señal de vida que tenemos es a ese otro lado del edificio”, ruega a un grupo de obreros contratados por un señor desconocido. Dicen que el barbero llegó a gritar algo pocas horas después de quedar sepultado. Reyes está en realidad en busca del “pluma”—como llama al líder del sector, una autoridad equivalente y que recibe el mismo nombre del cabecilla de un patio de cárcel—, el único capaz de coordinar y apaciguar a esos hombres de mala vida a quienes necesita de su lado. “Es un entorno delicado”, explica el bombero.

A pesar del despliegue urgente de maquinaria pesada y fuerza pública, hay lugares en Pereira donde aún se echa en falta más organización. “Aquí hace falta policía para organizar este desorden. ¿Sabe por qué? Porque no hay institucionalidad y no queremos accidentes”, advierte Reyes, funcionario local, mientras dos hombres sortean la calle en ruinas con una lavadora llena de ropa. No es un novato: atendió el terremoto de 1999, que dejó más de 1.000 personas muertas en la misma región, se ha formado internacionalmente en rescate en estructuras colapsadas, y ha sido instructor en esa especialidad en otros países de América Latina.

La vida normal está paralizada, pero todos están en movimiento. Incluido el presidente Abelardo de La Espriella, que en su fugaz paso por Pereira, en la mañana de este martes, aseguró que se le arrugaba el corazón al ver tantos comercios destruidos en el centro de la ciudad. El mandatario anunció la exención de pagos de servicios públicos durante tres meses y subsidios para los que perdieron sus viviendas. El ministro de Hacienda anunciaba, poco después, que el Gobierno decretará un estado de emergencia económica para atender la tragedia.

Voluntarios trabajan en los escombros de un edificio, en el centro de Pereira, este martes. Chelo Camacho

Mientras tanto, la búsqueda de los desaparecidos sigue en la calle y en las redes. Los mensajes se multiplican por grupos de WhatsApp. “Henry Palacio y Sonia de la Pava, dos personas de la tercera edad, son buscadas, no han tenido comunicación con ellos. Estaban en la Unidad Residencial Verona I de Pereira”. “Se busca a la familia Lozano Mora en Cali, ayúdanos a encontrarlos”. Entre las personas que no han podido ser localizadas después del terremoto hay 164 españoles, según ha informado el ministro de Asuntos Exteriores, José Manuel Albares.

En Cali, justamente, las autoridades buscan a por lo menos 21 desaparecidos. Entre ellos están Violeta, de 7 años, y su abuela Amparo. Allí, como en Pereira, tras el terremoto la ciudad entró en una operación de emergencia que movilizó a miles de personas entre miembros de los organismos de socorro y de las fuerzas de seguridad, y ciudadanos que salieron espontáneamente a ayudar. Con casi dos millones de habitantes, sus muertos se acercan al centenar, según los datos más recientes.

Hacia las nueve de la mañana del lunes, menos de hora y media después de la sacudida, los bomberos ya escalaban las montañas de ruinas. Uno de los que atendió la emergencia en La Alameda, una zona de comercio popular del centro de la ciudad, contaba que había llegado por sus propios medios, tan pronto pudo. Muchos de los rescatistas que se agolpaban allí eran voluntarios, espontáneos que se movilizaron orgánicamente. La escena se repetía en otros puntos.

Marlene Carrillo, una mujer de 70 años, cuenta cómo lo vivió en el barrio Cuarto de Legua, en el suroeste y a menos de un kilómetro del auditorio en el que, el viernes anterior, tomaba posesión el presidente de Colombia, Abelardo de la Espriella. “La respuesta ha sido muy rápida. Al ratico de que pasara todo, empezó a llegar la gente a ayudar a salir a los que quedaban adentro”, decía sobre las edificaciones desplomadas en las laderas de la ciudad, la zona más afectada.

Más información La ciudadanía en la primera línea de los rescates en Colombia, en imágenes

Los equipos de rescate han organizado las labores, coordinando a los voluntarios. Familias enteras han armado cadenas humanas para retirar los escombros con sus manos. Es una cooperación espontánea que ha aliviado a los habitantes de la tercera ciudad más poblada del país y que va más allá de los rescates. Así lo explica Amparo Olarte, encargada de regular el tránsito en una intersección en la que colapsó una edificación, una clínica veterinaria en la que aparentemente hay tres personas atrapadas: “La solidaridad de la gente es grande. Nos ha llegado comida, agua; las manos sobran para ayudar”.

No es una voz aislada. “Los centros de acopio están llenos de víveres y de agua. Hay mucha gente dispuesta a ayudar, médicos, personas del común como yo que llegamos para atender como podamos”, coincide Angie Osorio, residente del barrio El Trébol, en el noroeste de la capital del Valle del Cauca, informa Isabella Bernal Vega desde Cali.

Mientras tanto, en el Chocó, el cercano pero empobrecido departamento donde se dio el epicentro del terremoto, la búsqueda avanza más lentamente. Un territorio con dificultades de conexión, mucho más rural y de población dispersa, cuenta por ahora sus víctimas fatales en 13. De la Espriella lo visitó el martes y ha dejado allí al comandante del Ejército para coordinar las labores y servir de enlace entre el Ejecutivo nacional y las autoridades locales.

Este es el segundo gran terremoto que sacude la región en poco más de 50 días, después del doble sismo que dejó en Venezuela más de 6.300 fallecidos. Las comparaciones entre ambas tragedias se están multiplicando en redes. Unos ensalzan la eficacia de las autoridades colombianas frente a las venezolanas. Otros recuerdan que, igual que en el país vecino, aquí también ha sido la propia gente la que ha sacado a los suyos con sus manos y culpan a los periodistas de haber leído ese esfuerzo vecinal como un signo de indolencia del Gobierno de Delcy Rodríguez, y no una prueba de una sociedad solidaria y activa.

Ambos sismos son muy distintos, tanto por su naturaleza como por el tipo de edificios que han sido afectados y, en consecuencia, por el número de víctimas. Y también por la respuesta de cada Estado. En Venezuela, la magnitud del terremoto desbordó a todos y solo se podía acceder al lugar por una única vía que colapsó sin que las autoridades lograsen evitarlo. En Colombia se han decretado toques de queda nocturnos en Pereira y Cali, y se han desplegado con rapidez soldados, policías, bomberos, voluntarios y maquinaria, pese a que son varias las zonas devastadas y están muy distantes entre sí. Las vías de toda la región afectada enfrentan varios bloqueos por deslaves y caídas de rocas; algunos puentes se han desplomado o averiado, y los aeropuertos fueron cerrados, aunque han ido reabriendo a medida que se descartan daños mayores.

En Quibdó, la capital del selvático departamento del Chocó en la que murieron por lo menos nueve personas, la gobernadora sobrevuela drones junto a militares en busca de víctimas, aunque pide maquinaria para remover escombros. En Cali, quizás la ciudad más afectada, se juntaron en las primeras horas más de 1.600 personas entre bomberos, miembros de la Cruz Roja e integrantes de los equipos USAR (especializados en labores de búsqueda y rescate especializados), policía o militares. Las grúas, ese unicornio tan difícil de encontrar en La Guaira, la zona cero del terremoto en Venezuela, están frente a los edificios desde pocas horas después del sacudón.

Ciudadanos de Pereira trabajan quitando los escombros de un edificio en busca de sobrevivientes. Chelo Camacho

Por otro lado, la ayuda internacional coordinada por la ONU, que fue fundamental en Venezuela, en Colombia ni siquiera se ha pedido. El Gobierno de De la Espriella, que acusa de “globalista” a la institución multilateral, no ha organizado la recepción. El embajador de China le ha pedido públicamente definir un interlocutor para ella. Y Nayib Bukele, el presidente de El Salvador, de quien el recién inaugurado mandatario colombiano ha mostrado ser seguidor, ha explicado que Colombia dice no requerir ayuda para los rescates. “Nos han informado que sus equipos de rescate, médicos y demás cuerpos de emergencia se encuentran desplegados y atendiendo la situación, por lo que, en este momento, no requieren apoyo de personal”, escribía en X a inicios de la tarde de este martes. Informó que envía, entonces, 100 toneladas de ayuda humanitaria, insumos y no expertos.

Abelardo de la Espriella, que encaró el terremoto en su tercer día como presidente, ha encontrado en el terremoto un perfecto escaparate para vender a su nuevo Gobierno. El presidente se coordinó con gobernadores y alcaldes, distribuyó a los hombres fuertes de su gabinete por las regiones más afectadas y pasó la jornada actualizando datos de fallecidos, desaparecidos, heridos, personas atrapadas, rescatadas e infraestructuras dañadas. Pese a ello, no hay una cifra centralizada y actualizada de afectaciones. Si a fines de la mañana el presidente hablaba de 181 muertos, la Asociación de Ciudades Capitales tenía desde más temprano esa misma cifra solo en sus afiliadas, como Pereira y Cali, mientras otras autoridades suman decenas más en otros lugares.

También viajó: de Barranquilla a Bogotá para organizar, luego a Quibdó, el martes a Pereira. No perdió la oportunidad de soltar arengas religiosas y propagandísticas, pero ha ido recorriendo todas las regiones afectadas, parte de su promesa de gobernar en el territorio y no en el escritorio. Entrada la noche del lunes, cuando decenas de personas seguían buscando supervivientes con linternas, el expresidente Gustavo Petro recomendaba ver la segunda temporada de Cien años de soledad en Netflix.

World.title: Ukrainian soldier murdered by Soviets exhumed in Rotterdam
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

The remains of a Ukrainian soldier who was murdered in Rotterdam by the Soviet secret services in 1938 are being repatriated for a military burial.

Colonel Yevhen Konovalets, the founder of a Ukrainian nationalist group, was killed by a bomb concealed in a box of chocolates as he walked home from a meeting with an undercover agent.

The Soviet spy had infiltrated the Organisation of Ukrainian Nationalists (OUN) and handed Konovalets the chocolates as a gift during a meeting at a hotel in Rotterdam on May 23, 1938.

Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky announced on his official website that the colonel’s remains had been exhumed at Crooswijk Cemetery in Rotterdam so that they could be sent back to Ukraine.

He will be temporarily reinterred at the National Military Memorial Cemetery, in preparation for a farewell ceremony will be held at the Ukrainan Greek Catholic cathedral in Kyiv.

The OUN was founded in 1929 in Vienna as a right-wing nationalist organisation that aimed to establish an independent, ethnically homogenous Ukrainian state.

It was influenced in its early days by Italian fascism and German Nazism, but as Germany’s defeat in the Second World War drew nearer, the OUN adopted a more democratic ideology.

World.title: ABN Amro profit climbs to €781m as fees, lending grow
World.content:
ABN Amro has booked net profit of €781 million in the second quarter, up 29% on the same period last year and ahead of analyst forecasts, the bank said on Wednesday.

Analysts had expected earnings of around €686 million. The result beat even the highest forecast in that consensus, and shares in the group rose more than 5% to a record high.

The bank, which is now around one-fifth owned by the Dutch state after reducing its stake following the 2008 financial crisis, is in the process of a reorganisation that will cut 5,200 jobs by 2028.

The state is close to recouping the full €21.7 billion cost of the 2008 nationalisation of the bank, following a share price rally that took the bank’s stock above €40 this week.

World.title: Limburg wildfire wiped out rare juniper shrubland
World.content:
Fewer than 100 of the roughly 4,000 juniper bushes that grew in the Boschhuizerbergen nature reserve near Venray have survived this month’s wildfire in northern Limburg, the foundation that manages the site says.

The reserve held the largest juniper shrubland in the southern Netherlands, according to Het Limburgs Landschap, with some bushes more than 130 years old. Junipers grow slowly and thrive in the reserve’s nutrient-poor, drifting-sand soil – conditions that have become rare in the region.

The fire, which broke out on August 3, destroyed around 100 hectares, including 20 to 30 hectares of protected Natura 2000 land where the junipers stood. More than a week on, crews were still pouring water on smouldering hotspots to stop them reigniting.

The shrubland might not be able to be re-established, as the soil has changed over the decades and young plants may struggle to take root. “It is questionable whether we will ever get such a beautiful shrubland here again. I am afraid I will not live to see it,” the foundation’s Loek Hendrikx told broadcaster NOS.

Het Limburgs Landschap, set up in 1931 to stop the reserve being cleared for farmland, has appealed for donations towards a recovery it says will take years.

World.title: Human rights groups sue US government over Hague court sanctions
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Four US human rights organisations have sued the Trump administration over its sanctions against the International Criminal Court in The Hague, arguing the measures are unconstitutional and should be struck down.

The American Friends Service Committee, the Center for Constitutional Rights, Human Rights Watch and the Open Society Institute filed the complaint in New York on Tuesday.

It challenges the executive order signed by US president Donald Trump in February 2025, which authorised sanctions on court officials and on anyone assisting its investigations.

Washington has since used it against the court’s former chief prosecutor and two of his deputies, eight of its judges, a UN human rights expert and three Palestinian rights organisations.

The four organisations say the measures have forced them to drop work such as representing war crimes victims and making legal submissions to the court, in breach of their rights to free speech, association and religion under the US constitution.

They also argue the order exceeds the president’s powers and rests on a declared national emergency that has no basis in fact, describing it as a “blatantly illegal attack on international justice”.

Liz Evenson, international justice director at Human Rights Watch, said governments should step up to protect the court and those seeking justice before it.

The case follows Washington’s announcement in July of a campaign to dismantle the court, which the Netherlands hosts and has a duty as host state to protect.

Federal courts in New York and Maine ruled in 2025 that the order breached free speech protections, blocking enforcement against the claimants in those cases.

World.title: Roberto Martinez front-runner to be next Netherlands head coach
World.content:
The Dutch football association KNVB is reportedly lining up Roberto Martinez to take over from Ronald Koeman as coach of the national men’s team,.

The 53-year-old Spaniard emerged as a surprise contender after candidates such as former Feyenoord and Liverpool manager Arne Slot, former Ajax and Manchester United coach Erik ten Hag and PSV boss Peter Bosz ruled themselves out.

The KNVB held talks at the weekend with under-21 coach Michael Reiziger, but there have been no further discussions since Sunday, the Telegraaf reported on Wednesday.

Louis van Gaal also sent an open application to Zeist last week saying he was ready to step in for a fourth spell in charge, but the KNVB has not followed up with the 75-year-old former Ajax trainer.

Martinez was in charge of Portugal during the recent World Cup in North America, resigning after the team lost 1-0 to eventual winners Spain in the round of 16.

Previously he coached Belgium for six years, reaching the World Cup semi-final in 2018. He would be the first foreign manager to coach Oranje since Ernst Happel in 1978.

World.title: Uncertain future for Dutch bike brands after Accell goes under
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

The Netherlands’ largest bicycle manufacturer, Accell, has been declared insolvent, leaving an uncertain future for major brands such as Batavus, Sparta and the British-based bike maker Raleigh.

A court appointed curators last week when Accell applied to suspend payments to its creditors, the last step before insolvency in the Netherlands.

In a statement, the curators said they would explore all options, including a relaunch for Accell’s Dutch operations, based in Amsterdam. The company’s other European branches remain in business.

CEO Jonas Nilsson said: “Every realistic option for the future of the business has been tirelessly explored, and none has resulted in a solution to continue the group in its current form.”

Irish media reported that Quanta Capital, a Dublin-based investment firm founded by former road race cyclist Mel Sutcliffe, was preparing a bid with a number of other investors. Sutcliffe sold Eurotrek Raleigh Ireland to Accell 10 years ago.

Pandemic buyout

Accell was bought by a consortium led by New York-based private equity firm KKR for €1.8 billon in 2022 following a surge in demand for bicycles during the coronavirus pandemic.

But the company struggled to produce bikes fast enough and its costs rose after it ordered too many components in anticipation of a sustained rise in sales that never materialised.

By the time supply chains recovered after lockdown, Accell was left with a mountain of unsold bikes that it had to sell at a discount to limit its losses. Revenues fell 22% in 2024 to just over €1 billion.

Accell closed the Netherlands’ last remaining bike factory, the Batavus plant in Heerenveen, last year, shifting production to Hungary and shedding 160 jobs.

Babboe recall

The company was also hit by the mass recall of 22,000 Babboe cargo bikes after it received hundreds of complaints about the frames breaking on the road, which cost it tens of millions of euros as well as severe reputational damage.

The consumer standards agency NVWA briefly banned Babboe from selling new bikes and launched a criminal investigation amid allegations that the company had tried to cover up the flaws.

The collapse of Accell leaves the Netherlands with only one major bike maker, Gazelle, based in Dieren, as well as a handful of smaller manufacturers such as Kruitbosch (whose brands include Cortina) and Azor.

The consumer protection agency Consumentenbond has advised owners of Accell-made bikes to check the status of their guarantee with the shop or retailer where they bought it. Some replacement parts are still available because they were made by other companies.

World.title: Fire station break-ins soar as criminals steal rescue gear
World.content:
Break-ins at Dutch fire stations, which have risen sharply this year, are threatening life-saving work, the police have said. Criminal gangs are stealing the cutting equipment crews use to free people trapped in crashed cars, which they can be used for robberies.

There were 17 break-ins or attempted break-ins at fire stations in 2024 and 18 in 2025, broadcaster NOS reported. So far this year there have been 50. Stations in Maassluis, Aalsmeer and Ten Boer were all targeted in the past week.

The police, the fire service and the public prosecution department have begun working together nationally to stop the thefts. “One way or another, we are going to put a stop to this,” Jos van der Stap of the national police told NOS.

Police believe experienced criminals have discovered a market for the specialist tools. Van der Stap said they are being used in raids on jewellers and, abroad, to break open cash machines, and have turned up in several places across Europe.

Steven van der Looij of Brandweer Nederland, the national fire service organisation, said staff who work day and night at stations find it terrible thatpeople are coming into the buildings. Both quiet rural stations and busy city ones staffed around the clock have been hit.

Locking the equipment away is not straightforward. Everything on a fire engine is laid out so it can be grabbed at speed, Van der Looij said, and every extra lock has to be undone again. “Every second counts.”

Security cameras are being installed at some stations and windows are being replaced with mirrored glass.

World.title: Mental health services lose track of 62,500 people, says report
World.content:
A quarter of adults with a severe mental illness in the Netherlands – an estimated 62,500 people – are receiving no or insufficient care and have dropped out of sight of mental health services altogether, according to a report from the sector body de Nederlandse GGZ.

The organisation puts the total number of adults with a severe mental illness at around 250,000. What goes wrong, it says, is rarely the treatment itself but the handover – the point at which someone leaves a clinic, moves house or finishes a prison sentence.

“A discharge from a clinic, a house move or the end of a period in detention must not become the moment at which someone loses their support,” GGZ chair Ruth Peetoom said in a statement on Tuesday. “A psychological vulnerability does not disappear when a care pathway or an assessment comes to an end.”

Nowhere to go

The housing crisis is one of the biggest obstacles in helping patients through the transition out of care. The report calculates that 3,980 social housing units are needed each year for people leaving sheltered accommodation, but only 1,320 came free in 2023.

Around 33,000 people aged between 18 and 65 were registered as homeless at the start of 2024.

The pattern is similar for people leaving prison. Of the roughly 5,000 people released each year after more than three months inside, 27% are homeless or have no known address immediately afterwards, and almost half reoffend within two years.

Outreach

The report calls for assertive outreach – teams that actively go looking for people who are not asking for help – to be made a statutory duty for councils again.

It has not been one since social care was devolved in 2015, and funding is now split between health insurers, councils and central government, on top of the pressure on waiting lists that has already prompted legal action against the state.

Debate about severe mental illness in the Netherlands is dominated by figures on nuisance and public safety, the report says. It puts the number of people who pose a safety risk to others at around 1,500, against 24,000 to 60,000 who are a risk to themselves, through self-neglect, homelessness or avoiding care.

If you are struggling with your mental health, support is available. The MIND Hulplijn offers free, anonymous advice on 0900-1450, on weekdays from 9am to 9pm, or via mindhulplijn.nl. In a crisis, contact your family doctor or call 113.

The proportion of Poles who hold a negative view of Polish-Ukrainian relations has risen to 46%, the highest figure ever recorded by Polish state research agency CBOS. Only 12% think relations are good. By contrast, three years ago, in mid-2023, only 3% had a negative view and 64% a positive one. Meanwhile, CBOS also found that belief among Poles that reconciliation between the two neighbours, who share a difficult history, is possible is at its lowest level on record, 53%, down from 78% three years ago. The findings follow other polls showing worsening attitudes towards Ukraine and Ukrainians in Poland in recent years, and come amid an ongoing diplomatic crisis triggered by President Volodymyr Zelensky naming a military unit after a group that massacred Poles in World War Two. Przekonanie o możliwości pojednania między Polakami 🇵🇱 a Ukraińcami 🇺🇦 spadło do najniższego poziomu w historii naszych pomiarów. 📙 Więcej w komunikacie #CBOS "Stosunki polsko-ukraińskie" ⤵️ https://t.co/kw2o4upY3Q#Ukraina #Ukraińcy pic.twitter.com/LItCFC3f2m — CBOS (@CBOS_Info) August 11, 2026 Relations between Poland and Ukraine improved significantly in the wake of Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, as Poland welcomed millions of Ukrainian refugees and provided Kyiv with extensive military, humanitarian and diplomatic support. However, since 2023, those relations have been hit by a series of controversies over Ukrainian agricultural exports, border blockades by Polish farmers and truckers, and, above all, over the two nations’ difficult World War Two history. Among Poles who now hold a negative view of relations, CBOS also asked them who was responsible for the situation. A large majority, 65%, primarily blamed Ukraine, while only 4% said it was Poland’s fault and 28% placed responsibility on both sides. In its regular surveys since 1997, the agency has also asked Poles if they believe that reconciliation between Poles and Ukrainians is possible or not. In the early 2000s, that figure rose to a record level of 81%, and in 2023 it still stood at 78%. Now, however, it has dropped to an all-time low of 53%. There have long been tensions between Poland and Ukraine over their difficult, intertwined histories, in particular during the first half of the 20th century. In World War Two, Ukrainian nationalists killed around 100,000 Polish civilians, mostly women and children, in an ethnic-cleansing operation known as the Volhynia massacres. Poland has officially recognised that episode as a genocide. However, Ukraine rejects that label and also points to the persecution of Ukrainians who lived in the interwar Polish state, as well as to massacres of Ukrainians by Polish groups during World War Two. Long-simmering tensions between Poland and Ukraine over WWII massacres have finally boiled over, prompting a diplomatic crisis.@danieltilles1 looks at how we got here and what it may mean for the two countries and Europe more broadly https://t.co/a8tiYJJHRr — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 22, 2026 Those tensions recently boiled over after Zelensky, in May this year, approved a request to rename a military unit after the “heroes of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA)”, the group that led the Volhynia massacres but is remembered positively in Ukraine for its role in fighting Moscow-imposed Soviet rule. Zelensky’s decision prompted his Polish counterpart, Karol Nawrocki, to strip the Ukrainian president of Poland’s highest honour. While tensions have since calmed somewhat, the dispute remains unresolved. However, even before that diplomatic crisis broke out, polling showed increasingly negative attitudes in Poland towards both Ukraine and Ukrainians, who are by far the country’s largest immigrant group. In its annual survey of attitudes towards various national and ethnic groups, published in February, CBOS found that the proportion of Poles who said they disliked Ukrainians had increased by five percentage points year-on-year, to 43%. Only 29% said they liked Ukrainians. In January, CBOS reported that opposition to accepting Ukrainian refugees in Poland had risen to its highest ever level. In December 2024, a poll in Ukraine found that positive sentiment towards Poles had fallen by half in the space of two years. The proportion of Poles opposed to accepting Ukrainian refugees has reached its highest ever level of 46%, up from 3% in the wake of Russia's full-scale invasion. Other recent surveys have also indicated declining sympathy towards Ukrainians among Poles https://t.co/DLPGY2ToZG — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 7, 2026 Meanwhile, the number of reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland rose by 30% in the first half of 2026, including a number of high-profile incidents. Poland’s government has blamed increasing anti-Ukrainian rhetoric from the right-wing and far-right opposition. Last month, Ukraine’s foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, called on “Polish politicians to stop inciting hatred against Ukrainians”. CBOS’s new study shows that attitudes towards relations with Ukraine differ significantly depending on political affiliation. Whereas 35% of supporters of the centrist Civic Coalition (KO), Poland’s main ruling party, hold a negative view of relations, that rises to 52% among voters of the national-conservative opposition Law and Justice (PiS) party and 81% for the far-right Confederation (Konfederacja). Among those with a negative view, 49% of KO voters blamed Poland and Ukraine equally for the situation while 10% blamed mainly Poland. By contrast, 86% of Confederation supporters and 82% of PiS supporters placed responsibility on the Ukrainian side. Demonstrations took place in 25 Polish cities on Sunday against the “growing wave of hate and violence” against Ukrainians, who are Poland’s largest immigrant group. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland has unveiled its first frigate to enter service in decades at a ceremony in the Baltic Sea port of Gdynia, where the ship was constructed. The development marks a major milestone in a 15 billion zloty (€3.5 billion) programme to modernise the ageing Polish navy and strengthen NATO’s maritime defences. “Poland is becoming a maritime power in the Baltic Sea,” declared Prime Minister Donald Tusk at a ceremony to name the new ship, which he attended alongside opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki in a rare show of unity. Na terenie PGZ Stoczni Wojennej w Gdyni prezydent RP Karol Nawrocki, @PremierRP @donaldtusk oraz wiceministrowie @MON_GOV_PL @magdasobkowiak i @pawelbejda uczestniczą w uroczystości chrztu pierwszej jednostki programu „Miecznik”, fregaty wielozadaniowej – przyszłego ORP Wicher. pic.twitter.com/X2ftjoKTLZ — Ministerstwo Obrony Narodowej 🇵🇱 (@MON_GOV_PL) August 12, 2026 The ORP Wicher, a medium-sized warship designed for escort, air defence and other fleet protection duties, is the first of three multi-role frigates based on Britain’s Arrowhead 140 design being built under Poland’s Miecznik programme, the largest modernisation project in the history of the Polish Navy. It is due to be launched on Thursday in a complex manoeuvre involving its transfer and controlled launch from a semi-submersible barge. Shipyard officials have described the operation as one of the most demanding engineering projects undertaken by Poland’s shipbuilding industry. The three frigates are intended to form the core of Poland’s surface fleet and will replace Poland’s two current Oliver Hazard Perry-class frigates, which were constructed in the 1970s and transferred from the US Navy in the years 2000 and 2002. Ahead of Wicher’s launch, leading Polish officials attended the naming ceremony in Gdynia, including Tusk and Nawrocki, who are normally bitter rivals but have sought to present a more united front when it comes to national defence. “There can be no arguments or disputes when it comes to our country’s security,” said Tusk, who declared that Poland was seeking to play a role in “determining not only its own future, but also the entire region and Europe”. Nawrocki, meanwhile, said that the modernisation of the Polish navy “sends a clear message that we will develop our armed forces in every theatre – on water, on land, and in the air”. Both leaders also hailed the fact that the new frigates are being built in Poland itself, helping bolster the Polish shipbuilding industry. Prezydent RP @NawrockiKn w #Gdynia: Życzę, abyście zawsze szczęśliwie wracali do portu, któremu na imię Polska. pic.twitter.com/hHia2sCZfn — Kancelaria Prezydenta RP (@prezydentpl) August 12, 2026 The contract for the three frigates was signed in 2021 between Poland’s state Armament Agency (AU) and a consortium led by state-owned defence group PGZ, with British defence firm Babcock and other foreign partners also involved. The project was initially valued at about 8 billion zloty but had risen to around 15 billion zloty by the end of 2023 following amendments. Construction of the second frigate in Gdynia’s military shipyard began in May 2025, while work on the third began in April this year. The programme is scheduled to be completed by the end of 2031. Swedish defence giant Saab has signed a strategic collaboration agreement with Polish state defence group PGZ. The firms will cooperate on naval production, servicing and technology, including establishing an underwater technology centre in Poland https://t.co/dykKjMIAzX — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 15, 2026 The ships are more than 140 metres long and are based on Britain’s Arrowhead 140 design, developed by Babcock and adapted to Polish military requirements. The frigates will be equipped with British CAMM and CAMM-ER surface-to-air missiles, naval guns and anti-ship missiles capable of striking targets at ranges of more than 200 km. Their missions will include protecting shipping lanes and critical energy infrastructure and taking part in NATO naval groups. It now has the highest relative defence budget in NATO and is also the alliance’s largest arms importer. In recent years, Poland has also increasingly oriented itself towards the Baltic region, forming closer economic, energy and military ties with allies around the sea. Last year, Poland and Sweden signed a strategic partnership on defence and economic ties. They subsequently held their first ever bilateral military exercises in the Baltic. As part of its naval modernisation programme, Poland has selected Sweden’s Saab as the supplier for three advanced A26 stealth submarines. World.title: Negative views of Poland’s justice system have grown under Tusk government, finds state pollster
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The proportion of Poles who negatively assess their country’s justice system has increased under the current government, despite its promises to restore the rule of law and ensure that courts function more effectively and independently. New polling by state research agency CBOS found that, in June this year, 61% of Poles had a negative view of the functioning of the justice system, up from 55% in 2022 and 51% in 2017, when the former Law and Justice (PiS) government was in power. Only 26% now positively assess the system, down from 28% in 2022 and 36% in 2017. The last time positive views were lower was in 2005 (22%). The findings come two and a half years after the current government, a coalition ranging from left to centre right led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk, came to power in December 2023, replacing the national-conservative PiS administration. One of Tusk’s main promises was to restore the rule of law after eight years in which PiS had implemented a series of contested judicial reforms that experts, European courts and many Polish judges had condemned as undermining the independence and functioning of the judiciary. However, Tusk’s government has struggled to implement its promised changes. In many cases, its efforts have been blocked by PiS-aligned Presidents Andrzej Duda and Karol Nawrocki or other officials appointed under the former government. But in other cases, such as with a pledge to separate the functions of justice minister and prosecutor general, which were fused by PiS in 2016, the current ruling coalition has simply not followed through on its promises. In its latest polling, CBOS found that supporters of the current opposition are most dissatisfied with the functioning of the justice system: 72% of PiS voters have a negative view, as do 71% of those who support the far-right Confederation (Konfederacja). However, even among voters of Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) party, a majority, 53%, have a negative opinion, with only 38% holding a positive one. Interestingly, public attitudes towards judges themselves have hardly changed. Currently, 19% of Poles have a positive view towards them and 23% a negative one. That is similar to findings in 2017 (22% positive, 24% negative) and 2012 (19% positive, 23% negative). More Poles (35%) think that the rule of law has got worse under Tusk's government than believe it has improved (24%). A further 28% think there has been no change, finds a new poll https://t.co/KkiuY2vDSW — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 5, 2025 When asked to identify the greatest problems with the justice system, Poles instead often point to structural issues – that is, those that are under the control of politicians. The most commonly identified problem (chosen by 38% of respondents, who could select up to three main problems) was “prolonged proceedings” in court cases. The second biggest issue was “politicisation of courts” (18%). Only 4% said that “judges’ neglect of duty, incompetence and impunity” were among the biggest problems. However, 23% of respondents were unable to name a single major issue that the justice system faces. Fifteen months since the change of government, Poland's rule-of-law crisis continues – indeed, many Poles think the situation has got worse.@J_Jaraczewski explains the roots of the crisis, what its impact has been, and how it might be resolved https://t.co/7KOCURV3dU — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 17, 2025 CBOS’s findings echo a number of other polls. After the first year of Tusk’s government, a survey by SW Research for the Rzeczpospolita daily found that 35% of Poles thought the rule-of-law situation had got worse, compared to only 24% who thought it had improved. Another poll by the same agency for Onet, a news website, in January this year similarly found that 40% of Poles believe the justice system has not improved under the current government, while only 33% think it has got better. In response to the latter poll, justice minister Waldemar Żurek admitted to Onet that there had been problems in addressing the rule of law. But he blamed the “hurdles [put] in our path” by Presidents Duda and Nawrocki. Opposition-aligned President @NawrockiKn has vetoed a government bill intended to reform a judicial body at the heart of Poland’s rule-of-law crisis. He argued that the measures would simply create even greater “legal chaos” https://t.co/I7FHRKIoP1 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 19, 2026 In 2024, Duda refused to sign government bills overhauling the Constitutional Tribunal (TK), which still contains judges illegitimately appointed under the former PiS administration. As a result, Tusk’s government refuses to recognise rulings issued by the TK. In February this year, Duda’s successor, Nawrocki, vetoed a government bill intended to restore the legitimacy of the National Council of the Judiciary (KRS), the body responsible for nominating judges to positions on courts. In 2017, the KRS was overhauled under PiS in a manner that rendered it illegitimate, according to multiple Polish and European court rulings. That in turn has led to doubts over the legal status of around 3,000 judges appointed by the KRS since 2017 and all the rulings issued by them. Nawrocki has also refused to swear in four new TK judges nominated by parliament this year, despite an order by the European Court of Human Rights that they be allowed to take up their positions. The European Court of Human Rights has ordered Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) to accept four judges whom opposition-aligned President Nawrocki refused to swear in. The decision was welcomed by the government but rejected by the TK itself https://t.co/9NxInPdYk9 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 6, 2026 ​ Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Indians and Colombians now third and fourth largest groups of foreign workers in Poland
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Indians are now the third-largest group of foreign workers in Poland, followed by Colombians, according to new data from the country’s Social Insurance Institute (ZUS). Ukrainians remain by far the largest immigrant group, followed by Belarusians. The figures also show that the overall number of registered foreign workers has risen more than 8% over the last year, a faster rate of growth than in recent years. However, the government official responsible for migration strategy says this is because stricter government measures have pushed some employers to register previously uninsured workers. The ZUS data, reported by Dziennik Gazeta Prawna (DGP), a leading daily, show that there were 1.34 million foreign workers registered in ZUS at the end of June, up from 1.24 million at the same point last year. That 8.2% increase is larger than the growth rate of around 6% seen in each of the previous two years, notes the newspaper. Maciej Duszczyk, the deputy interior minister responsible for migration, commented that the rise actually reflects the government’s tougher migration strategy, which he said “forces employers to report for insurance those who arrived earlier” but were working unregistered The official pointed to recent data showing that, in fact, in the first half of this year, Poland issued 50% fewer work permits to foreigners than in the same period of 2025. Dane ZUS pokazują dokładnie to co zakładaliśmy w Strategi Migracyjnej. Radykalny spadek liczby wydawanych, nowych zezwoleń na pracę (ponad 50% rok do roku) wymusza na pracodawcach zgłaszanie do ubezpieczenia, tych którzy przyjechali wcześniej. Tylko w pełni legalne zatrudnienie! — Maciek Duszczyk (@MaciekDuszczyk) August 11, 2026 Ukrainians remain by far the largest group of registered foreign workers, with 901,000 now in the system, a 10.1% rise from a year earlier. Belarusians (144,000, up 4.9%) remain in second. But two non-European migrant groups whose numbers have been growing rapidly in recent years now occupy third and fourth place: Indians (25,500, up 4.9%) and Colombians (23,000, up 31%, which was the fastest growth of any national group). Georgians, who had previously been the third-largest group, saw their number fall by 17% to 22,000, meaning they are now in fifth, ahead of Filipinos (15,400, down 2%), Moldovans (14,200, down 1%), Nepalis (13,400, up 8.3%), Vietnamese (12,200, up 6.1%), and Russians (11,800, down 2.5%). Latin American migration to Poland is booming, with 45,000 work permits issued last year, five times more than in 2022@Gosia_Tomczak looks at what is driving this trend and what challenges and opportunities it has created for both the migrants and Poland https://t.co/tl1wUTCaC0 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 15, 2025 ZUS’s data also show that foreign workers are increasingly establishing their own businesses in Poland, which Dziennik Gazeta Prawna notes is a sign that they are establishing longer-term ties with the country but also a result of an easier online system for registering businesses. In 2021, only 22,700 foreigners had a registered business in Poland, a figure that now is now almost five times higher, at 102,000. The rise has been driven in particular by Ukrainians, many of whom are legally entitled to establish companies in Poland under the same terms as Polish citizens. As a result, 7.6% of foreign workers now run their own business, up from 6.7% a year ago and from 2.7% before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, which led to a wave of Ukrainian refugees settling in Poland. Ukrainian refugees boosted Poland’s GDP by 2.7% last year while not raising unemployment or lowering wages, finds a report by the UN @Refugees agency and @Deloitte "Whoever thinks refugees are a burden on the economy should think again," says @UNHCRPoland https://t.co/rOvtOvBNwG — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 12, 2025 Over the last decade, even before the war in Ukraine, Poland has experienced a wave of migration unprecedented in its history and among the largest anywhere in Europe. For six years running, between 2017 and 2022, it issued more first residence permits to immigrants from outside the European Union than did any other member state. Much of the surge in immigration came during the rule of the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government from 2015 to 2023, despite its strong anti-migrant rhetoric. The current government, a more liberal coalition led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk, came to power pledging to reduce immigration, which it said had got out of control under PiS. Under Tusk’s government, in 2024, Poland issued the lowest number of residence permits to non-EU immigrants in a decade. In 2025, the government introduced tougher entry requirements for foreign workers and students. It has also stepped up deportations of foreigners who have broken the law. However, Duszczyk notes that the current government still sees “selective and responsible migration” as a way to “maintain the competitiveness of the economy without limiting wage growth”. ​ Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Mother bear and cubs spotted on busy hiking trail in Poland
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! We cannot do what we do without your support. A female brown bear and her three cubs have been spotted in Poland’s Tatra mountains crossing a popular trail filled with hikers, with the animals coming unusually close to people. According to an official from Tatra National Park, where the incident took place, the behaviour could be a survival strategy by the mother to protect her young from male bears, which can kill cubs but tend to avoid humans. In a video posted on Sunday, the mother and three cubs were seen crossing the Chochołowska Valley trail in broad daylight, as crowds of people looked on Videos of the bear family have appeared increasingly often on social media, prompting questions about whether the animals are becoming less wary of people. But park officials say the female’s behaviour may have a biological explanation. “As we know, male brown bears are infanticidal. They kill not only other bears’ cubs, but their own as well. So the females, to avoid contact with the males, tend to stay closer to people,” Tomasz Zwijacz-Kozica, a park official, told local newspaper Gazeta Krakowska. “Females sense this instinctively and generally use the presence of people as a sort of shield to defend themselves against these males,” he added. The park staff hope to gather more detailed data on the female bear’s movements and behaviour in the future by possibly fitting her with a telemetry collar. They note that similar behaviour has been seen before. Around 20 years ago, a female bear drew attention when hundreds of tourists photographed her. They advise visitors to remain calm if they encounter a bear and to follow several basic rules, including staying calm and not running or making sudden movements, which may trigger a pursuit; not approaching the animals; and not attempting to take close-up photographs or use a flash. If a bear is encountered, visitors should slowly retreat in the direction from which they came while maintaining eye contact with the animal. Particular caution is required when cubs are present. Visitors should also avoid feeding bears or leaving rubbish behind. The smell of food can attract animals to trails and encourage behaviour that brings them into dangerous contact with people. A woman has died after being attacked by a bear in a forest in southeastern Poland. Such incidents are extremely rare, with the last fatal bear attack in the country reported in 2014 https://t.co/sAC2MPAvfh — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 23, 2026 Estimates of Poland’s brown bear population vary between 120 and 400, with most found in the southeastern Bieszczady mountains as well as the Tatras and Beskids further west. The population is thought to be growing, with a rise in reports of encounters with humans. In April this year, a woman was killed in a bear attack, Poland’s first such fatality since 2014. Another bear attack earlier in the year in the same region left a man with head and limb injuries. In March, the government launched a new 16 million zloty (€3.7 million) scheme aimed at both protecting bears and ensuring the safety of their human neighbours. It includes the creation of a special force to monitor and respond to bear sightings, including fitting the animals with tracking collars. In 2022, the town of Zakopane, located at the foot of the Tatra mountains, installed bear-proof rubbish bins to prevent animals from foraging in them – and thereby coming closer to areas of human population Poland has launched a new programme to protect brown bears and ensure the safety of their human neighbours, amid growing reports of encounters. World.title: Kaczyński appeals to President Nawrocki to unify Poland’s right-wing opposition ahead of elections
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. Jarosław Kaczyński, the leader of Poland’s largest opposition party, the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), has called on opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki to help unify the country’s various right-wing opposition forces ahead of next year’s parliamentary elections. His appeal comes as PiS, which for the last two decades has dominated the Polish right, is in crisis, amid falling polling numbers, a split by a breakaway faction, and a growing challenge from far-right parties that have long been critical of PiS. That has created a fragmented opposition, with parties competing against one another as much as or more than with Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s ruling coalition. Some on the right hope that Nawrocki, who enjoys good relations with various parts of the opposition, could act as a unifying figurehead bridging those divides. 🔴 Jarosław Kaczyński ujawnił, o co osobiście poprosił Karola Nawrockiego. Podczas miesięcznicy smoleńskiej prezes PiS odniósł się do podziałów na prawicy i przyznał, że widzi dla prezydenta wyjątkowo ważną rolę: ma pomóc scalić zwaśnione środowiska. „Ja prezydenta swego czasu… pic.twitter.com/qwXhmccun2 — Super Express (@se_pl) August 10, 2026 Speaking on Sunday at a monthly commemoration of the 2010 Smolensk air disaster that killed his identical twin brother, then-President Lech Kaczyński, Jarosław was reported by a variety of Polish media outlets as saying that he had asked Nawrocki to act as a “patron” for a unified right. “I asked the president some time ago, and I hope he will do it,” said Kaczyński, quoted by newspaper Fakt. “It would be very good if the president took up this matter energetically.” “We could continue to develop – as we did during our years of government – not only in terms of achieving GDP growth, but also by undertaking major investments, by undertaking everything that would truly change Poland.” Kaczyński was referring to the period between 2015 and 2023 when a PiS-dominated coalition, known as the United Right (Zjednoczona Prawica), ruled Poland. In the latter year, it was ousted from power by a more liberal coalition led by Tusk, Kaczyński’s great rival. Since then, the landscape on the Polish right has changed dramatically. One of PiS’s partners in the United Right, the hard-right Sovereign Poland (Suwerenna Polska), merged with PiS in 2024. The other, the centre-right Agreement (Porozumienie), is now defunct. Meanwhile, support for PiS itself has collapsed. Having won 35% of the vote at the 2023 elections, it now averages only around 20% in polls – the party’s lowest figures for almost 20 years. To make matters worse, last month, around a fifth of the party’s MPs formed a breakaway group in parliament led by PiS deputy leader and former Prime Minister Mateusz Morawiecki. They plan to soon form their own, separate party, Development Plus (Rozwój Plus), with a more moderate, centre-right agenda than PiS. At the same time, PiS has found itself challenged by a growing far right. Confederation (Konfederacja), which won 7% of the vote in 2023, is now polling around 12-13%. The even more radical Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP), which broke away from Confederation last year, is at 9%. The split in PiS is a blow to the party and its leader, Jarosław Kaczyński. But the potential emergence of a new centre-right party led by Mateusz Morawiecki could actually help the opposition win a majority at next year's elections, writes @danieltilles1 https://t.co/xMP7e4rOFf — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 31, 2026 That has resulted in a much more fragmented right, with four separate entities not only opposed to Tusk’s government but also competing with one another for overlapping electorates. With parliamentary elections scheduled for autumn 2027, there have been questions over whether and to what extent the opposition should seek to cooperate with one another. One option would be an agreement not to stand candidates against one another for seats in the upper-house Senate, which are contested on a single-member-district system rather than through the proportional representation that decides the share of seats in the more powerful lower-house Sejm. Parties in Tusk’s current ruling coalition themselves formed such a “Senate pact” at the 2019 elections, helping them win control of the upper house, then repeated that in 2023, when they retained control. Although the Senate has a limited legislative role, it would be a significant prize for Nawrocki and the opposition, especially if Tusk’s coalition wins the Sejm, because the Senate has the power to approve or reject national referendums proposed by the president. An even more ambitious plan that has been rumoured is for some elements of the right-wing opposition to run joint electoral lists for the Sejm. That would require a far greater degree of programmatic consensus and longer negotiations over how to distribute places on lists. The government's majority in the Senate has, for the second time, rejected a proposal by opposition-aligned President Nawrocki to hold a referendum on whether Poland should continue implementing the EU's climate policies, which he argues are too costly https://t.co/Idm6dnzQEH — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 6, 2026 Nawrocki is seen as key to any such plan coming to fruition. He was elected last year to the presidency as an independent, but with the formal backing of PiS. Ahead of the second-round run-off vote, he also received endorsements from defeated first-round rivals Sławomir Mentzen, one of the leaders of Confederation, and Grzegorz Braun, the leader of KKP. Since taking office, Nawrocki has continued to cultivate good relations with PiS and Confederation, as well as with Morawiecki’s new breakaway faction. However, he has kept his distance from Braun, whose anti-Americanism, antisemitism and sympathy towards Russia makes him something of a pariah. The European Parliament has again voted to strip Polish far-right leader Grzegorz Braun of immunity to face further charges for Holocaust denial as well as various antisemitic, anti-Ukrainian and anti-LGBT incidents during last year's presidential campaign https://t.co/4EHVEuSDnM — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 26, 2026 Media reports have suggested that Nawrocki is planning to play a role in creating a “broad patriotic camp” among the opposition ahead of next year’s elections. Last week, during an event celebrating the first anniversary of his swearing in, the president also hinted at this role. He noted he will, in the coming months, be presenting “a presidential development strategy”, which “I believe will become a point of reference in the upcoming parliamentary elections for all those who aspire to govern Poland, a real plan for the future of the republic”. The strategy would be aimed in particular at “patriotic forces” who are “ready for dialogue between the offices of the president and future prime minister”. Given that Nawrocki and Tusk’s government are bitterly opposed to one another, that was a clear reference to opposition parties. A report on Sunday by Newsweek Polska, based on unnamed inside sources, claimed that Kaczyński is hoping to form a single electoral list for the Sejm elections compromising PiS, Development Plus and all or parts of Confederation, under the patronage of Nawrocki. 💥 Nowa obsesja Jarosława Kaczyńskiego, w jaki sposób odzyskać władzę. Prezes PiS naciska na Karola Nawrockiego, by prezydent stworzył "listę Nawrockiego" prawicy do Sejmu. To najbardziej ryzykowna, ale też o ogromnej stawce, decyzja prezydenta.https://t.co/sqRPFUuiZ7 — Jacek Gądek (@JacekGadek) August 9, 2026 Other leaders on the right have expressed varying degrees of willingness to work with one another. Speaking to broadcaster TVN on Saturday, Krzystof Bosak, another of Confederation’s leaders, expressed support for the idea of a Senate pact. On Friday, Morawiecki said that he can “fully imagine working with Sławomir Mentzen”, who “I believe is absolutely part of the patriotic camp”. However, Mentzen himself quickly ruled out the idea, tweeting that he’d rather “quit politics than join this gang leading Poland to disaster”, adding that Tusk, Kaczyński and Morawiecki are “one and the same”. Whereas Bosak represents a nationalist faction of Confederation seen as more compatible with PiS, Mentzen represent’s a libertarian wing that is bitterly opposed to the former PiS’ government’s high social spending, support for Ukraine, and the restrictions it introduced during the COVID-19 pandemic. Tusk, Kaczyński, Morawiecki, Czarzasty, jeden pies. Dla nich wszystkich słupki sondażowe są ważniejsze od przyszłości… — Sławomir Mentzen (@SlawomirMentzen) August 7, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Protests against anti-Ukrainian violence held in 25 Polish cities
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! We cannot do what we do without your support. Demonstrations took place in around 25 Polish cities on Sunday against a “growing wave of hate and violence” against Ukrainians, who are Poland’s largest immigrant group. The protests came after police data showed a significant increase in reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland so far this year, including a number of high-profile incidents of verbal and physical aggression. Sunday’s demonstrations, which took place under the slogan “Do Not Be Indifferent”, were organised by the Committee for the Defence of Democracy (KOD), an NGO, with support from other groups, including Amnesty International. “[This is] a nationwide campaign aimed at expressing opposition to the growing wave of hate, xenophobia, nationalism and violence directed against Ukrainians and members of other minorities,” wrote KOD ahead of the events. Ukrainians are by far Poland’s largest foreign national group, with around 1.6 million living in the country. World.title: Remains of Poles massacred by Ukrainian nationalists in WWII exhumed in Ukraine
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The remains of a further 55 victims of massacres of Poles by Ukrainian nationalists during World War Two have been exhumed in Ukraine. Around half were children, and most show signs of brutal deaths, including skulls pierced with farming tools (as pictured above). The announcement comes amid ongoing tensions between Poland and Ukraine over the so-called Volhynia massacres, sparked by President Volodymyr Zelensky’s recent decision to name a military unit after the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), which was responsible for leading the killings of around 100,000 Poles. However, both sides have expressed hope that continued exhumations of victims – most of which are believed to still remain buried in unmarked mass graves in Ukraine – can ease that path towards reconciliation. 📣 Zakończenie tegorocznych prac ekshumacyjnych ofiar Zbrodni Wołyńskiej w Ostrówkach i Woli Ostrowieckiej ❗ Od 13 lipca do 7 sierpnia br. pracownicy Instytutu Pamięci Narodowej, przedsiębiorstwa „Wołyńskie Starożytności” oraz specjalista z zakresu medycyny sądowej z… pic.twitter.com/iDJR5NmdEn — Instytut Pamięci Narodowej (@ipngovpl) August 7, 2026 The new findings were made in Ostrówki and Wola Ostrowiecka, two neighbouring former villages, now depopulated, that were previously part of Poland but, after postwar border changes, are now located in western Ukraine. There, on 30 August 1943, the UPA massacred over 1,000 Poles and razed the villages to the ground. Similar massacres took place in many other villages, as part of an ethnic cleansing operation by the UPA to remove Poles and other minorities from what they saw as Ukrainian territory. Exhumations previously took place in Ostrówki and Wola Ostrowiecka in the 1990s, and again in 2011 and 2015, uncovering the remains of hundreds of victims. However, hundreds more are believed to remain buried. In 2017, Ukraine imposed a ban on searches for victims on its territory in response to the dismantlement of a monument to the UPA in Poland. However, in a diplomatic breakthrough last year, it allowed them to resume, including granting permission in December for work in Ostrówki and Wola Ostrowiecka. In April this year, mass graves were discovered there, with exhumations then beginning in July. Poland’s state Institute of National Remembrance (IPN) has now announced the result of that work. They have uncovered the remains of 55 victims, 26 of them children (mostly under 12 years of age, with the youngest a few months old) and 20 women. In the Volhynia massacres as a whole, the majority of victims were women and children. The locations and conditions of the remains reveal much about the manner of their death. Most were buried “at random” without coffins, which is consistent with contemporary accounts that they were killed in a barn and then thrown into a mass burial pit, notes the IPN Most of the remains, in particular skulls, show signs of injuries that are also consistent with contemporary accounts, which said that victims were ordered to lie on the ground before being killed with farm tools, including hammers for slaughtering cattle. Material from the bones has been secured for genetic testing, which was recently used for the first time to identify massacre victims exhumed at another location in Ukraine last year. Around 300 personal items, including rosaries, crosses and clothing, were also found during the recent excavations in Ostrówki and Wola Ostrowiecka. On 30 August, the 83rd anniversary of the massacre, the newly found remains will be buried in a funeral ceremony at the cemetery in Ostrówki. The IPN believes that over 300 further victims still remain buried at unknown locations in the two former villages. Poland has for the first time used DNA testing to identify the remains of Poles massacred by Ukrainian nationalists in WWII. “After more than 80 years, families are receiving the answer they have awaited for generations,” says the culture minister https://t.co/c1gM3kQ83s — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 14, 2026 The Volhynia massacres have long been a point of tension between Poland, which recognises them as a genocide, and Ukraine, which rejects that label. The decision by Kyiv to allow exhumations to resume last year was regarded as a major step towards reconciliation. However, that process was undermined in May this year, when Zelensky decided to name a military unit after the “heroes of the UPA”. That prompted an angry response from Warsaw, where President Karol Nawrocki stripped Zelensky of Poland’s highest honour. There have since been efforts to reach a diplomatic solution. Last month, Zelensky pointed specifically to the exhumation work in Ostrówki and Wola Ostrowiecka as evidence that “Ukraine is doing its part to fairly establish the facts about those who were killed in those years”. Subsequently, he announced a five-point plan to alleviate the crisis, including allowing more exhumations and opening up historical archives. Poland welcomed the move but said that it would wait to see how it was implemented in practice. Poland has cautiously welcomed President @ZelenskyyUa's announcement of a five-point plan to alleviate the diplomatic crisis triggered by his earlier decision to name a military unit after a group that led massacres of Poles during WWII https://t.co/M3GXD9vtAr — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 18, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers.
