Tech.title: Brendan Carr is one firing away from an unchecked FCC
Tech.content:
is a senior policy reporter at The Verge, covering the intersection of Silicon Valley and Capitol Hill. She spent 5 years covering tech policy at CNBC, writing about antitrust, privacy, and content moderation reform.

President Donald Trump already holds a Republican majority in the agency tasked with regulating America’s communications systems. But with a new nomination to the Federal Communications Commission, he could move to shut out opposing voices altogether — albeit at a legal risk.

The FCC is currently composed of two Republicans and one Democrat — Republican Chair Brendan Carr and Commissioner Olivia Trusty, and Democratic Commissioner Anna Gomez. This mixed group gives the agency a three-member quorum that allows it to vote on major actions, though it still falls short of the five members (no more than three from a single party) the FCC is meant to have. But late last week, Trump nominated a third Republican, Carr adviser Danielle Thumann Severs. If she’s confirmed, it won’t change the basic math of which policies win votes. But it would mean there’s a quorum even without Gomez. That could open the door to Trump firing the FCC’s lone Democrat, something she herself has wondered why he hasn’t already done.

Gomez may not have much hard power in the current FCC, but her removal would be a blow to the public interest. Commissioners often have access to information that the public might not otherwise know about, and can raise non-confidential issues in their public dissents and statements. And even in situations where dissenting voices are overruled, they can push the majority to offer more robust reasoning in their decisions. During the Trump administration, Gomez has used her post to call attention to FCC actions she thinks violate the First Amendment, and pushed back on policies loosening broadcast consolidation rules.

Gomez may not have much hard power in the current FCC, but her removal would be a blow to the public interest

Trump could well be able to remove Gomez, given that he fired the Federal Trade Commission’s two Democrats without cause and got away with it. Like the FTC, the FCC was created as an independent agency, with a bipartisan panel of staggered terms that would supposedly insulate it from a given administration’s whims. But under the unitary executive theory, which Trump allies including Carr and FTC Chair Andrew Ferguson endorse, all power held by them belongs to the president. The Supreme Court’s ruling affirming Trump’s ability to fire the FTC’s Democrats bolstered this.

But there are still good reasons Trump could spare Gomez, particularly that firing her could put the FCC’s legitimacy in question, as former FCC senior staffer Blair Levin writes. Even after SCOTUS legitimized the FTC firings, the Communications Act’s language grants the FCC unique quirks. It could provide stronger legal ground to argue that one party can’t hold all the seats on the panel, Levin adds, and a court could determine it is more like the Federal Reserve, insulated from presidential firings, than the FTC.

Gomez’ term is technically lapsed, but she can stay on until the end of 2027 unless her seat is filled sooner, or she’s re-nominated. With limited Senate floor time ahead of the midterm elections and key Democrats’ opposition to confirming a Republican nominee without a Democratic one, the FCC could remain in a holding pattern for quite some time.

Tech.title: Insta360’s next 360-degree action cam puts bigger sensors in a smaller design
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Insta360 announced the next iteration of its popular 360-degree action cameras that have helped the company expand its offerings. The new X6 introduces a design that’s smaller than last year’s X5 and X4 Air but with improved video capabilities thanks to an even larger pair of custom 1/1.1-inch square sensors from Sony. While last year’s models offered 8K recording at up to 30fps, the new X6 can capture 8K at up to 50fps. It also carries forward the X5’s replaceable lenses, which are now five times more scratch-resistant and 60 percent cheaper, according to the company.

The Insta360 X6 is available today in black or white through the company’s online store and other retailers starting at $699.99, which is $150 more expensive than last year’s $549.99 X5. It’s also available as part of a $799.99 Essentials Bundle that adds an additional battery, an invisible selfie stick, a fast charging case, and other accessories.

The X6 is available in white or black color options. Image: Insta360

The most obvious upgrade for the X6 is a smaller design that’s a little wider and thicker than the X5, but a full inch shorter and 4 grams lighter, making it more pocketable than its predecessor. Shrinking the X6 did result in a slightly smaller 2.32-inch touchscreen on the back, but while the X5 featured a 2.5-inch LCD display, the X6 gets an upgrade to OLED.

While the new X6 doesn’t feature full 1-inch sensors like the DJI Osmo 360, its new 1/1.1-inch square sensors come very close and offer 33 percent more sensor area and “four times the light intake per frame” when compared to the 1/1.28-inch sensors in the X5. Those sensors work alongside multiple AI chips, including two dedicated to imaging, to give the X6 better low-light performance with improved denoising. It’s also the first 360-degree camera, Insta360 claims, with in-camera Dolby Vision support so that brightness and contrast metadata is captured frame by frame to ensure HDR footage looks accurate on supported displays.

When capturing 360-degree footage using both cameras the X6 maxes out at 8K/50fps, but you can boost that to as high as 6K/120fps or 4K/240fps in a “Bullet Time” mode designed for capturing slow-motion footage. You can use the X6 as a 2D action camera by recording with just one sensor at a time, but that’s limited to a maximum resolution of 5K/60fps, or 120fps if you drop to 4K. Still photography with the X6 is also getting an upgrade to 120 megapixels when capturing 360-degree images, or 42 megapixels when using just one side of the camera.

The X6’s battery life can be boosted by pairing it with accessories like a selfie stick featuring an extended battery. Image: Insta360

Despite the camera being smaller, Insta360 managed to squeeze a slightly larger 2,600mAh battery into the X6 that the company claims will keep it recording up to 51 percent longer than the X5, which came with a 2,400mAh battery. The X6 will record for around 140 minutes at 8K/30fps before it dies, but you can extend that with the optional X6 Power Selfie Stick accessory, which adds an extra 180 minutes of runtime.

Other upgrades include improved waterproofing to a depth of 66 feet and a better invisible dive case that can be used to film underwater as deep as 60 meters without the case itself showing up in footage.

Insta360 has also upgraded the InstaFrame feature introduced with the X5 that can produce a social media-friendly flat 4K video without requiring any manual editing by tracking and focusing on people, pets, or other subjects in frame. For those who don’t want to edit 360-degree footage either, a new feature called PanoMind uses an AI model trained on 10,000 hours of 360-degree footage to automatically create a highlight reel from footage on the camera while the X6 is charging.

Tech.title: Google’s Pixel 11 lineup offer fewer hardware changes, but much more Gemini
Tech.content:
For the last few years, Google’s Pixel has been a showcase of new AI features, with few hardware changes from the previous year’s devices. Similarly, the Pixel 11 series isn’t too different in design and internals from its predecessor.

However, this year’s devices have more Gemini features to complete tasks in the background, including a new Wispr Flow-like transcription feature, a live translation feature that works across content, and a new camera feature that captures the right frames.

Image Credits:Google

AI advances on the Pixel 11

With this year’s Pixel 11 series launch, Google is thinking more agentic AI to complete your tasks. With Gemini, U.S.-based users will be able to order groceries, book rides, or get coffee, for instance. Plus, Gemini can call businesses on users’ behalf for table reservations or appointments. Google said that users can take over or stop tasks at any point in time and also review transcripts for AI-operated calls.

The company has also evolved the “Magic Cue” feature from last year to use Gemini, which proactively surfaces contextual information, to now display information from across your apps to help you find suggestions for things like a dinner spot or show.

In May, Google announced a dictation product called Rambler to take on competitors like Wispr Flow and Aqua. Now, that product is making its way to the Pixel phones.

The new Pixel series phones have some other helpful features that might be handy for daily usage, too. First, the device can translate videos, podcasts, and voice messages in the target language. The company is also making its “Circle to Search” gesture-based feature available directly in the camera, something that Apple also did in iOS 27 by making Siri available in the camera.

What’s more, Google is adding an accessibility feature to the camera, which uses Gemini to translate sign language into text to help people communicate with others who have hearing impairments. And the company has redesigned the live transcribe interface for improved communication.

Camera features

Google also added a few AI tricks embedded into its camera. One feature is called “Magic Capture,” which picks the best frames out of hundreds of frames it captures between when users press start and end. The idea is to take a video and get photos as a byproduct. Google said that the feature also auto-crops and unblurs the frames to make them ready for sharing.

The company has upgraded its super zoom from 100x to 120x for Pro phones, and from 20x to 30x for the base Pixel 11. With the new devices, users will be able to create custom looks for the camera, which are specialized filters that appear when users are snapping images.

Image Credits:Google

The Pro phones are also getting faster capture with a feature called “Instant Night Sight,” which takes 4.5x less time than the previous-gen phone’s Night Sight. Google enhanced video shooting, too, with support for 8K resolution with video boost and better stability.

For creators, Google added a “creator suite” mode in video settings, which lets you use Pixel 11 devices as a teleprompter while shooting clips. When you are done shooting, the clip is saved in a dedicated folder, making it easier to find for editing.

Hardware upgrades

All the Pixel phones now run the latest Tensor G6 processor, which has 20% better power efficiency and

allows for 25% faster browsing, as per Google. Plus, it lets users take faster low-light photos with Night Sight Instant.

The new image signal processing on the chip also enables 120x magic zoom on the Pixel 11 Pro XL. The company said that the new processors run the latest models with lower latency, but didn’t offer any specific metrics.

The display size on all phones is the same, but the Pro models get a slightly brighter display, which could be helpful in the daylight.

Image Credits: Google Image Credits:Google

Google said Pro models get an updated main camera sensor that takes higher-quality photos than the previous generation without specifying any numbers. It also said the new telephoto sensor allows for 32% more light while capturing an image.

Image Credits:Google

London-based startup Nothing made its phones recognizable by Glyph bars and then a Glyph interface. Google is not that extravagant, but it has now placed an LED light on the back, which is built around the flashlight. This acts as an indicator for calls or messages from favorite contacts when Gemini is thinking or listening.

All these devices are available to pre-order starting today and will start with a base storage of 256GB.

The Pixel 11 starts at $899, the 11 Pro starts at $1,099, and the 11 Pro XL starts at $1,299. (The prices of the Pixel 11 and the Pixel 11 Pro are the same as last year’s 256GB models, but you could buy a 128 GB model at that time with a $100 lower price tag.)

With the rising prices of components, the company has bumped the price of the top model by $100 compared to the Pixel 10 XL.

A new lineup of Pixel 11 accessories is also arriving alongside the phones, including new Pixelsnap cases (which now include clear) and Pixelsnap Ring Stand colors.

Tech.title: Google unveils the Pixel Watch 5 with a smarter Gemini and advanced health monitoring
Tech.content:
At its Made by Google event on Wednesday, Google unveiled the Pixel Watch 5 with a smarter Gemini experience, as well as advanced fitness and health monitoring. The new smartwatch, which starts at $399, can track blood pressure patterns and insulin resistance, as well as deliver personalized help and better sleep tracking.

Google says it’s designed the watch to deliver personalized and proactive help right when it’s needed. For example, the watch will proactively suggest relevant actions or information based on a text message’s context, like instantly pulling up a smoothie place your sister sent you.

You can raise your wrist to ask Gemini a question, handle requests like finding a nearby lunch spot with navigation, or use Gemini offline to manage timers, alarms, and workouts with your voice.

The watch will also dynamically surface timely updates right at the bottom of the watch face, like flight info, ETAs, and other helpful reminders.

Image Credits:Google

As for the new health features, the tech giant says the smartwatch uses sensors and machine learning to track blood pressure patterns before they can put strain on your heart. Google says the feature was tested against 24-hour blood pressure monitors and uses an advanced waveform model trained on more than 1 billion minutes of data from over 500,000 people.

The insulin resistance feature is designed to identify changes in metabolic health that may be associated with insulin resistance and an increased risk of developing prediabetes or type 2 diabetes. The feature combines signals from sleep, heart rate, physical activity, and other health data. A large sensor model then analyzes these signals over time to identify long-term changes in insulin resistance.

Google will give users a summary of their blood pressure and insulin resistance trends every month.

There’s also a new feature that can detect a persistent drop in oxygen saturation and will contact emergency services if the watch determines that a breathing emergency may be occurring. This feature is launching in select European countries before expanding to additional regions.

Image Credits:Google

Additionally, the watch’s sleep-stage tracking is 15% more accurate and there’s also a new bedtime watch face that reduces nighttime distractions. A new “Smart Wake” feature wakes users at an optimal point in their sleep cycle, while a new sleep breathing quality metric tracks minute-by-minute changes in blood oxygen levels.

As for fitness, Google says the Pixel Watch 5 delivers its most accurate GPS route tracking yet, with route mapping that’s two times more accurate than previous generations. The improved accuracy is designed to provide users with more precise workout and running data, including a closer match between your recorded route and the actual course.

The Pixel Watch 5 features the Qualcomm Snapdragon W5 Gen 2 platform and has 12% more CPU performance and 50% more RAM than the previous platform. Google says the Watch 5 is 20% faster overall.

The Pixel Watch five supports up to 40 hours of battery life and is available in new colors, including Canyon Fog and Olive. The 41mm version starts at $399, while the 44mm starts at $429. The smartwatch is available for pre-order starting Wednesday and will be available on August 20.

Tech.title: Google takes on AirTag with the new $29 Pixel Tag
Tech.content:
Alongside its announcement of a new lineup of Pixel 11 smartphones, Google on Wednesday introduced its answer to Apple’s AirTag. At its livestreamed “Made by Google ’26” event, the company unveiled a new product designed for keeping track of your valuable items: the $29 Google Pixel Tag.

Similar to how Apple’s AirTag leverages its network of iPhones to find lost devices, the new Pixel Tag taps uses Google’s Find Hub network, which taps into Android devices around the world. Android users can add the tag to their phone’s built-in Android Find Hub, which is already used to help users find their lost Android smartphones and other devices, similar to Apple’s Find My.

Helpfully, you can locate and ring your Pixel Tag directly from your Pixel Watch, too, not just your phone.

Image Credits:Google

Where the Pixel Tag differs from AirTag is in its look and feel.

Apple’s lost-item finder is small, round, and engravable; Google opted for a slimmer, elongated device instead. Spec-by-spec, the Pixel Tag is 1.1 inches wide, compared to the AirTag’s 1.26 inches. As the Pixel Tag is oval-shaped, it’s 1.8 inches high from top to bottom. Thickness-wise, the Pixel Tag clocks in at a depth of 0.2 inches, compared with the AirTag’s 0.31 inches (which Apple calls its height).

By weight, the two competitors are comparable, as the Pixel Tag weighs 0.4 ounces with the battery, and the AirTag comes in at 0.39 oz.

Both are also rated IP67 for splash, water, and dust resistance, meaning they can withstand submersion in a maximum depth of 1 meter for up to 30 minutes.

Image Credits:Google

Taking other cues from AirTag, the Pixel Tag offers connectivity via Bluetooth and Ultra Wideband for precision finding; however, it doesn’t include NFC. Pixel Tag has a built-in speaker to help you find the lost device when nearby, and it’s powered by the user-replaceable CR2032 coin cell battery — the same used by the AirTag. This allows the Pixel Tag to work for roughly a year before the battery needs to be replaced.

Designed to be attached to items like keychains and bags, the Pixel Tag will cost $29 for a one-pack and $99 for a four-pack when it becomes available for purchase on November 11, 2026.

Tech.title: Google’s new Pixel 11 Pro Fold offers a stronger build and brighter screens
Tech.content:
Samsung’s short and wide foldable is the talk of the town, but Google is not experimenting with its design with today’s unveiling of the new Pixel 11 Fold, which appears largely unchanged on the outside. The company said that the new foldable is stronger and lighter than the previous-gen phone, but it’s also costlier.

Google said that it developed a new, stronger hinge for this year’s Pixel 11 Pro Fold. It’s also adding a Super Actua display to the outer display with 3,600 nits of peak brightness. Both the inner and outer displays are 20% brighter than its predecessor, according to the company.

There is a bit of a battery downgrade, however, as it now offers a 4,750 mAh capacity battery instead of 5,015 mAh from last year’s model. On the plus side, this is probably the reason why the phone is 1mm thinner and roughly 20 grams lighter.

Image Credits:Google

Another small upgrade on the charging front is that the new foldable supports 25W wireless charging.

The Pixel 11 Pro Fold is getting an updated 48-megapixel sensor that pulls in more light for more detailed photos in different lighting conditions. Because of the new G6 Tensor chip and the updated image processor, the phone can digitally zoom at 30x, up from 20x.

The device will be available in both the Olive and Obsidian colors, and will cost $1,899.

Tech.title: AI code-testing startup Blacksmith’s valuation jumps almost 10x in less than a year
Tech.content:
As AI makes coding dramatically faster, the next big challenge in software development is testing and validating all that code. Blacksmith has raised a new $45 million round to capitalize on that shift.

The Series B, led by Peak XV Partners, values Blacksmith at $550 million, up from the $60 million valuation it was assigned when it raised a $10 million Series A less than a year ago. Existing investors GV and Y Combinator also participated, bringing the startup’s total funding to $58.5 million.

Founded in 2024, Blacksmith helps companies build, test, and verify software before it reaches production. The startup now serves more than 5,000 customers, including Mercury, Supabase, Clerk, Ashby, and Expensify, up from more than 700 customers less than a year ago, co-founder and CEO Aditya Jayaprakash said in an exclusive interview.

The rise of AI coding tools such as Cursor, OpenAI’s Codex, and Anthropic’s Claude Code has made it significantly easier for software teams to generate code, but the quality of AI-generated code is not a given.

“Validating code is still a bottleneck, and it’s an even bigger bottleneck because people are writing even more,” Jayaprakash said.

Blacksmith started as a cloud provider for continuous integration (CI) workloads, helping companies run the software builds and tests needed to validate code before it reaches production. The startup has since broadened its platform with Codesmith, an AI coding agent that can automatically fix failed code checks.

Jayaprakash said Blacksmith reached a $10 million annualized revenue run rate with just 10 employees and has since grown its workforce to about 30 and grown revenue to “tens of millions of dollars.” He declined to provide a specific updated ARR figure, though did say some of its largest customers now spend more than $1 million a year on the platform.

While that appears to be solid and fast progress, Blacksmith is operating in a crowded market. Its key competitors include GitHub Actions, Cursor Automations, validation capabilities baked into Codex and Claude Code, numerous other startups, and AI code-testing services offered by Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud.

Jayaprakash said his startup is competing on the speed of testing code as well as affordability.

Looking ahead, Jayaprakash said that Blacksmith plans to expand into a broader suite of coding tools, aiming to help developers write, validate, and merge software faster.

Tech.title: Reservoir raises $8M to make water heaters that people — and the grid — will actually want
Tech.content:
It’s hard to imagine a home appliance more forgotten — yet more consequential — than the water heater. Most people only think of water heaters when their shower runs cold, but they represent about 18% of a household’s total energy budget and are one of the main causes of residential water damage.

To Luke Winston-Almanzar, water heaters are in clear need of an upgrade. “The typical water heater is devoid of intelligence, it’s using a god-awful amount of energy, and my air fryer is smarter than it,” he told TechCrunch. “I was using more energy to heat my water than it takes to drive my electric car.”

So Winston-Almanzar, who was previously chief business officer at 3D printing startup Formlabs, co-founded Reservoir along with Gabriel Parisi-Amon and Jake Felser to make a water heater that they would want to buy.

Reservoir announced Wednesday that it has raised $8 million in a seed round led by Asymmetric Capital Partners with participation from Founder Collective and MCJ.

The funding will help the company install more of its water heaters in homes around the Boston area, it’s initial market. Reservoir has installed about 100 devices to date, and Winston-Almanzar said his company hopes to have around 1,000 installed by the end of next year. “That’s when you start talking about a megawatt-scale in terms of capacity,” he said.

Storing megawatt-hours of energy as hot water could go a long way to stabilizing the grid. Today’s water heaters tend to be dumb devices, responding only to changes in temperature in the tank. But Reservoir, by predicting when people will need hot water, can heat the tank when electricity demand is low and prices are cheap. Plus, the device’s heat pump is nearly four times more efficient than an electric water heater and five times more efficient than a natural gas version.

The startup has been able to show that it can relieve strain on the grid at the neighborhood level, Winston-Almanzar said. Eventually, Reservoir could aggregate its fleet of water heaters to participate in utility demand response programs, which pay handsomely for large users to avoid tapping the grid at certain times. Winston-Almanzar said he’s looking at ways to use those payments to keep Reservoir’s prices down.

While energy storage might get grid experts excited, it won’t sell many water heaters. Most people replace their water heaters with whatever their plumber has on hand. The Reservoir team knew they needed to do more than build another heat pump water heater. “The sustainable product need to just be the better product,” he said.

To make an appliance that customers will seek out, Reservoir has included a number of features that aren’t found in typical water heaters.

The predictive heating feature ties in with energy storage. Reservoir’s water heater will spend the first month in a home gathering information about water usage patterns to train a model. Once trained, it will run the unit’s heat pump at the most efficient and cost effective times to save money while also ensuring ample supply.

Reservoir also added an ultrasonic flow sensor to help detect plumbing leaks throughout the home, sending homeowners an alert through its app. In the Max version, Reservoir added more features, including a recirculation valve to provide instant hot water and a mixing valve that can prevent pipes from freezing in cold snaps. In the Max version, a 50-gallon tank can deliver up to 150 gallons of hot water in “party mode,” which can be set either on the device’s touchscreen or through the app.

To keep pricing simple and to speed up the sales process, Reservoir has also started its own plumbing company. Winston-Almanzar said that decision was inspired by his experience at Formlabs. “We built direct relationships [there] because, in a lot of cases, distributors weren’t embracing the new technology.”

Reservoir’s “Max” version costs $6,500, while the base “Core” version costs $5,000, installation costs included. Massachusetts residents qualify for a $1,050 rebate, bringing the price down significantly.

At $3,950, the Core model is competitive with or cheaper than existing heat pump water heaters. For comparison, the 80-gallon AO Smith that’s sitting in my basement currently costs about $3,500, and installation would add about $1,000. Traditional electric water heaters might cost less up front, at about $1,700 for an 80-gallon tank. But Winston-Almanzar said a Reservoir would save typical Boston homeowners up to $1,000 per year in energy costs. Breakeven should happen long before the Reservoir dies since the company offers a 10-year warranty.

“We don’t think it’s enough just to have great technology. We think it needs to be affordable,” Winston-Almanzar said.

Water heating is ripe for some new technology. The newest advance, heat pump water heaters, have failed to make a dent, commanding a small part of the market. If Reservoir succeeds, it might finally push them into the mainstream — and in the process take some pressure off the grid.

Tech.title: India’s Yulu raises $93M as quick-commerce boom fuels e-bike demand
Tech.content:
As India’s quick-commerce platforms race to deliver everything from groceries to smartphones in minutes, electric mobility startup Yulu has seized the boom, raising $93 million in fresh funding.

The Bengaluru‑based startup offers electric two‑wheelers on weekly subscription plans, so delivery drivers can jump straight into the gig economy without buying their own vehicles. With around 50,000 vehicles in its fleet, Yulu reports that it logs about 1.6 million zero‑emission miles each week and powers more than 750,000 deliveries a day. The new funding will let Yulu grow that fleet to 200,000 bikes over the next two years and launch faster electric two-wheelers aimed at new logistics use cases.

The Series C round comprised $63 million in equity led by GEF Capital Partners and $30 million in debt financing. About $5.5 million of the equity component was used to buy shares from seed investors whose funds were nearing the end of their investment life, co-founder and CEO Amit Gupta said in an interview.

The deal valued Yulu at about $170 million post-money, people familiar with the matter told TechCrunch. Gupta declined to comment when asked about the valuation and did not dispute the figure.

Existing investors Bajaj Auto and Magna International did not participate in the round after waiving their pre-emptive rights, allowing GEF to acquire its target ownership stake, Gupta said. He added that the startup expects this to be its final equity fundraising before an eventual public listing, with future fleet expansion financed primarily through debt and lease financing.

The business moves toward becoming profitable before interest and taxes next year, after achieving positive EBITDA last financial year, Gupta told TechCrunch. The startup also grew its revenue seven-fold between fiscal 2023 and fiscal 2026, he said, without sharing specifics.

The COVID shift

Founded as a bike-sharing startup for urban commuters in 2017, Yulu found its biggest opportunity during the COVID-19 pandemic as demand for food and grocery deliveries accelerated.

Today, Gupta told TechCrunch that about 95% of Yulu’s revenue comes from renting electric bikes to gig workers on weekly subscriptions, while the rest is generated by its station‑based rental service in Bengaluru. The startup has also dropped an earlier plan to sell bikes directly to consumers.

To fuel its next growth phase, Yulu is introducing a full-sized, higher‑speed electric scooter, called Yulu Express. It is designed for longer‑haul e‑commerce deliveries, bike taxis, and express parcel services — areas that its slower fleet could not previously cover.

About a third of the planned 200,000‑vehicle fleet will be made up of this new model, Gupta said.

While Yulu’s current low‑speed fleet is built by Bajaj Auto, the new high‑speed scooter comes from a different Indian manufacturer that Gupta declined to name.

About 500 of the new bikes are already running in Bengaluru and are being trialed in three additional cities, Gupta told TechCrunch.

Currently, Yulu operates in 12 Indian cities, running its own operations in Bengaluru, Mumbai, Delhi‑NCR, and Hyderabad, while partnering with franchisees in eight other markets. The startup, Gupta said, aims to reach roughly 20 cities within the next year, with Chennai and Pune among the key targets for expansion.

Gupta stated that Yulu partners with almost every major quick‑commerce, food‑delivery, and e‑commerce platform — including Amazon and Walmart-owned Flipkart — though its customers are the gig workers who rent the bikes, not the platforms themselves. He compared Yulu’s role to “the AWS of mobility,” supplying the infrastructure that lets delivery workers operate without any third-party logistics providers taking a cut.

Tech.title: Phoebe Gates and Sophia Kianni reportedly knew Phia was ‘cookie stuffing’ for months
Tech.content:
Phia, the shopping startup co-founded by Phoebe Gates and Sophia Kianni, is once again under fire for its alleged business practices. The latest issue stems from earlier this year when Bloomberg published an investigation that mapped out how Phia was taking credit and commission for affiliate purchases it did not help to generate, known as cookie stuffing.

It’s a controversial practice that can get startups sued, mainly because it’s seen as taking referral revenue away from other affiliate marketers. Usually, when affiliate platforms like Phia sign on to work in a marketplace, they sign a contract stating that cookie stuffing is banned because it’s unfair.

When Bloomberg reported on Phia’s cookie stuffing, a Phia spokesperson told the publication that the company was only made aware of the issue when Bloomberg reached out to them.

But new reporting by Bloomberg shows that Gates and Kianni knew their startup was cookie stuffing as far back as December, based on leaked Slacks and sources familiar with the matter speaking to the publication.

The latest reporting found that cookie stuffing made up a good chunk of Phia’s sales and the company saw a sizable drop in daily revenue once it stopped the practice. The outlet also gained insight into the affected retailers, including Nike and Nordstrom.

Back in early July, a Phia spokesperson referred to the cookie stuffing as a bug, but Bloomberg now reports that this was a purposefully built feature that could be switched on and off. The leaked Slack messages also show Gates and Kianni talking about cookie stuffing practices with other executives and engineers.

Regarding the new allegations, a Phia spokesperson told Bloomberg that it rebuffed some of the publication’s claims, but said the company would “learn from this.”

When reached by TechCrunch, an unnamed spokesperson for Phia said in a statement: “Any features causing misattributions were immediately removed over a month ago on July 7. We are reviewing every transaction, we are fully committed to and have already begun issuing all transaction reversals to brand partners as a result of any misattribution, and we are hiring a head of compliance to make sure something like this never happens again.”

The company added that it would “learn” from this incident.

Phia launched last April with the promise to be a more effective Google Flights-like site for shopping — helping users find the best prices across various retailers.

A few days after Bloomberg’s investigation in July, Puck also dug around and found that Phia lost almost half its full-time employees since the beginning of the year; that several brands were unaware that they were listed on the app; and that investors got the ick from how aggressively Phia was leaning into affiliate marketing. It has also faced controversy in the past, like about how it was secretly collecting swaths of sensitive data, including tracking user behavior across the web and sending it back to their servers.

Updated with a statement from Phia.

Tech.title: Google Pixel 11 Series, Pixel Watch 5, Pixel Tag: Specs, Features, Price, Release Date
Tech.content:
Google is dialing things up to 11 this year with its Pixel phones. Ahead of its annual Made by Google event in New York City, the company unwrapped the Pixel 11 smartphone family—which includes the Pixel 11, Pixel 11 Pro, Pixel 11 Pro XL, and Pixel 11 Pro Fold—alongside the Pixel Watch 5 smartwatch. There's also a new hardware addition: the Pixel Tag, which seems designed to be the AirTag of the Android world.

Here's everything you need to know about the hardware changes and software upgrades on Google’s latest devices. Preorders open today, and the phones and watches go on sale August 20.

The Pixel 11 and Pixel 11 Pro Fold

The Pixel 11 starts with 256 GB of storage and comes in an eye-popping Hibiscus color. Photograph: Julian Chokkattu

It was inevitable, but prices are up across the board for Google's Pixel 11 series. The Pixel 11 now starts at $899, and on the highest end of the spectrum, the Pixel 11 Pro Fold is now $1,900. This means both devices got $100 price bumps. There's some good news: Google has bumped the base storage up to 256 GB on every device, a move matching Samsung's and Apple's latest handsets.

The Pixel 11 series is powered by Google's Tensor G6 chipset, which the company says is 20 percent more power efficient, 25 percent faster for browsing, and 15 percent faster when loading apps. Many of the camera improvements in the new devices are thanks to an improved imaging signal processor on the chip and a 50 percent more powerful tensor processing unit.

One big design change across the entire Pixel 11 series is on the oval camera bar on the back—it's now an all-glass surface, as opposed to a mix of metal and glass on its predecessors. Google says the camera bar on the Pixel 11 is more than 40 percent thinner, and when you pop on Google's case, the camera bar disappears and is completely flush. The Pixel 11 has the most striking color of the lot—Hibiscus—joined by more muted Pistachio, Frost, and Obsidian.

Tech.title: 4 New Camera Tricks on Google’s Latest Pixel 11 Smartphones
Tech.content:
The new Pixel 11 Pro, announced today, can zoom up to 120X, though in addition to the digital stitching, it relies on AI-generated pixels to fill in some details. Reynolds says maybe having that capability is enough to get someone interested in, say, wildlife photography. After experimenting on their phone, they’d be ready to invest in a professional camera and a big zoom lens.

“There's a reason I work on low light and zoom every single year," he says. "Because no matter how much I do it, when I do the user study with thousands of respondents, people always want more."

Every year, Google debuts a new Pixel phone, and every year, there's a slew of new camera tricks—largely powered by software wizardry—to deliver better photos than ever before. Last year, there was the Pro Res Zoom, which bumped up digital zoom on the Pixel 10 Pro to 100X. Two years before that, Google introduced “Add Me,” which lets two people take a group photo together without asking a stranger to take the pic for them.

For the Pixel 11 series, Google has demonstrated a handful of upgrades that can drastically alter the look of your photos, and even take some of the work out of capturing photos. Here's a closer look at a few top new camera capabilities on the Pixel 11 series.

Magic Capture

Photograph: Julian Chokkattu

So you want to capture a video of an important event—a concert of your favorite band, singing happy birthday to a loved one as a waiter brings a cake over, or your kid's recital. Too often, you see people holding their phone up during these milestones, trying to capture the moment, instead of being present. That's the problem Google's new Magic Capture feature is trying to solve.

Tech.title: Honor’s Robot Phone Has a Gimbal-Powered Camera for Vloggers
Tech.content:
The gimbal-powered 200-megapixel camera isn't the only camera, either. It's joined by a 200-megapixel telephoto camera and a 50-megapixel ultrawide, not to mention the 50-megapixel selfie shooter. The gimbal has 4 degrees of freedom, and you can activate it in the camera app or by making a palm motion on the selfie camera. And since it can rotate 300 degrees, you can use it as a selfie camera too.

The phone is shockingly light at 248 grams (the aforementioned iPhone 17 Pro is 206 grams). I wholly expected the Robot Phone to be top-heavy, with all those camera components at the top and the massive 7,060-mAh silicon-carbon battery inside powering the whole system. But in fact it’s decently balanced.

A glass cover protects the gimbal camera, and you can slide it to the right when you're ready to activate the gimbal. Once the camera is out, you can manually control the gimbal for ultra-smooth video capture through the camera app, or use preset motions to give your clips a cinematic look. There's even voice control with natural language, so you can say “turn around for 5 seconds.”

The motorized stabilization in the camera makes action shots—which can typically look shaky on traditional smartphones—look amazingly smooth. There are tracking modes as well, such as a subject tracker that keeps the selected person in the frame even as they move around. You can imagine how helpful that can be for solo travelers vlogging their way through a trip.

Specs Honor Robot Phone Display 6.31-inch, 120 Hz, OLED Processor, RAM, and Storage Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5, 12 or 16 GB RAM, 512 GB or 1 TB storage Cameras 200-MP gimbal main, 200-MP telephoto, 50-MP ultrawide, 50-MP selfie camera Battery and Charging 7,060 mAh, 120-watt wired, 50-watt wireless Size and Weight 151.43 x 72.86 x 9.59 mm, 248 grams Colors Silver, Gray Water Resistance IP54

Some of these features extend past content creation. For example, the subject-tracking mode works in video calls, meaning you can set the phone up on a table (Honor includes a case and a magnetic stand) and the camera can follow you around. I also took a group selfie, and instead of taking a normal picture, the gimbal took three photos—left, center, and right—and stitched them like a panorama for a wide shot of everyone. Quick and seamless.

There's a less effective and quite gimmicky integration with Honor's Yoyo virtual AI assistant, where the gimbal camera acts like an enigmatic robot with a pair of eyes on the phone's screen. Ask it to dance to music, and the gimbal camera will move to the beat. It can pretend to be happy or angry, making the appropriate movements to indicate its mood. The camera also serves as the AI's eyes; ask it to describe the scene in front of you, and it'll take a peek.

Tech.title: This Coin-Sized Device Can Hack a Boeing 737
Tech.content:
Even as the digital components of so many life-critical systems have proven susceptible to cybersabotage—cars, medical devices, even water utilities and power grids—the computer systems of airplanes have, thankfully, remained uniquely inaccessible to hackers. But one group of academic researchers has spent years testing a different, devious approach to aviation cybersecurity. Perhaps, they suggest, a plane could be hacked the same way that spies and saboteurs have targeted other high-value, offline computers: by surreptitiously gaining physical access to one and plugging in a device designed to silently run the attackers' malicious code.

Tomorrow at the Usenix Cybersecurity Conference, researchers from the University of California at San Diego and Oberlin College will present a hacking technique capable of commandeering the autopilot of a Boeing 737 to redirect its navigation or silently altering key values in the plane's takeoff and fuel calculations while spoofing the results on the pilot's screen—subtle changes the researchers say could potentially cause anything from runway overruns on takeoff to diversions to a different country's airspace to catastrophic crashes.

To carry out that hacking, they've built a roughly coin-sized, Wi-Fi-enabled prototype device that costs less than $100. In less than a minute, that hardware implant can be fitted into a port accessible via a hatch on the exterior of the plane, one that's routinely within reach of maintenance workers or other airport and airline staff between flights. Once it's in place, the device can send electrical signals on one of the 737's internal networks to spoof commands to sensitive computer systems that guide its autopilot and show the pilot variables like the plane's total weight and outside air temperature, which play a critical role in a 737's takeoff calculations.

Tech.title: How to Select the Office Chair That’s Right For You
Tech.content:
I spent years taking office chairs for granted. But when I began working from home six years ago, I learned quickly that the right office chair is the difference between pain and no pain. I prefer “no pain.” Turns out the human body was not designed to sit in the same position for long hours at a time. An ergonomic office chair can mitigate the strain on your back from long hours of sitting and help you keep good posture.

But what’s the best office chair? The answer is not the same for everyone. (See WIRED’s guide to the Best Office Chairs to examine your options.) The highest-end chairs offer excellent adjustability for a wide range of heights and builds, but almost none will serve everyone—and some styles and builds tend to suit tall or short people better.

Here are the main questions and considerations when finding an office chair, in consultation with Kristianne Egbert, an ergonomist at workplace-injury company Briotix Health with two decades' experience in the field.

How Much Should You Spend on an Office Chair?

Top-end picks like the Herman Miller Aeron ($2,195)—a favorite of many WIRED reviewers over the years for its elegant design, wide-ranging adjustability, and breathable Pellicle mesh—can rival the price of a good mattress or sofa. The price buys beauty and comfort, sure, but also durability (and a 12-year warranty, in Herman Miller’s case).

Top-end ergonomic chairs are designed for people who expect to spend long hours in their chairs and at their desks. If you have the budget, WIRED’s favorite premium chair, the Steelcase Gesture ($1,510), is an investment meant to last for your entire working life—elegant and near-infinitely adjustable to your shape and frame.

Tech.title: Ego 1300 Electric Mower Review: Tame Your Lawn Without Gas
Tech.content:
My old 21-inch gas mower was a Toro that a friend of mine found for free at the side of the road. He gave it to me, I replaced the carburetor, and it fired right up. Score! It ran fine for over a year. And mowing 5 acres with a small gas mower at an hourly rate made my son a relatively wealthy 11-year-old. But then it died again. And again. And at some point, small engine repair isn't fun anymore.

While I was spending weekends cleaning carbs, tracking down air filters, and not mowing, the grass was growing. In northern Wisconsin, grass grows so fast I'm pretty sure you can see it happening if you take the time. A wet June ensured that by the time the Ego arrived for testing, the grass was well out of control, up to 10 inches in the lower, wetter areas of the property.

I figured it would make a good torture test for the Ego, but I'd still need to go in afterward to hack it back with my string trimmer. To my surprise, the Ego 1300 plowed right through almost all of it in a single pass.

For the first pass, I set the height to 4.5 inches, which is easy to do using the height adjustment lever. Unlike an alarming number of mower makers, Ego's height adjustment system is a thing of beauty. The height markings aren't arbitrary letters or symbols that require you to consult a manual to translate to inches. On the Ego, the height adjustment is plainly printed in inches. Imagine that. This lets you know that if you set it to 4.5 inches, your grass will be 4.5 inches high when you're done.

Photograph: Scott Gilbertson

Starting at 4.5 inches and running in Turbo mode allowed the Ego, in a single pass, to cut just about anything I pointed it toward. There is one patch of grass, below an active seeping spring, that was long enough and wet enough that I had to make two passes to get a nice even cut. After that initial mow, I then went back over it a few days later at 3 inches to finally get the height back to what I could call normal. The second mow was, dare I say, incredibly easy. Even the lowest self-propelled speed was generally fast enough for me, though I did crank it up to about the middle to get up the steeper slopes (and then turned it off entirely going downhill).

Tech.title: The Job-Interview Tattoo Guy Everyone Got Mad at Finally Explains Himself
Tech.content:
Jordan Zietz wants to be clear: He has never, and will never, force anyone to tattoo his startup’s logo on their body.

The 24-year-old briefly became the internet’s most hated person after LemonLime, his AI-for-small-business startup, hosted a party following Y Combinator's Startup School in late July. In a LinkedIn post, Zietz wrote that he brought an “actual tattoo artist” to the party and “offered an instant interview to anyone who got a LemonLime tattoo.” Seven people, Zietz wrote, left with ink.

The backlash was quick. Zietz’s LinkedIn posts were flooded with angry comments calling him “disgusting” and “very unfair,” the perpetrator of a “textbook display of predatory corporate behavior, a gross abuse of power, and a profound violation of professional ethics.” A screenshot of his post went viral on X. One representative response read: “The job market cannot be this cooked that kids have to get permanent tattoos to get interviews.”

In an interview with WIRED on Tuesday, Zietz attempted to set the record straight.

He says that, despite what his original post suggested, no one permanently branded themselves with LemonLime’s corporate logo at the party. While there were predesigned tattoos of lemons and limes, attendees could pick any design. (At least one said she got a personal tattoo; she added that she was “not seeking a job.”) According to Zietz, he told everyone at the party that getting a tattoo—citrus-themed or otherwise—was not a job requirement. In fact, he says, any attendee who wanted an interview got one.

“A decent amount of people who got tattoos never wanted to even take us up on any offer to chat” about a job, Zietz says. “They just wanted to get a tattoo for free.”

Three of LemonLime’s five employees received LemonLime-themed flash tattoos, including Zietz and his cofounder, Daniela Muñoz. So did at least one person who didn’t work for the startup, according to Zietz.

On Monday, Zietz got his second tattoo in less than month: the actual LemonLime logo, on his other shoulder. It is one of many. He got his first ever tattoo on a first date, and his thigh tattoos include a dinosaur doodle and text that says “This Is The Correct Knee,” with an X underneath.

“I would never ask anyone to do something I would not do myself,” Zietz says, while emphasizing, again, that he is the only person, to his knowledge, with the actual logo tattooed on his body. He plans to release a glossy video of himself getting the tattoo on social media.

Though Zietz insists the tattoos weren’t a prerequisite for employment at his startup, you’d be forgiven for assuming that was the case, and the language of his LinkedIn post certainly made people think it was. After reading various angry comments and posts, he says he understands why people were uncomfortable with the power dynamic.

Still, part of the reason Zietz hired the tattoo artist was to identify candidates who would be a good cultural fit for LemonLime. Zietz says his original post was “half-and-half” earnest, serving as something of a test for cultural alignment. He didn’t want people to feel obligated to get tattoos. But he did want people to see the tattoo station and think that what LemonLime was doing was “out there.” Then he wanted them to make a judgement call: Did they love it or did they hate it?

If partygoers were turned off by the tattoo station, they probably wouldn’t be a good fit for the startup, he reasons. Sure!

Zietz is trying to hire people who appreciate what he calls his “eccentric” approach to life. When he was a student at Stanford, Zietz was suspended from his role as the university’s mascot, the Tree, after unfurling a banner that said “Stanford Hates Fun” during a football game. Prior to LemonLime, Zietz cofounded a social-media platform called Confetti, and part of the hiring process, Zietz wrote last year on LinkedIn, involved an interview while skydiving.

Tech.title: The Best Action Cameras for All Your Craziest Adventures (2026)
Tech.content:
The B-Roll

About all those cheap cameras on Amazon: Readers often ask, why spend $400 on a GoPro when they can get a camera with 4K video for $100? It's a fair question, and the answer comes down to software, primarily image stabilization. Action cameras are designed to be strapped to helmets or clipped to your chest while you skydive, rock climb, or race through the city on a scooter. Without stabilization, the results are something even your closest friends won't sit through. So yes, you'll get 4K footage with the cheaper cams, but it'll be footage no one wants to see. In our view, you're better off spending another $100 for an older GoPro or DJI Osmo Action on sale.

Best Accessories to Trick Out Your Camera

Photograph: Scott Gilbertson

Once you have an action camera, you're good to go for most use cases. GoPro, Insta360, and DJI all provide helmet mounts and other ways to stick your camera where you want it. But there are some nice extras that can make getting that shot you're dreaming of even easier. Here are a few:

A good microSD card: The action camera you buy may include an SD card. Insta360's SD cards are pretty good, actually, but I tend to use SanDisk's Extreme cards because they're fast and waterproof. You can pick up a 512-GB card for around $110. DJI has some specific recommendations for microSD cards to use with the Action 6. Of their list, the one I recommend is the Lexar Professional Silver Plus 512-GB card ($165). Sadly, like all flash-memory products, a shortage has led to skyrocketing microSD card prices.

GoPro Media Mod ($100): The Hero 13 Black's sound capture is OK out of the box, but if you want higher-quality audio, this is where you start. Not because the Media Mod mic captures great sound—it's better than the camera, but still not great. What it offers is a microphone jack. Plug in a high-quality microphone, and you'll finally have awesome sound. GoPro has listened to users and wisely included this feature out of the box for the Mission 1 Pro, which will have a media mod as well, but not necessary just to connect external audio.

Handlebar/seatpost/pole mount ($40): This is my favorite mount for mountain biking, but it'll also work on ski poles and any other round object you want to clamp it to.

Motorcycle accessory bundle ($60): If you ride, this mount for Insta360 cameras (Ace Pro, X5, etc.) is a must-have. It's one of the most secure clamps I've ever used, almost as good as a bench vise.

Yallsame tripod mount ($12): Action cameras offer many ways to mount them, but one that's curiously missing is the traditional quarter-inch tripod screw mount. The GoPros have them, but this three-pack of adapters solves the problem for the others.

Polarizer and ND filters: If you shoot around water, through glass, or in any other high-glare situation, a polarizing filter will help cut that glare. Neutral density (ND) filters hold back light to let you shoot at a wider aperture in bright light, helping to increase the amount of intentional motion blur. Both are great additions to your action camera kit. Here are the filters by camera:

GoPro Mission 1 ND filters ($100) : These are hot off the press, and I have not tested them yet, but they work the same way the Hero 13 ND filters below do, automatically adjusting the camera settings when they are attached. This is a godsend for most of us since figuring out the best settings to use with an ND filter on is complicated. GoPro has done all the hard work for you.

: These are hot off the press, and I have not tested them yet, but they work the same way the Hero 13 ND filters below do, automatically adjusting the camera settings when they are attached. This is a godsend for most of us since figuring out the best settings to use with an ND filter on is complicated. GoPro has done all the hard work for you. GoPro Hero 13 Black ND filter Four-Pack ($90) : These work like the Mission 1 ND filters above when it comes to automatic adjustment, but I have used these quite a bit. They're great for increasing the motion blur in fast shots on bright, sunny days—especially if there's snow on the ground.

They're great for increasing the motion blur in fast shots on bright, sunny days—especially if there's snow on the ground. DJI ND filter set for the Action 6 ($79) : The Action 6 does not automatically detect and adjust settings, but depending on what you're shooting, there are plenty of guides online to getting good results with these filters.

: The Action 6 does not automatically detect and adjust settings, but depending on what you're shooting, there are plenty of guides online to getting good results with these filters. Insta360 Ace Pro 2 ND Filters ($122) : These strangely expensive filters work well with the Ace Pro 2.

: These strangely expensive filters work well with the Ace Pro 2. Third-party ND filters: These are very hit-or-miss. Beware of slip-on filters as they often cause internal reflections. Others I've tried have had some pretty bad vignetting. For older GoPros, I like Freewell's polarizing and ND filters ($20). I suggest starting with an 8-stop ND or combo ND and polarizing filter.

Floaty ($35): Another one for the water shooters, but well worth the money since it'll keep your GoPro from ending up at the bottom of the sea. I haven't tried it, but there's one for the Insta360 Ace Pro 2 ($26) as well. DJI doesn't make an official case for the Action 6, but there is a floating grip ($59).

Selfie stick ($25): Surprisingly for someone who hates being on camera, I've tested a lot of selfie sticks, and they're almost all fine, but I keep grabbing this Insta360 version when I head out the door. It's lightweight, small enough to fit at the bottom of my bag, and it's affordable. If you want to go big, this Insta360 Extended Edition Selfie Stick ($100) can imitate a low-flying drone, perfect for use in national parks and other places where drones are forbidden.

Tech.title: Exclusive: New Crunchyroll Collab Brings Anime Streaming to Cars
Tech.content:
Nothing like kicking back in your car to stream Daemons of the Shadow Realm, right? But instead of watching on your phone, the in-car entertainment system lets you catch the latest episodes on your BMW’s dash. Crunchyroll and automotive app store Appning are partnering to bring the streamer’s catalog to a selection of vehicles, starting with BMW and Mini and eventually expanding to more than 40 auto brands. The companies announced the team-up on Wednesday, sharing that the anime app will soon arrive in cars.

Appning, Forvia’s app store, is an in-car platform where customers can access built-in apps for YouTube, Zoom, Spotify and more. The addition of Crunchyroll’s streaming service will make anime available to drivers around the world, including North America, Europe, Asia, Latin America and Australia. While Appning is the hub behind the experience, TiVo’s tech is surfacing titles and personalized recommendations for Crunchyroll subscribers tapping in while chilling in their cars.

Also see: Crunchyroll and Starz Bundle Up on Prime Video

Using safety-first features, the venture will allow anime fans to watch more than 50,000 episodes of TV shows and movies, plus 25,000 hours of content when the vehicle is parked. So, no streaming while driving, OK? Video playback will be blocked if you attempt to watch while the car is moving.

“Today’s consumers expect their entertainment to be available wherever they are, including in their vehicle, said Brian McGarvey, Crunchyroll’s SVP of global distribution and business development. “With Crunchyroll coming soon to global automotive partners, the anime experience will be even more accessible on every journey. Through this collaboration with Appning, we’re glad to provide another way for this passionate, global fan community to enjoy their favorite anime.”

You will still need a paid Crunchyroll subscription to watch favorites like Demon Slayer, Solo Leveling or Gachiakuta, and plans start at $10 per month in the US. Appning, which is available in car brands such as Mercedes-Benz, Lotus and Volkswagen, is an Android-powered system that carries more than 300 apps.

Tech.title: Honor Has Radically Reinvented the Phone for the Robot Age. I Played With It, and It’s Wild
Tech.content:
When Chinese phone brand Honor first teased the concept of its Robot Phone last year, I thought it sounded too outlandish to be real and too good to be true. The device it was proposing occupied the center point in the Venn diagram of my interests in robotics and unconventional phone design.

Even when I saw a mockup of the phone with its pop-out camera gimbal at CES in January, and then an early working demo at MWC in February, I was skeptical that it would actually go on sale. In my decade-plus as a tech journalist, I’ve seen plenty of bright and interesting concepts fall at the last hurdle. I’m always the first to advocate for less boring tech, so I hoped the Robot Phone wouldn’t be one of them.

On Wednesday, in the Chinese city of Guangzhou, I was thrilled that Honor proved me wrong once and for all. At the Robot Phone’s launch event, I got to play with the final version of the phone, which will go on sale in China imminently, priced at 9,999 yuan ($1,483) for the version with 12GB of RAM and 12,999 yuan ($1,923) for the 16GB version.

In the age of AI, not every phone should be just “another black slab,” said Honor CEO James Li at the company’s launch event. Given Honor’s growing expertise in the world of robotics (it has also built a humanoid robot), it wanted to find a way to fuse its innovation in the fast-expanding field of embodied AI with its phones.

From the front, you might not notice anything immediately unusual about the Robot Phone. Available in silver and grey and sporting a 6.3-inch OLED screen, it could just be another Android device. Flip it over, and that’s where the fun begins.

Unlike other phones with a camera bump on the back, the protruding module on the Robot Phone slides open to reveal a camera system on a three-axis gimbal that swings out on a robotic arm. It’s a radical departure from any phone I’ve been allowed to handle before, and it packs the kind of tech that realistically requires more than just a few hours of experimentation to truly master. Still, I was determined to give it a go.

The Robot Phone in action

Ahead of the event, I used the phone’s in-built Yoyo AI voice assistant to order a boba tea from a nearby shop to my hotel in Shenzhen. All I needed to do was tell Yoyo what I wanted, and it went into the app, placed my order and paid for me. Less than 20 minutes later, I was happily chugging my boba while still playing with the phone.

Powered by Qualcomm’s top-of-the-line Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 chip, the Robot Phone should be highly capable of handling AI requests you throw at it. But it’s also great to see Honor harness the chip’s power to bring physical AI features to a phone — something no other phone-maker has yet attempted.

The obvious standout feature of the Robot Phone is the robotic arm that swings out from the rear to bring up the camera. You can activate it two ways – either manually from within the camera app, or using gestures, which I tried out at MWC. If you choose the latter, the Yoyo app will open automatically, immediately turning your phone into your robotic personal assistant.

Katie Collins/CNET

In this mode, it has around 10 gestures it can perform to express itself to you — including nodding, shaking its “head” (the camera), curious peeking and dancing in sync with a musical beat. This is complemented by over 100 emoji options that can appear on the screen simultaneously.

When you switch apps with the gimbal open, a pop-up gives you the option to close it, which I especially liked. I could easily imagine myself leaving it open in a moment of forgetfulness after using it, and I’d want to minimize the potential damage.

That said, the gimbal is made of tough stuff. Honor has used an all-titanium gimbal, into which it’s packed over 100 micro-precision components. It’s powered by a titanium alloy gimbal motor and a steel flip motor. Still, probably best not drop it.

To show quite how powerful and versatile the Robot Phone truly is, Honor has partnered with Chinese robotics company Seeed Studio, which has built various robot bodies that the phone can sit inside. The phone acts as the “brain” of the robots — one with wheels and arms, one bipedal bot — and allows people to interact with them using AI or a controller. The robot kit with wheels is available as open-source hardware for people to download. This means that if you buy a Robot Phone and have access to a maker space or kit, you can transform it into a robot that can actually move.

A cinematographer’s dream phone

The most obvious reason someone might be interested in buying the Robot Phone is that it packs handheld camera technology popular among creators, such as the DJI Osmo Pocket series and its rivals, into the body of a phone. This means carrying one device where once you might have had two, and being able to immediately edit and upload your footage without having to transfer files.

The phone features three cameras: one 200-megapixel main camera, one 200-megapixel telephoto camera and one 50-megapixel ultrawide camera. Co-developed with Hollywood cinematography darling ARRI, the main camera sits atop the swing-out module. When I used it in vertical mode, I was disappointed that the camera cropped in rather than flipped, which caused a drop in resolution from its standard 4K.

ARRI cinema mode is available from within the camera app. Katie Collins?CNET

The three smart tracking modes allow you to choose between gimbal tracking, smart tracking and pre-composition framing. The phone also has six dynamic camera modes, including AI SpinShot, default stabilization, tilt locked, super steady, FP and FPV vertical. I played with the AI SpinShot feature, which allows you to spin the gimbal either 90 or 180 degrees with the touch of a button while recording, creating some very cool shots.

Honor’s partnership with ARRI is a shrewd move in establishing the Robot Phone as a serious filmmaking device. The gold standard of cinematography equipment, ARRI footage is often used as a benchmark for quality in video circles, and its cameras are the go-to for big-budget Hollywood productions.

Quality isn’t something I’m able to judge for myself at this stage, but when you enter cinematic mode within the camera app, the sheer number of manual controls is no joke. This might take some getting to grips with for those of us who aren’t pro cinematographers, but it’s great to have the opportunity to learn for enthusiastic amateurs. The inclusion of ARRI cinematic filters will also allow you to apply a range of classy filmic looks to your footage.

A bold, radical reinvention of the smartphone

In my early hands-on time with the Robot Phone, I was impressed with its features and versatility, but more so by Honor’s boldness. It’s the closest thing I can think of in the phone world to the avant-garde.

Cutting-edge design for every other phone-maker right now means foldables — and Honor is doing that too. Its Magic V6 might be the most stunning foldable I’ve had the pleasure of holding in my hands. But the company isn’t content to simply compete on the same playing field as all of its competitors.

With the Robot Phone, it’s blazing a new trail and going where no other phone-maker has dared. Is it a wise move to rip up the rulebook that dictates the parameters of conventional hardware design? It’s obviously a big risk, but it shows daring on Honor’s part.

There’s nothing quite like this in the phone world. Katie Collins/CNET

“They are showing the art of the possible with a highly differentiated product, which will get a lot of attention amongst technology enthusiasts,” said Ben Wood, chief analyst at CCS Insight. The Robot Phone “represents the ambition that Honor has,” he added. “This is not unique for Honor because let’s bear in mind that they were the pioneers when it came to the thin foldables.”

The Robot Phone will be a China-only product for now, and the country makes an ideal testbed. DJI’s products fly off the shelves here, and the nation is deeply familiar with Honor as a brand.

Many Chinese phone brands struggle to distinguish themselves from one another — especially in the international market — and building a robot arm into a phone is certainly one way to cement your reputation as a pioneer.

“You’re going to see lots more of this from Honor in terms of them trying to push the envelope to relentlessly try and build the brand in the face of immense dominant competition,” said Wood.

Editors’ note: Katie Collins’ travel costs for the Honor event were covered by Honor. The judgments and opinions of CNET are our own.
